# Preface

Thus far speaks the one—honored reader, according to your status and dignity—who gave birth to this child and let it travel out into the world with a **French mouth** <note>A metaphor for the original author, Nicolas Lemery, and the original French language of the text.</note>: But one will not take it amiss if he who has also taught it to **speak German** <note>The translator referring to himself and his work in translating the text.</note> adds a few small things. I do not wish to make a great fuss in order to recommend this book to the reader’s favor based on all its perfections. 

For, to begin with, its author **Mr. Lemery** has already been known throughout the learned world for over twenty years as an exceedingly perfect **chemist** and **physicist**: Thus he already has a favorable **presumption** <note>original: "Præsumption". In this context, it refers to a "preconceived positive reputation" or the benefit of the doubt earned through past merit.</note> in his favor, suggesting that with this book he has brought no imperfect fruit or misshapen monstrosity into the world; especially since he presided over the **laboratory** of a King as curious as he was glorious <note>A reference to King Louis XIV of France, known for his patronage of the sciences.</note> for such a long time, to the King’s great pleasure and the good **satisfaction** of the **curious** <term>the curious: From the German *Curiosen*, referring to the "virtuosi" of the 17th century—intellectuals and collectors who were dedicated to investigating new scientific phenomena.</term> in **France**. Secondly, the book has already so well legitimized itself by its own merits that in France itself, just last year, for the ninth [time]...

# Preface

Germans, wishing to serve them therewith, we have endeavored as much as possible to please German eyes and ears, and have adopted such a measure that we either retained the **technical terms** <term>technical terms: the original *Kunst-Wörter* refers to the specialized vocabulary used within a specific craft or science.</term> with their **Latin** sound—where they have already been, so to speak, **naturalized** <note>original: *naturalisiret*, referring to foreign words that have been adopted into common German usage.</note> among us—or expressed them with an understandable **German** name, or even presented both forms together. Should this seem somewhat strange to anyone, let him not laugh at it, lest he otherwise laugh at himself for not having better pursued and practiced his **mother tongue**; or should another complain of **obscurity** here and there, he must assign the blame neither to the **translator** nor to the first **author** <note>original: *Uhr-heber*.</note> of the book, but rather to the profound and thorough presentation of the most **intricate** matters, or perhaps even to his own **prejudices** and his own head, for not having cleared its contents better.

For indeed, nothing is more difficult than to present, or even to understand, the **physical** and **medical disciplines** in the **German language**, because hitherto people have been so negligent in characterizing the words and giving them a certain meaning

This testimony, where a profoundly learned Frenchman speaks on behalf of the Germans against his own countrymen, certainly belongs among the **defenses of the German name** <note>original: *Vindiciis nominis Germanici*</note>. In this work, Mr. Cramer—the highly-appointed Counselor to His Electoral Serenity of Brandenburg—defends and maintains with commendable zeal and a gallant manner the merits of the Germans in the advancement of the arts and sciences against certain Pharisaical <note>In this context, "Pharisaical" implies an air of intellectual or moral superiority.</note> Frenchmen who would rather reduce them to mere zeros in the **Republic of Letters** <term>Republic of Letters: the international community of scholars and intellectuals during the 17th and 18th centuries who shared knowledge across borders.</term>.

In general, however, all readers will find something here that will partly instruct them, partly provoke reflection, and partly entertain them. For the learned, the new and tangible explanation of **chemical principles** in the introduction will provide occasion for many fine thoughts. If gardeners and **heads of households** <note>original: *Haußväter*; referring to the 18th-century "housefather" who managed a self-sufficient estate</note> study the second part regarding plants with mature reflection and thoughtful patience, they will learn from it—or at least find the opportunity—how to produce new species of plants or improve common ones. This is achieved by assisting nature in their cultivation with various additives that either increase the **spirit** <note>original: *Spiritum*; in alchemy, the volatile essence or "mercury" of a substance</note>, the **salt**, or the **oil** <note>These three—Spirit, Salt, and Oil—represent the *Tria Prima* or three primary chemical principles of the era.</note>, or change their composition and mixture.

The final part can help every person to better know their own body and learn to treat it more carefully when they see what can be prepared from the parts of animal bodies and their **waste products** <note>original: *Excrementen*; in this context, biological discharges like urine or bone used to create chemical medicines or phosphorus</note>, which were already present within the body’s substance and roots. ## Highly and Well-Born,
## Highly Commanding Gracious Lords,

I serve the world as best I can, because I cannot yet serve as I wish. Indeed, I would have gladly consecrated the first bloom of my years to the service of God in His church, as they appeared mature enough for such a task in the eyes and ears of my teachers and patrons, and even the local, Highly Reverend Ministry of the Holy Cross <note>original: *Creuz-Ministerii*; the clerical body associated with the Kreuzkirche in Dresden, responsible for ecclesiastical affairs</note>. 

However, Divine Wisdom <note>original: *Göttl. Weißheit*</note> has seen fit otherwise, and has not yet chosen to accept them—just as the firstfruits of the year were accepted as an offering in His temple in the Old Testament—up to this date. 

In the meantime, I shall not be acting wrongly if I come forward with a secondary work <note>original: *Nebenwercke*; a project or publication produced alongside one's primary professional calling</note> that specifically concerns itself with the well-being of the human body <note>original: *Wohlstand des Menschlichen Leibes*</note>: since God has not yet deemed me worthy...

# Appendix.

## The Powers and Virtues of the Medicines which are Described in this Book.

Many people have requested such a list,
and I myself believed it would
have its uses; therefore, I
should not withhold it from the reader.
However, I must still mention this
to everyone: although one finds the
dosages <note>original: "Dosin," the plural of *Dosis*</note> for the medicines provided here,
they cannot be used without careful caution:
For because temperaments <note>The four "humors" or constitutional types (sanguine, choleric, melancholic, and phlegmatic) which 17th-century medicine believed dictated how a person reacted to treatment.</note> are
differently distinguished in countless ways, it is
impossible to bring everything under general rules.
A remedy can succeed very well
with one patient, and yet disagree
with another: To one, a person must
give much; to another, less:
Some sick persons must first
be prepared <note>original: "præpariren"; in early modern medicine, this often involved balancing the body's fluids through diet or mild purgatives before a stronger medicine could be safely administered.</note> when they are to
take certain medicines, while for
others, conversely, no preparation is needed:
For some, this time is suitable; for
another, that time. Thus, it depends
on the understanding of the physician,
that he carefully considers all circumstances
and prescribes the remedies at the right time.
In this, one must at every moment

account for the way in which Nature exerts her power to rid herself of her burden, and to come to her aid: <note>original Latin: "qvo natura vergit eo ducere oportet" – *whither nature tends, thither one ought to lead.* This is a fundamental principle of Hippocratic medicine, suggesting that a doctor should observe which way the body is naturally trying to expel "bad humors" and assist that specific process.</note> This is precisely the main point that one must watch for, and without which one can hardly find a successful outcome.

## Vomitives and Emetic Medicines.
<note>Emetics are substances used to induce vomiting, a practice central to early modern medicine for "purging" the stomach of excess or corrupted fluids (humors).</note>

Mineral Turbith. The dosage is 2 to 6 grains. <note>A "grain" (Gran) was the smallest unit of pharmaceutical weight, roughly 65 milligrams.</note>
Ordinary Regulus of Antimony <term>Regulus: the metallic form of a mineral, in this case antimony, which was a favorite chemical remedy of the era.</term> and Martial Regulus. <note>Martial Regulus is an alloy of antimony and iron (associated with the planet Mars).</note> The dosage is 4 to 8 grains.
Antimonial Sulfur of Gold. <note>original: "Antimonialischer Gold-Schwefel," a reddish-orange powder made from antimony and sulfur, often used to induce sweating or vomiting.</note> The dosage is 2 to 6 grains.
Glass of Antimony. <note>original: "Vitrum Antimonii," a translucent, glass-like substance produced by melting antimony ore; it was a potent emetic.</note> The dosage is 2 to 6 grains.
Liver of Antimony or Saffron of Metals. <note>original: "Leber Antimonii" or "Crocus Metallorum," a brownish-yellow chemical compound used as a strong purge.</note> The dosage is 4 to 8 grains.
Emetic Wine, or Vomiting Wine. <note>original: "Vinum emeticum," usually wine in which antimony had been steeped, allowing the wine to absorb the mineral's emetic properties.</note> The dosage is half to 3 ounces.
Flowers of Antimony. <note>original: "Flores Antimonii," the white sublimate (vapor that turned back to solid) formed when heating antimony.</note> The dosage is 2 to 6 grains.
Algaroth Powder. <note>A white powder of antimony chloride, named after the Italian physician Vittorio Algarotti.</note> The dosage is 2 to 6 grains.
Gilla Vitrioli. <note>An old term for white vitriol (zinc sulfate), which acted as a rapid emetic.</note> The dosage is 10 grains to one drachm. <note>A "drachm" (or dram) was equivalent to 60 grains.</note>
Salt of Vitriol. The dosage is 10 to 30 grains.
Tartar Emetic. <note>original: "Tartarus emeticus," a compound of antimony and potassium tartrate that remained a standard emetic well into the 19th century.</note> The dosage is 3 to 10 grains.
Soluble Tartar Emetic. The dosage is 4 to 15 grains.
Spirit of Tobacco. <note>A distilled extract of tobacco. Though highly toxic, it was used in small doses to trigger immediate vomiting.</note> The dosage is 2 to 6 drachms.

## For the Stilling of Vomiting.
<note>In early modern medicine, after a patient had been "purged" or if they were suffering from excessive vomiting, "astringent" or "binding" medicines were used to settle the stomach.</note>

Fulminating Gold. <note>original Latin: *Aurum fulminans*. This was a volatile gold compound. In tiny doses, it was believed to have calming or "refrigerating" effects on the spirits.</note> The dosage is 2 to 6 grains.
Astringent Extract of Iron <note>original Latin: *Extractum Martis adstringens*. Iron was known as "Mars" in the chemical tradition.</note> or binding iron extract. The dosage is 10 grains to 2 scruples. <term>Scruple: an apothecary weight equal to 20 grains.</term>
Diaphoretic Iron. <note>original Latin: *Mars Diaphoreticus*. A "diaphoretic" is a substance that induces sweating, believed to release toxins through the skin.</note> The dosage rises from 10 up to 20 grains.
Diaphoretic Antimony. <note>original Latin: *Antimonium Diaphoreticum*. A white powder made by reacting antimony with saltpeter.</note> The dosage goes from 6 up to 30 grains.
Mineral Bezoar. <note>original Latin: *Bezoardicum Minerale*. This was not a real bezoar (a stone from an animal's stomach) but a chemical preparation of antimony intended to mimic the stone’s supposed life-saving properties.</note> The dosage goes from 4 up to 16 grains.
Prepared Corals. <note>Ground and purified coral was used as an antacid to settle the stomach.</note> The dosage is 10 grains up to one drachm. <term>Drachm (or Dram): an apothecary weight equal to 60 grains.</term>
Salt of many virtues from Rochelle. <note>original: *Sal polychrestum Rupellanum*. Known today as Rochelle salt (sodium potassium tartrate), it was a famous mild laxative and digestive aid discovered in the mid-17th century.</note> The dosage permits 1 to 6 drachms.
Amber. <note>original German: *Agtstein*, an archaic term for amber.</note> The dosage goes from 10 grains up to half a drachm.
Essence of Ambergris. <note>original: *Ambra-Essentz*. Ambergris is a rare substance from the digestive system of sperm whales, highly prized as a restorative.</note> The dosage is 2 to 12 drops.
Essence of Cloves. The dosage is one to 3 drops.
Essence of Cinnamon. The dosage is 1 drop.
Oil of Nutmeg; this is to be smeared upon the stomach.
Cream of Tartar. <note>original Latin: *Cremor tartari*. A sediment from winemaking used to treat various stomach ailments.</note> Half to 3 drachms of it are administered.

## Purgatives for the Lower Body.
<note>This section lists laxatives intended to "purge" the bowels of "corrupt humors."</note>

Silver Crystals <note>original: *Silber-Chrystallen*. Likely silver nitrate, though highly caustic, it was used in minute, diluted doses in early chemistry.</note> / the dose is 2 to 6 grains.
Sweet Sublimate <note>original: *Sublimatum dulce*. Also known as Calomel (mercury chloride), a very common but toxic purgative used for centuries.</note>, the dose is 6 to 30 grains.
A perpetual pill <note>original: *pilula perpetua*. A pill made of metallic antimony that was intended to pass through the body entirely. It could then be retrieved from the stool, washed, and reused indefinitely.</note>, eternal pill.
Salt of Many Virtues <note>original: *Sal polychrestum*. Usually potassium sulfate, valued for its many ("poly") medical uses ("chrestum").</note>, the dose is 1 to 6 drachms.
Vitriolated Tartar <note>original: *Vitriolierter Tartarus*. Potassium sulfate produced by reacting oil of vitriol (sulfuric acid) with salt of tartar.</note>, the dose is 8 to 30 grains.
Crystals of Tartar <note>original: *Tartar-Chrystall*. Purified potassium bitartrate, derived from the sediment left in wine barrels.</note> / the dose is half a drachm to 3 drachms.
Soluble Tartar <note>original: *Tartarus solubilis*. Potassium tartrate, a common mild laxative.</note>, the dose is one scruple to one drachm. <term>Scruple: an apothecary weight equal to 20 grains.</term>
Jalap <note>original: *Jalappa*. A powerful purgative derived from the root of a Mexican climbing plant.</note> / the dose is 10 grains up to one drachm.

## vapor of mercury.
<note>Treating syphilis with mercury often led to mercury poisoning. Early doctors believed that heavy salivation (ptyalism) was a sign the "venereal poison" was leaving the body, but it often became a dangerous condition itself, leading to lost teeth and internal damage.</note>

Powdered or **gold leaf** <note>original: *Bläthgen-Gold*. In early chemistry, gold was considered the "king of metals" and the spiritual opposite of mercury; it was believed gold could "soak up" and neutralize mercury inside the body.</note>, the **dose** is 6 to 30 **grains**.

**Fulminating gold** or **crackling gold** <note>original: *Aurum fulminans* or *Prassel-Gold*. An unstable gold compound that could explode if heated; medically, it was used as a sedative or to promote sweating.</note>, the **dose** is 2 to 6 **grains**.

**Poterius’s stomach remedy** <note>original: *Stomachicum Poterii*. A chemical preparation of gold and antimony named after the 17th-century French physician Pierre Potier.</note>, the **dose** is 6 to 30 **grains**.

## For the flow of seed.
<note>original: *Vor den Saamen-Fluß*. A historical term for gonorrhea or any involuntary discharge from the reproductive organs.</note>

**Turpentine** <note>original: *Terpentin*. A resin from pine trees used as a diuretic and to treat infections of the urinary and reproductive tracts.</note>, the **dose** is 20 **grains** to 1 **drachm**,

**Spirit of turpentine** <note>original: *Terpentin-Spiritus*. A distilled oil from pine resin used to treat urinary tract issues and "cleansing" the body.</note>, the **dose** is 4 to 12 **drops**.
**Rose-colored mercury precipitate** <note>original: *Rosenfarbigtes Præcipitat Mercurii*. Also known as red precipitate or mercuric oxide; it was a potent chemical used both externally and occasionally internally for syphilis.</note>, the **dose** is 4 to 20 **grains** <note>A grain is a small unit of weight, roughly 65 milligrams.</note>.
**Green mercury precipitate** <note>original: *Grünes præcipitat Mercurii*. A mercury compound often containing copper, used for its caustic and "purifying" properties.</note>, the **dose** is 2 to 6 **grains**.
**Mercurial panacea** <note>original: *Panacea Mercurialis*. Literally a "mercurial cure-all," this was usually a highly refined form of calomel intended to be safer for the patient.</note>, the **dose** is 6 **grains** to 2 **scruples** <note>A scruple is about 1.3 grams.</note>.
**Sweet sublimate** <note>original: *Sublimatum dulce*. Another name for calomel (mercurous chloride), used as a milder alternative to more toxic mercury salts.</note>, the **dose** is 6 to 30 **grains**.
**Mineral crystal** <note>original: *Mineralischer Chrystall*. Likely *Sal Prunellæ*, a purified saltpeter (potassium nitrate) used to cool the blood and treat fevers.</note>, the **dose** is 20 to 30 **grains**.

## How to stop the flow of seed.
<note>original: *Saamen-Fluß*. This term refers to involuntary seminal discharge or gonorrhea (then called "the clap").</note>

**Antihectic of Poterius** <note>original: *Antihecticum poterii*. A famous 17th-century chemical remedy made from tin and antimony, used for wasting diseases and chronic discharges.</note>, the **dose** is 10 **grains** to 2 **scruples**.
**Medicinal stone** <note>original: *Lapis medicinalis*. A fused mineral compound, often containing alum and vitriol, used for its drying and astringent effects.</note> dropped into a drink; this is done with one **drachm** <note>A drachm is roughly 3.9 grams.</note> put into 8 **ounces** of **smithy water** <note>original: *Schmiede-Wasser*. **Prepared coral** <note>original: *Præparirte Corallen*. Ground red coral, used as an antacid and to stop "fluxes" or discharges.</note>, the **dose** is 10 **grains** to 1 **drachm**.

**Astringent saffron of Mars** <note>original: *Crocus Martis adstringens*. An iron oxide powder; "Mars" was the alchemical name for iron, used here to stop bleeding or fluid loss.</note>, the **dose** is 10 **grains** to 1 **drachm**.
**Astringent extract of Mars** <note>original: *Extractum Martis adstringens*. A liquid or resinous concentrate of iron.</note>, the **dose** is 2 **scruples** to 1 **drachm**.
**Laudanum** <note>original: *Laudanum*. An opium preparation used to suppress pain and bodily functions.</note>, the **dose** is half a **grain** to 2 **grains**.

## Venereal mouth-sores / Fig-warts and genital pustules.
<note>original: *Venerische Maul-Drüsen / Feig- Warzen und Gemächts- Blattern*. This section deals with the visible symptoms of syphilis and other sexually transmitted infections. "Fig-warts" refers to what we now call genital warts.</note>

**Red precipitate** <note>original: *Præcipitatum rubrum*. Mercuric oxide, a heavy red powder used to cauterize or "eat away" diseased flesh.</note>.
**Burnt alum** <note>original: *Gebrannter Alaun*. Alum that has been heated to remove water, making it a powerful astringent used to dry up sores.</note>.
**Infernal stone** <note>original: *Lapis infernalis*. Silver nitrate, a caustic chemical used to cauterize wounds or warts.</note>.
**Green precipitate of mercury** <note>original: *Præcipitatum viride Mercurii*.</note>.
**Mercurial panacea** <note>original: *Panacea Mercurialis*. A "universal" mercury-based remedy, typically a highly purified form of calomel.</note>.
**Caustic stone** <note>original: *Lapis causticus*. Potassium hydroxide or a similar strong alkali.</note>, and the kind used for **fontanelles** <note>original: *Fontanellen*. In historical medicine, these were "issues"—deliberate, surgically created wounds kept open to allow "corrupt humors" to drain from the body.</note>.
**Oil of Mercury** <note>original: *Oleum Mercurii*.</note>, placed upon the injury.
**Sweet sublimate** <note>original: *Sublimatum dulce*. Also known as calomel; a milder form of mercury used internally.</note>, the **dose** is 6 to 30 **grains**.
**Decoction of antimony** <note>original: *Decoctum antimonii*.</note>, **guaiacum** <note>original: *gayaci*. A resin from the "holy wood" tree of the Americas, famously used as a treatment for syphilis.</note>.
**Purgatives** <note>original: *Purgantzen*. Medicines used to induce bowel movements to "cleanse" the system.</note>.

## Aperients and opening remedies for dropsy and for milk-blockage.
<note>original: *Aperientia und eröffnende Mittel vor die Wassersucht und vor Milch- Verstopffung*. "Aperients" are remedies meant to "open" the body's channels or pores. "Dropsy" is an old term for edema (fluid retention). "Milk-blockage" refers to issues with lactation or breast engorgement.</note>

**Silver crystals** <note>original: *Silber-Chrystallen*. Likely silver nitrate crystals, though here given in a very specific internal dose.</note>, the **dose** is 2 to 6 **grains**.
**Opening Crocus of Mars** <note>original: *Crocus Martis aperiens*. A name for various iron oxides (Mars being the alchemical symbol for iron). It was used to treat anemia and "open" the flow of blood or other fluids.</note>, the **dose** is 10 **grains** to 2 **scruples** <note>A scruple is an apothecaries' weight equal to 20 grains, or about 1.3 grams.</note>.

**Acid Spirit of Sal Ammoniac**, the **dose** is 4 to 8 **drops**.
**Mercurial Panacea** <note>original: *Panacea Mercurialis*. A "universal" remedy made from mercury, processed to be less caustic than other mercurial salts.</note>, the **dose** is 6 **grains** to 2 **scruples**.
**Nut-Salt** <note>original: *Nuß-Saltz*. Likely a salt prepared from walnut shells or other botanical nuts, used for its specific chemical properties.</note>, the **dose** is 6 **grains** to 1 **scruple**.

**Volatile Salt of Amber** <note>original: *Sal volatile succini*. Succinic acid, obtained by distilling amber; it was highly regarded for treating nervous disorders and "hysteria."</note>, the **dose** is 4 to 16 **grains**.
**Jalap** <note>original: *Jalappa*. A powerful purgative root from Mexico (*Ipomoea jalapa*).</note>, the **dose** is 10 **grains** to 1 **drachm**.

**Spirit of Sugar** <note>original: *Spiritus sacchari*. A distillate of fermented sugar or molasses.</note>, the **dose** is 4 to 10 **drops**.

## For Hypochondriacal Melancholy.

# For the Quartan Fever.
<note>Quartan fever is a form of malaria characterized by paroxysms that occur every fourth day (every 72 hours).</note>

*Diaphoretic Iron* <note>original: *Mars diaphoreticus*. In alchemy, "Mars" represents iron. A diaphoretic is a substance used to induce sweating.</note>, the dose is 10 to 20 **grains** <note>A grain (Gran) was approximately 65 milligrams.</note>.
*Salt of Iron* <note>original: *Sal Martis*. Usually refers to iron sulfate, used to treat "impure" blood or anemia.</note>, the dose is 4 to 12 **grains**.
*Tincture of Iron* <note>original: *Tinctura Martis*. An alcoholic extract of iron.</note>, the dose is 1 **drachm** <note>A drachm (Drachma) was approximately 3.9 grams.</note> to half an **ounce** <note>An ounce (Unze) was approximately 30 grams.</note>.
*Extract of Iron* <note>original: *Extractum Martis*.</note>, the dose is 10 **grains** to 2 **scruples** <note>A scruple (Scrupel) was approximately 1.3 grams.</note>.
*Sweet Sublimate* <note>original: *Sublimatum dulce*. Another name for Calomel (mercurous chloride), a common though toxic purgative.</note>, the dose is 6 to 30 **grains**.
*Antimonial Gold-Sulphur* <note>original: *Antimonialischer Gold-Schwefel*. Antimony pentasulfide, used as a powerful emetic or to induce sweating.</note>, the dose is 2 to 6 **grains**.
*Glass of Antimony* <note>original: *Vitrum antimonii*. A transparent brownish glass made by roasting antimony, used as a very strong emetic.</note>, the dose is 2 to 6 **grains**.
*Emetic Syrup* <note>original: *Brech-Syrup*.</note>, the dose is 2 **drachms** to one and a half **ounces**.
*Saffron of Metals* <note>original: *Crocus Metallorum*. A liver-colored preparation of antimony used as a powerful emetic.</note>, the dose is 2 to 8 **grains**.
*Emetic Wine* <note>original: *Vinum emeticum*. Also known as Antimonial Wine, made by letting wine sit in a vessel made of antimony.</note>, the dose is half to 3 **ounces**.
*Gilla of Vitriol* <note>original: *Gilla vitrioli*. Purified white vitriol (zinc sulfate), used to clear the stomach.</note>, the dose is 20 **grains** to one **drachm**.
*Soluble Emetic Tartar* <note>original: *Tartarus emeticus solubilis*. Antimony potassium tartrate, a standard emetic in early modern medicine.</note>, the dose is 4 to 20 **grains**.
*Cornachini’s Powder* <note>original: *Cornachinisches Pulver*. A famous multi-ingredient purgative powder named after the physician Marco Cornacchini; it typically contained scammony, tartar, and antimony.</note>, the dose is 20 to 45 **grains**.
*Flowers of Antimony* <note>original: *Flores antimonii*. A white powder (antimony trioxide) produced by sublimation.</note>, the dose is 2 to 6 **grains**.
*Powder of Algaroth* <note>original: *Algarothisches Pulver*. Named after Vittorio Algarotti; a violent emetic made from antimony chloride.</note>, the dose is 2 to 6 **grains**.
*Nut Water* <note>original: *Nuß-Wasser*. Likely distilled from green walnuts.</note>, the dose is 1 to 7 **ounces**.
*Nut Extract* <note>original: *Nuß-Extract*.</note>, the dose is 1 **scruple** to one **drachm**.
*Saltpeter fixed with coals* <note>original: *Mit Kohlen fixirter Salpeter*. Potassium carbonate, created by reacting saltpeter (potassium nitrate) with charcoal.</note>, the dose is 16 to 30 **grains**.
*Flowers of Sal-ammoniac* <note>original: *Flores Salis armoniaci*. Ammonium chloride prepared by sublimation.</note>, the dose is 6 to 20 **grains**.

--- Page 93 ---
<meta>This page marks a significant transition in the manuscript. While the previous page concluded a practical apothecary's list of dosages for ailments like the hiccups, this page begins a formal theoretical treatise titled "Cursus Chymicus." It shifts from the "what" of pharmacy to the "how" and "why" of chemistry as a foundational science.</meta>

# CHEMICAL COURSE,
->Or:<-
## A Proper Discourse on CHEMISTRY,
->And specifically its<-
## I. Necessary Introduction or Preparation.

---

### Chapter I.
### On Chemistry in General.

->§ 1.<-

The name Chemistry comes either from the Greek word for "juice" <note>original: χυμὸς (chymos); referring to the extracts or essences of plants</note> or from the Greek verb "to pour" <note>original: χέειν (cheein); referring to the melting and casting of metals</note>. # Chapter 3.
## Observations on the *Active Principles* and the Working Fundamental Parts.

### §. I.

The name **Principle** <note>original: *Principium*</note> must not be taken in a strictly exact or entirely accurate sense: For the substances that are so named are only **principles** in relation to ourselves, as we are unable to carry the division of **bodies** <note>original: *Cörper*; physical matter or substances</note> any further. One admits readily, however, that these principles could still be decomposed into infinitely many parts, which could more rightfully be titled **principles** in the first place. Thus, by **chemical principles** <note>original: *principiis Chymicis*</note>, one understands nothing other than substances separated and divided as far as our weak abilities allow. And just as **chemistry** <note>original: *Chymia*</note> is a <term>demonstrative science</term> <note>original: *scientia demonstrativa*; a field of study where conclusions are reached through visible experiments and empirical proof</note> (since everything depends on obvious **evidence** <note>original: *Beweißthümer*</note>), so too can it [know] nothing

§. 2. The beautiful imaginings that other philosophers <note>original: *Welt-Weisen*; literally "world-wise ones," a common term for natural philosophers or scientists</note> conceive regarding their physical principles <note>original: *Principia physica*</note> certainly puff up the mind with grand ideas; but they provide no demonstrations <note>original: *demonstrationes*</note> with which they can prove even the smallest thing with convincing emphasis. Therefore, if one wishes to know the right path and get to the bottom of their principles, each of them has a different system <note>original: *Systema*</note>, a different method of teaching. But if one wishes to approach the true principles <note>original: *principiis*</note> of nature as closely as possible, one can choose no surer way than that which chemistry <note>original: *Chymie*</note> shows us. This art will serve as a ladder upon which we can reach the secrets of those very principles <note>original: *principiorum*</note>: and its division of substances <note>original: *Substanzen*</note>—though still somewhat crudely devised—will nevertheless provide us with a magnificent outline of nature and the shape of the first little bodies <note>original: *Cörpergen*; referring to "corpuscles" or the smallest particles of matter</note> from which mixtures <note>original: *mixta*; compound substances made of different elements</note> are composed.

§. 47. I therefore always guide myself by my **principle** <term>principle: the foundational theoretical framework for his chemical observations</term>, and believe that instead of the **effervescence** <note>original: "Auffgären"; refers to the bubbling chemical reaction between acids and bases</note> of **acid** <note>original: "Acidi"</note> and **alkali** originating from a salt which one adds to earthly substances, it is these earthly substances themselves that are the alkali; furthermore, the salt cannot be this alkali until it has been driven through the fire and reached the form of **calx** <term>calx: the powdery residue left after a mineral or metal has been heated; an early term for an oxide</term>. In speaking of **volatile salt** <note>original: "flüchtigen Sal"</note>, I have demonstrated that fire changes substances excessively; and just as I have credibly shown that there is only one salt in plants, and that volatile salt is merely a substance changed by fire, I will also stand by this and say: there is no **fixed alkali salt** <note>original: "Sal alkali fixum"</note> in a plant. Rather, the fire, through **calcination** <note>original: "Calcination"</note>, has **fixed** <note>original: "figiret"; converted into a non-volatile state</note> a portion of the **essential acid salt** <note>original: "Sale acido essentiali"</note> together with the earthly substances; the fire has broken off its most subtle points, created wide **pores** <note>original: "poros"</note> within it, and brought it to the state of a calx. <note>The author is using "corpuscularian" imagery common in the 17th century, where acids were thought to be sharp needles or spikes. However, to explain this matter quite clearly, one must consider as precisely as possible what **acid** <note>original: "Acidum"</note> and **alkali** truly are.

of which it consists, assigning it such **figures** <note>original: "Figuren"; referring to the geometric shape of the microscopic particles</note> that agree with all its effects: so I will say, the **acidity** <note>original: "aciditas"</note> of a **liquid** <note>original: "liqvoris"</note> or the sour sharpness of a fluid thing consists in the pointed particles of the **salts** <note>original: "Salium"</note> which are in motion. But a complete **demonstration** <note>original: "Demonstration"</note> and conviction that an acid consists of pointed particles can be given to us by this observation: that not only does every **acid salt** <note>original: "Sal acidum"</note> **crystallize** <note>original: "chrystallisiret"</note> in the shape of points, but also all solutions of different substances that are performed through **acid liquids** <note>original: "liqvores acidos"</note> take on this figure during their **crystallization** <note>original: "Chrystallisation"</note>. These little crystal pieces consist of such points, where one differs from the others in length and thickness: which difference arises according to whether their points are more or less sharpened by the various types **of acids** <note>original: "acidorum"</note>. This difference, which manifests in the **subtlety** <term>subtility: the degree of fineness or sharpness of the microscopic particles</term> of the points, ensures on the other hand that one acid can easily penetrate and divide a **mixture** <note>original: "mixtum"</note>, while another cannot dissolve it.

<margin>§. 49. Alkali described.</margin>
§. 49. As for **alkali**, one becomes acquainted with it when one adds some **acid** <note>original: "Acidum"</note> to it: for immediately, or shortly thereafter, a violent **effervescence** <note>original: "Auffgährung"; literally a bubbling up or fermentation</note> arises, which lasts until the acid finds no more body to dissolve. This effect allows us to rationally suspect that alkali is a substance consisting of rough and broken particles, whose **pores** <note>original: "Lufft-Löcher"; literally 'air-holes,' referring to the gaps between solid matter</note> are so shaped that as the points of the acid penetrate them, they break and clear everything out of the way that hinders their movement: And depending on whether the particles of this substance are more or less solid and coarse, the **acids** also find more or less resistance and produce a stronger or weaker surge: which, for example, is much gentler in the dissolution of **corals** than in the separation of silver.

->§. 1.<-

# Chapter 5.
## On the Furnaces and Vessels belonging to Chemical Operation.

**§. 1.**
My intention is not at all to provide an exhaustive account of every type of vessel and furnace that craftsmen have invented for chemical work, as that alone would fill a large book; rather, I wish only to describe those with which one can successfully carry out all common chemical operations <note>original: "Chymiſche Operationes"</note>. For the rest, however, I refer those eager to learn, who desire a detailed and comprehensive report on everything, to the laboratories <note>original: "Laboratoria"</note>, where they will learn more than if they were to rummage through every book on the subject.

§. 9. The **portable furnaces** <note>original: *Trag-Oefen*</note> must be constructed from a **lute** <note>original: *Leim*; a refractory paste or cement used to seal or build chemical apparatus</note> made of 3 parts powdered earthenware vessels and two parts fatty earth or **clay**, which is worked together thoroughly in water. §. 10. It is also very beneficial to have a **portable melting furnace** made of the very same material as the others. It must be round, stand upon a **tripod**, and have a single iron bar at the bottom and 6 registers or holes on the sides to provide more air to the fire. From the same material, one should make a **roof** to place over it and a kind of small earthenware **chimney** <note>original: *Feuer-Esse*</note> to be set upon the hole in the roof; all of this is done so that the intensity of the fire may be maintained for longer.

§. 11. One must always add <term>sand</term>, or broken <term>pots</term>, or similar materials into the paste used in the construction of both fixed and portable <term>furnaces</term>, so that they do not develop cracks while drying. It is useful to have a <term>vapor bath</term> <note>original Latin: *balneum vaporum*; a steam bath where the vessel is heated by steam rather than being submerged in water</note> which should consist of three pieces: The first is a large copper kettle with 2 handles, having 3 air-holes with their lids, in order to prevent the broadly expanding steam from bursting everything, and to allow one to pour new water into the kettle as soon as the first amount has been consumed. One must place this kettle in a furnace that is specially made for it, which has its firebox, its ash pit, and two iron bars to support the kettle. The second piece is a large copper kettle, tinned on the inside, with 2 handles, which sits inside the first one up to a third of its height and fits quite snugly, being fastened firmly to it with three hooks; this second kettle must have the shape of a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>original Latin: *Cucurbitæ*; a gourd-shaped vessel used in distillation</note> at the top. The third piece is a <term>Moor’s Head</term> <note>original: *Mohren-Kopff*; a specific type of still head or "cap" that has a built-in reservoir for cold water to aid condensation</note> with its beak and <term>condensers</term> <note>original: *Refrigeranten*</note>, which is tinned on the inside and is attached to the other vessel in the usual manner. You can see the illustrations of these on the third and fourth copperplates.

§. 20. When one wishes to distill in this <term>vapor bath</term> <note>original Latin: *balneo vaporum*</note>, one must put the material into the other kettle that is shaped like a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>original Latin: *Cucurbita*</note>, and fill the first kettle halfway with water: this water is then heated by the fire made in the furnace—

<margin>§. 22. Advantage of the steam bath.</margin>
§. 22. This distillation proceeds much faster than that performed by <term>Mary’s Bath</term> <note>original Latin: *balneum Mariæ*; a water bath where the vessel is submerged</note>: because the steam from the water, which has been forced upward, is far hotter; moreover, it penetrates the upper vessel, which the water—no matter how warm it may be—does not do when it touches the vessel in Mary's Bath.

### §. 24.
One can also distill via <term>Mary’s Bath</term> <note>original Latin: *Balneum Mariæ*; a method of heating a vessel by surrounding it with hot water</note> in this vessel if one has a large lid made with holes in three or four places through which to insert the <term>cucurbits</term> <note>original: *Cucurbitas*; gourd-shaped glass or ceramic distilling vessels</note>. You will find an illustration of this figure on the 4th copperplate. One places and clamps the lid onto the first kettle, into which water has been poured, and inserts as many cucurbits as the lid has holes. One then puts the material from which one wishes to extract water into the cucurbits and attaches the <term>helmets</term> <note>original: *Helmen*; the still heads or alembics that fit over the cucurbits</note> and the <term>receivers</term> <note>original: *Recipienten*; the vessels that catch the condensed liquid</note>. Afterward, a fire is made in the furnace to heat the water, and consequently the cucurbits with everything inside them, so that the moisture is loosened and distilled through the helmets into the receivers. 

One must diligently add new water to the kettle as soon as the first has been consumed; however, it is of great importance to warm this water beforehand. For if one were to leave it cold and add it in that state, the cucurbits—which must be blown from glass or <term>Greitz earth</term> <note>original: *Gretz-Erde*; a high-quality refractory clay, likely from Greiz, used for making heat-resistant laboratory vessels</note>—would shatter. The cause of this is that the "air-pores" of these vessels, previously opened by the heat, are suddenly blocked by the coldness of the water. Since the <term>fire-particles</term> <note>original: *Feuer-Theilgen*; in early chemistry, heat was often thought to consist of physical particles that moved through matter</note> now strike about with force but no longer find free passage, they violently drive the material apart.

They are also excellently suited for many <term>sublimations</term> <note>the process of heating a solid into vapor and then back into a solid form</note>. When the neck of one <term>matrass</term> is inserted into another, they are called a <term>vessel of encounter</term> <note>original: *Vaisseau de rencontre*; a setup where two flasks are joined neck-to-neck, allowing vapors to rise and fall back between them</note>. These are made when one wants to let certain <term>spirits</term> <term>circulate</term>, at which time all the joints are <term>luted</term> <note>original: *verlutiret*; sealed with "lute," a specialized paste or clay to prevent the escape of vapors</note> with great diligence.

## Chapter 7.
## On Sealants.

->§. 1.<-

Because of the intensity of the fire, glass flasks often shatter in the reverberatory furnace <term>reverberatory furnace: a furnace that reflects or "reverberates" heat from the roof onto the material being heated</term>. For this reason, one must coat them with a paste which, once it has become dry, is capable of containing the distilled matter and preserving it unharmed. This paste is called a *lutum* <note>Latin: *lutum*, meaning mud or clay</note>, that is, a sealant or cement <gloss>Leim</gloss>, and it is made in the following manner.

§. 2. Take sand, iron slag <term>iron slag: the stony waste matter separated from metals during the smelting of ore</term>, and powdered clay—5 pounds of each; one pound of horse manure or finely chopped fibers <note>Early chemists used manure or hair as binding agents to provide structural integrity and prevent the clay from cracking during heating.</note>; crushed glass and sea salt—4 ounces of each. Mix everything together and make a paste with enough water. With this paste or sealant <gloss>Leim</gloss>, one coats the retort <term>retort: a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</term> up to the middle of the neck and then lets it dry in the shade. One can also use this same sealant to tightly seal the joints between the flask and the inserted receiver <term>receiver: the vessel placed at the end of a still to collect the condensed liquid</term>. However, since it becomes very firm once dry and is very difficult to remove, one must wrap a wet cloth around it when wanting to detach the receiver from the flask.

§. 3. The sealant that I typically use on such occasions consists of only two parts: namely, two parts sand and one part clay, which are well-kneaded and worked together with water.

§. 4. If one requires a sealant that should come off very easily once the operation is finished, one must allow sifted ash to soften in water and make a paste from it. However, this has much larger air holes <note>meaning it is more porous</note> than the previous ones. Once it has been removed, one can moisten it again and reuse it as often as one wishes.

## Chapter 8.
### Regarding the Degrees of Heat. <note>original: *Graden des Feuers*, literally "degrees of fire." In early laboratory practice, heat was measured by the quantity of fuel rather than with a thermometer.</note>

->§ 1.<-

If one wishes to create a **fire of the first degree**, one requires only 2 or 3 small burning **coals** <note>original: *Kohlgen*, a diminutive form of coals</note>, which are sufficient to maintain a very slight warmth.

§ 2. For a **fire of the second degree**, one needs 3 or 4 coals, which provide enough heat to make the vessel noticeably hot, yet such that one can still endure holding their hand against it for a short while.

§ 3. For a **fire of the third degree**, one requires as much heat as is needed to bring a pot with 5 or 6 **measures** <term>measure: *Maaß*, a historical German unit of liquid volume, often roughly equivalent to 1.07 to 1.5 liters depending on the region</term> of water to a boil.

§ 4. For a **fire of the fourth degree**, one adds as much coal or wood as is required to awaken the extreme intensity of the fire.

§ 5. Fires of **sand**, of **iron-filings**, and of **ashes** <note>These refer to "baths" (e.g., a sand bath or *balneum arenae*), where the vessel is nested in a dry medium to distribute heat evenly and prevent the glass from cracking.</note> are employed when a vessel—containing the **matter** <note>original: *Materie*, the chemical substance being processed</note> to be heated—is surrounded at the bottom and on the sides with sand, iron-filings, or ashes; by this means, the vessel is heated quite gradually.

§. 6. These fires all have their degrees; however, the **ash-fire** is the most leisurely and gentle, because the ash does not retain as great a heat within itself as other materials do.

§. 7. The **reverberatory fire** <term>reverberatory fire: *Reverberir-Feuer*, a furnace designed so that the heat or flame is reflected (reverberated) from the roof back down onto the material being heated</term> is prepared in a furnace covered with a roof, where the heat or flame—which always seeks to escape upward—strikes back down upon the exposed vessel placed on the grate or on the two iron bars. While this fire indeed has its degrees, one can force it with much greater intensity than the others.

§. 8. The **wheel-fire** <note>original: *Rade-Feuer*, likely referring to a fire where coals are arranged in a circular "wheel" around a crucible</note> or **melting-fire** is prepared when one heaps burning coals around a **crucible** <term>crucible: *Schmelz-Tiegel*, a container made of material like ceramic that can withstand very high temperatures for melting metals or minerals</term> in which the matter is to be melted.

§. 9. A **Mary's bath** <note>original: *balneum Mariæ*, now commonly known as a water bath or bain-marie</note> is thus brought about when one places the **alembic** <term>alembic: *Alembicum*, a chemical apparatus used for distillation</term>, along with the matter that is to be heated within it, into a vessel full of water, but builds a fire underneath so that the hot water also heats the contents of the alembic.

§. 10. The **vapor bath** <note>original: *Balneum vaporum*</note> or **sweat-bath** is made when a glass vessel, together with its enclosed matter, is heated by the steam of hot water.

## Chapter 9.
# Explanation of most Chemical Terms and Technical Words.

->§. 1.<-

**To alcoholize** <note>original: *Alkoolisiren*</note> or **to make into an alcohol** means to make something very subtle <note>In early chemistry, "subtle" refers to a substance being refined into its smallest possible particles.</note>, as when one pulverizes a mixture so thoroughly and for so long that the powder can no longer be felt between the fingers. The word is also used for a very pure spirit; thus, **rectified spirit of wine** <note>original: *spiritum vini rectificatum*, or high-proof distilled alcohol</note> is called an **alcohol of wine**.

§. 2. **To amalgamate** or **quicken** <note>original: *verquäcken*, derived from *Quecksilber*, the German word for mercury or "quicksilver"</note> means to mix **mercury** <term>mercury: *Mercurius*, a liquid metal used extensively in alchemical processes</term> with a molten metal. This is done so that the metal can be applied to a surface, or so it can be turned into a very subtle powder. This happens when one throws an **amalgam** <term>amalgam: *Amalgama*, a blend of mercury and another metal</term> into a **crucible** <term>crucible: *Schmels-Tiegel*, a heat-resistant pot for melting minerals or metals</term> over the fire; for as the mercury escapes and vanishes into the open air, it leaves the metal behind as an impalpable powder. Iron and copper do not amalgamate.

§. 3. **To cement** <note>original: *Cœmentiren*</note> or **to lute** <note>original: *verkütten*, meaning to seal or bond</note> is a method of purifying gold. It occurs when one layers the metal with a hard paste <note>original: *Past*</note> made from one part **sal ammoniac** <term>sal ammoniac: *Salis Armoniaci*, ammonium chloride, used in refining and as a flux</term>, two [parts]...

§. 7. **To cohobate** <note>original: *Cohobiren*</note> means to distill a liquid once more and pour it back onto the **dregs** <note>original: *Hefen*, the sediment or residue left after distillation</note> in the vessel, by which means the bodies are opened— <meta>catchword: eröff-</meta>

Thus, one revivifies **cinnabar** <note>mercury sulfide; a bright red mineral</note> and other **preparations of mercury** <note>original: *præparationes Mercurii*</note> back into flowing **mercury**.

§. 29. **Stratification** <term>Stratificiren: from the Latin 'stratum', meaning to arrange in layers</term> means to place different things on top of one another in layers. This is done when one wishes to **calcine** <term>calciniren: to heat a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to achieve decomposition or oxidation</term> a **mineral** or **metal** with a **salt** or another substance.

§. 30. **Sublimation** <term>Sublimiren: a process where a volatile solid is heated until it turns into vapor and then collects as a solid again on a cooler surface</term> means allowing a volatile **substance** to rise through fire into the height of the **alembic** <note>original: *Alembici*; the cap or lid of a distilling apparatus</note> or into the helm <note>the top part of a still where vapors collect</note>.

# The Treatise Itself.
## The First Chapter.
### A. Regarding Gold.

->§. 1.<-

Gold retains the first rank among the seven metals because it is the most perfect and the heaviest; and, as they say, it is deemed worthy of the influence <note>The author refers to the traditional alchemical belief that the Sun radiates a celestial "influence" that forms gold within the earth.</note> of the most beautiful celestial body, the Sun. For this reason, it is also called the King among metals. It is a matter of the greatest density, which allows itself to be hammered <note>The property of malleability, allowing the metal to be beaten into thin sheets.</note>, and consists of unequal particles: for which reason one can also see the various shapes of its pores <note>original: *pororum*; the tiny spaces or channels within the structure of the metal.</note> through a good microscope.

->§. 2.<-

Gold is found in many ore mines, both in Europe and in other parts of the world. It is regularly surrounded by water and stone, or very hard marcasite <note>A brittle mineral, often iron pyrite or "fool's gold," frequently found in the same veins as precious metals.</note>, so that one has difficulty extracting it. Many stones contain gold particles within them, such as the gold-marcasite stone, <term>lapis lazuli</term> <note>original: *lapis lazuli*; a deep-blue metamorphic rock prized since antiquity.</note>, and <term>Armenian stone</term> <note>original: *lapis armenus*; a blue carbonate of copper, likely azurite, historically associated with healing properties.</note>. In many countries, one also finds gold grains <note>original: *Gold-Kräupgen*; small, high-purity grains or nuggets found in alluvial deposits.</note> in the sand of rivers, because the water that has run through such gold mines has carried them away.

<margin>§. 3. Gold leaf.</margin>

<margin>§. 4 and following. Gold-making.</margin>
§. 4. Just as greed has always ruled the human mind, so too has it prevented the minds of chemists <note>original: *Chymisten*; in the 17th and 18th centuries, the term "chemist" was often used interchangeably with "alchemist."</note> from being satisfied without the pursuit of making gold. They believed that the generation of this metal was the primary goal and the highest stage toward which Nature aimed within the ore-mines <note>original: *Ertz-Gruben*.</note>; they thought Nature had only been hindered or led astray whenever she produced other metals, which they labeled as "imperfect."

<margin>§. 20. The improbability of the art of gold-making.</margin>
§. 20. For just as gold and silver are dug from such mines that are surrounded by water: it is probable that these waters bring with them **salt particles** from the places they originate, which freeze together and become such bodies in the earth that have a quite singular composition, and whose *pores* <note>original Latin: *pori*; refers to the microscopic gaps or internal structure of a substance</note> are arranged in such a way that art can never imitate it. # B. Purification or Refining of Gold.

## §. 1.

To **purify** or **refine** gold means as much as separating other metals that have been mixed into it.

## §. 2.

Take as much gold as you please / let it become glowing in a **melting crucible** <term>Schmelz-Tiegel: a ceramic or graphite container capable of withstanding very high temperatures</term> over a strong fire / and when it begins to melt / then throw in four times as much powdered <term>Antimonium</term> <note>original: *Antimonium*; in this period, this usually referred to stibnite (antimony trisulfide), which was used to "eat" base metals away from gold.</note> / then the gold will immediately be brought into **flux** <note>original: *Fluß*; the state of being liquid or molten.</note> / but maintain the strong fire for so long / until the matter sparks.

## §. 3.

Then lift your melting crucible away from the fire / and shake it / until the <term>Regulus</term> <note>original: *Regulus*; literally "little king," this refers to the metallic button or lump that settles at the bottom of the crucible beneath the waste material.</note> goes to the bottom. Break the crucible apart / when it has become cold / and separate the **regulus** or **king** from the **slag** <term>Schlacken: the stony waste matter separated from metals during smelting</term> / that is underneath. If you want to keep your melting crucible whole / then take it / place an iron mortar inside / let it become a little warm beforehand / smear it with <term>Unschlitt</term> <note>original: *Unschlitt*; animal fat or tallow used here to prevent the metal from sticking to the mortar.</note> / and melt the matter into this, and beat or tap with the <term>Zwick-Zänglein</term> <note>original: *Zwick-Zänglein*; small pincers or nippers used for fine handling.</note> against the mortar for so long / until the matter has melted into a lump.

Let it cool a little / pour it out afterward / and separate with a

§. 6. The most certain method of all is the **purification** <note>original: *purification*</note> of gold by **antimony** <note>original: *antimonium*; a semi-metal used in alchemy to "devour" impurities in gold, often symbolized by the wolf</note>: only the density and firmness of gold is a match for this "devourer." §. 7. ->§. 1.<-

<margin>pure</margin> Silver holds the second rank among the metals; it is a very dense, unified, or less rough matter than gold, and its <term>sulfur-pores</term> <note>original: *Schwefel-Löcher*; early chemists believed metals were composed of sulfur and mercury particles; the "pores" were the spaces between these particles</note> are also much more uniform in their shape. ## B. The Purification or Refining of Silver.

->§. 1.<-

To <term>purify</term> <note>original: *purificiren*</note> or refine silver means as much as separating it from other metals that it carries with it. # C. Observations on the Purification of Gold <insert>and Silver</insert>

->§. 1.<-

The <term>cupel</term> <note>original: *Capelle*; a shallow, porous vessel used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals</note> is an earthen vessel that has the shape of a bowl and withstands fire. One fills it with a paste prepared from unsalted ash, specifically the kind of ash provided by bones that have lost their overly <term>volatile salt</term> <note>original: *flüchtiges Salz*; refers to ammonia or other salts that evaporate easily when heated</note> during burning. One makes a hole in the center into which the material to be placed on the cupel is put; afterwards, one lets it dry in the shade.

§. 2. According to the proportion of impurities that may be in the silver, one must also put lead into the cupel; normally, however, one throws in four times as much. <margin>§. 1. What is a cupel?</margin> What is called "impurity" here is nothing other than various particles of other metals that remained attached to the silver when it was extracted from the mine <note>original: *Fund-Grube*</note>. These metals mix much more readily with lead than with silver, because lead is filled with sulfurous and hook-like particles <note>In the 17th century, scientists often believed chemicals reacted because their atoms had physical shapes, like "hooks," that latched onto each other.</note> that easily entangle other bodies within themselves. Silver, on the other hand, has very tightly closed particles and can only be penetrated and linked with such materials from the surface; these [impurities] separate immediately during melting, and

## Chapter 3.
# A. On Tin.

-> §. 1. <-

Tin / which the ancients called **white lead** <note>original: "weiß Bley"; historically known in Latin as *plumbum album* to distinguish it from "black lead" or lead proper (*plumbum nigrum*)</note> / is a metal that comes very close to silver in color / but which is greatly different from it in the shape of its **pores** <term>Lufft-Löcher</term> <note>original: "Lufft-Löcher"; literally "air-holes," referring to the internal structure or porosity that 17th-century chemists believed determined a metal's properties and how it reacted with acids</note> / in its firmness and density, and in its weight. It has been given the name of the planet **Jupiter** <note>original: "*Jovis*"; in alchemical tradition, tin is governed by Jupiter and shares its astrological symbol</note> / as it is said to receive its **influence** from it: It is a substance / that can be hammered / contains much **sulfur** <note>In early modern chemical theory, "sulfur" was one of the three primary principles, representing the soul of the metal and its flammability or oiliness</note> / and melts easily. It is found in many mines / especially in England / which for this reason is called the **Isle of Tin** <note>original: "*Isle d'Etain*"; likely referring to Cornwall and the British Isles, which were the primary source of tin for the ancient world</note>. This does not dissolve entirely in **nitric acid** <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "*Aqua fort*"; unlike silver, which dissolves clearly, tin reacts with nitric acid to form a white, insoluble paste (metastannic acid)</note> / as some would like to claim / only a part is dissolved / which indicates / that it consists of different particles / and its pores have different shapes. A power is attributed to it against **liver and uterine complaints** <term>Leber- und Mutter-Beschwerungen</term> <note>original: "Mutter-Beschwerungen"; "mother-complaints" or "the mother" was a common historical term for hysteria or uterine distress, though the author here expresses skepticism about tin's medicinal value for these conditions</note> / but this consists of mere imagination / because experience has in no way confirmed it.

## C. Concerning the Calcination of Tin.

->§. 1.<-

To **calcinate** <term>calciniren</term> tin means nothing other than to bring it into the form of a **lime** <term>Kalck</term> <note>original: "Kalck"; in early chemistry, a "calx" is the powdery substance, usually a metal oxide, left after a metal has been roasted or "burnt" in fire.</note> through the assistance of fire.

§. 2. # Chapter 4.
## A. Concerning Bismuth,
### Which one calls *stannum glaciale* <note>Latin: "icy tin."</note>, or Ice-Tin.

->§. 1.<-

<margin>§. 1. Artificial Bismuth.</margin>
Bismuth is a metallic, white, polished, sulfurous substance similar to tin, yet it is simultaneously hard, acidic <note>Early chemists often described brittle or sharp-edged minerals as "acidic" in nature.</note>, and slaty. It consists of cubic and gleaming plates or layers which shimmer like small ice floes, from which it also received its name. Scholars do not agree in its description. The ancients categorized it as a natural *marcant* <note>A historical term for marcasite or similar metallic ores.</note> or an imperfect tin found in tin mines. The moderns believe with greater probability that it is a *regulus stanni* <note>Latin: "king of tin"; the pure metallic portion of the metal after smelting.</note> or tin-king, artificially prepared by the English. Be that as it may, one can prepare a fine bismuth from tin, tartar <term>Weinstein</term> <note>Potassium bitartrate, a common chemical reagent in early labs.</note>, and saltpeter, into which some also mix arsenic <note>original: "arsenicum".</note>.

§. 2. The air-holes <term>Lufft-Löcher</term> <note>Also called "pores"; early scientists believed metals had tiny openings that allowed fluids to enter.</note> of bismuth are arranged more widely than those of tin; this is evident from the solvent <note>original: "menstruo"; a liquid used to dissolve a solid.</note>, which dissolves the bismuth but does not dissolve the tin at all.

§. 3. <margin>§. 3. Use.</margin> Bismuth is not administered internally to anyone, as it is believed that it carries something of **arsenic** <note>original: "Arsenico". Early chemists were wary of bismuth's toxicity due to its frequent association with arsenic in mineral deposits.</note> within it. Pewterers <note>Artisans who make vessels and tools from pewter (an alloy of tin).</note> mix it into tin so that it becomes bright, hard, and resonant.

§. 4. <margin>§. 4. What is **marcasite**?</margin> **Marcasite** <note>original: "Marcant"; a historical term used broadly by early chemists for various metallic minerals or ores before they were fully classified as distinct elements.</note> is a general name suitable for all metallic substances; however, bismuth is called this specifically and above all others because it surpasses all other **marcasites** in beauty.

§. 5. <margin>§. 5. What is **zinc**?</margin> There is another kind of **marcasite** called **zinc**, which indeed resembles bismuth but is not as brittle. It is used to purify tin of its impurities <note>original: "Unart"; literally "bad nature," referring to the dross or base qualities that make tin soft or dull.</note> and to make it even brighter, adding only a little to a large amount of tin melted over the fire. This **marcasite** is also used for soldering.

## Concerning the **Magistery** of Bismuth.

->§. 9.<-

The **magistery** of bismuth is a dissolved **ice-tin** <note>original: "Stannum glaciale"; a historical name for bismuth because of its crystalline, ice-like appearance.</note>, or bismuth-tin, which has been **precipitated** into a very white powder.

<margin>§. 10. Weight. Spanish White.</margin>
§. 10. Dissolve one ounce of coarsely powdered bismuth with 3 ounces of **spirit of nitre** <note>original: "Spiritus nitri"; nitric acid.</note> in a **matrass** <note>A long-necked glass chemical flask.</note>: pour the **solution** into a very clean earthenware basin, and pour 5 or 6 pounds of spring water over it, in which you have previously dissolved half an ounce of sea salt; thus a white powder will **precipitate** to the bottom. ### §. 1.

One must use a fairly large **matrass** <note>A long-necked glass chemical flask.</note> to dissolve the **bismuth** / so that the violent **effervescence** <note>A bubbling or fizzing reaction.</note>, which occurs immediately after the **spirit of nitre** <note>original: "Spiritu nitri"; nitric acid.</note> is poured on, has enough space. §. 2. To which is added / that also a considerable **quantity** of fire-particles <note>The text ends here with "Feuer-" and the catchword "Theil-," referring to the contemporary theory that heat was caused by the release of physical "fire-matter" trapped within chemicals.</note> contained in the **spirit of nitre**—

### §. 6.
Here a difficulty arises: why, specifically, can common water alone dissolve the **bismuth** / the **lead** / and the **antimony** <note>original: "Antimonium"</note> which has been joined with an **acid** <note>original: "acidum"</note>; whereas it cannot **precipitate** <note>To cause a solid substance to separate and fall out of a liquid solution.</note> **gold** / **silver** / and **mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> on its own, but only with the help of a salt or another body? I maintain it is because the former have **pores** <note>In 18th-century chemistry, it was believed that substances had tiny holes or "pores" (poros) where acid particles could lodge themselves.</note> that are somewhat too wide, so the **acids** have not settled themselves so firmly within them that the water cannot drive them out. Conversely, **gold**, **silver**, and **mercury**, having narrow **pores** compared to the others, hold the **acid** so firmly that it cannot be torn loose by the shaking and rattling of the water alone, unless another substance comes to the aid of the water to give the **acid** more forceful blows.

### §. 7.
The addition of the **bismuth** in the **magistery** <note>The "Magistery of Bismuth" was a popular white cosmetic powder and medicinal skin treatment.</note> arises from a portion of the **spirit of nitre** <note>original: "Spiritus nitri"; nitric acid.</note>, which remained settled inside despite the **precipitation** and washing.

### §. 8.
One normally puts one **dram** <note>original: "Drachmam"; a historical unit of weight, about 3.9 grams.</note> of this **magistery** into 4 ounces of lily-water or well-water, or into one ounce of **pomade** / then it is good for the **itch** <note>original: "Kräze"; a general term for skin eruptions or scabies.</note>, because it eats away the **acids** or salts that harbor and sustain this evil.

# Chapter 5.
## A. On Lead.

->§. 1.<-

**Lead** is a metal full of **sulfur** <note>In historical alchemy, "sulfur" referred to the principle of combustibility and color, rather than just the chemical element S.</note> or resinous earth, which makes it soft and very ductile <note>original: "zach"</note>; it also appears as if it carries **mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> within it. Its **pores** <note>Tiny internal spaces believed to determine a metal's density and reactivity.</note> are very similar to the air-holes of **tin**. It is called **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturnum"</note> because of the influences it is said to receive from the planet of that name <note>Alchemists associated lead with the planet Saturn because both were considered heavy, slow, and "cold" in nature.</note>.

->§. 2.<-

<margin>§. 2. Where lead is found.</margin> This metal is to be encountered in many lands in various types of stones and earths, some of which contain **silver**, while others contain **gold** and **silver**.

->§. 3.<-

Lead ore specimens.</margin> The **lead ore** or specimen <note>original: "Bley-Stuffe"</note> looks as black as **antimony** <note>original: "Spieß-Glaß"; specifically stibnite, a dark grey mineral.</note> and is sprinkled with small shiny points and glitters. However, the ore that carries **gold** looks much brighter, much more polished, and more radiant.

->§. 4.<-

It is remarkable that the **effervescence**, which occurs in other lead processes when one adds such an **acid** <note>original: *acidum*</note> to it, is much stronger: because the acid finds a more closed **body** <note>original: *Corpus*; the solid physical form of the substance</note> than in **white lead** <note>a white pigment consisting of lead carbonate</note>, it must therefore apply more force to penetrate it, and consequently lifts and swells the matter in the process.

§. 3. In these and many other effervescences, one can perceive no degree of heat if one simply feels it with the hand: But one will still become aware of it if one places a **thermometer** <note>original: *thermometrum* or *Wetter-Glaß* (literally "weather-glass"); early instruments for measuring temperature</note> into the **liquid** <note>original: *liqvorem*</note> during the ongoing **fermentation** <note>here meaning a vigorous chemical reaction or agitation</note>: For the **spirit of wine** <note>original: *Spiritus vini*; alcohol, which was used as the liquid inside early thermometers</note> contained within will rise several degrees, which is an indisputable sign of warmth.

§. 4. The wine-vinegar loses all its power in the **penetration** of the lead and takes on a **sugary taste** <note>Lead acetate is notoriously sweet to the taste, leading to its historical name "Sugar of Lead," though it is highly toxic.</note>.

## §. 5. Revivified Salt of Lead.

# I. Observations.

### §. 1.

Keep this well in mind: you must not fill more than a third of the flask with the matter, and you must attach a fine, large receiver <note>the glass vessel used to collect the distilled vapors</note>, because the volatile spirits <note>original: *Spiritus volatiles*; the gaseous vapors</note> rush forth with such force that the vessels could shatter into pieces if they did not find enough room to expand.

<margin>§. 2. Weight of the Salt</margin>
### §. 2.

If you have distilled 6 ounces of salt, you will draw out one ounce and 6 drachms <note>original: *drachmas*; a unit of weight equal to 1/8th of an ounce</note> of liquid <note>original: *liqvoris*</note>, and 6 ounces and 6 drachms of blackish and yellow matter will remain in the flask. If you then place this matter in a crucible under burning coals, it will melt, and you will get out 4 ounces of lead and half an ounce (or sometimes 6 drachms) of yellow earth, which has the color of litharge <note>original: *Gold-Schaums*; literally "gold-scum," referring to lead monoxide or litharge</note>.

# Chapter 6.

## A. On Copper.

§. 1.
Copper is a metal extracted from many ore mines in Europe, but it is particularly mined in Sweden and Denmark. It is found in powdered form and in such <term>specimens <note>original: *Stuffen*; mineral samples or high-quality ore pieces</note></term> that resemble iron ore. These are washed thoroughly to purify them from the earth that is always mixed in. After this, they are melted with a strong fire, and the molten matter is poured into molds or forms; this is common copper. One can make it far more beautiful and pure if it is recast once or twice, because with every <term>smelting <note>original: *Fluß*; literally "flow," referring to the state of the metal when melted</note></term>, some coarse and earthy particles are separated. This is called *rosette copper* <note>original: *cuivre de rosette* / *cuprum rosatum*</note>, or rose-red copper.

§. 2. Copper contains much <term>copper water <note>original: *Kupfferwasser*; also known as blue vitriol or copper(II) sulfate</note></term> or vitriol and sulfur. It is called *Venus*, because it was believed that this planet ruled over it and filled it with its influences...

Then, take your plates from the fire while they are still quite warm and separate them from one another; thus you have <term>burnt copper: <note>original: *Æs ustum*</note> a copper oxide produced by heating copper with sulfur, historically used in alchemy and medicine</term>, which is used in several external remedies for drying <note>referring to its medicinal use in drying out wounds or sores</note>.

## Observations.

->§. 3.<-

<margin>§. 3. Layer upon layer <note>original: *Stratum super stratum*</note>.</margin>
In stratification, one begins with a layer of sulfur / and over that one lays a layer of copper plates / then another layer of sulfur / and yet another layer of copper plates. One continues in this way / until the melting-crucible is full: however, the first and the last layers must be of sulfur.

§. 4. This calcination <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to change its chemical or physical properties</note> is performed so that the burning sulfur may cleanse the copper of its superficial and surface-level sulfur; however, it is cleaned even further in the following manner.

## C. Regarding the Purification of Calcined Copper.

### §. 1.

This second refining of the copper is intended to make its color beautiful and intense <note>literally "high in color," referring to a rich, vibrant hue desired in the finished product</note>.

### §. 2.

Take as much as you like of the copper calcined in the aforementioned manner; let it become glowing hot in a melting crucible under burning coals. Throw it, while completely glowing, into a pot which must already contain enough linseed oil <note>original: *Lein-Oel*</note> so that it rises four fingers' height above the material. Cover the pot immediately, otherwise the oil would catch fire. Let the copper harden <note>this refers to the quenching process where the metal is rapidly cooled in a liquid</note> until the oil has cooled halfway; take the copper out, put it back into the melting crucible to make it glowing hot again, and place it back into the linseed oil while glowing. Continue this process of heating the copper and cooling it in linseed oil a total of nine times. One must use fresh oil every three times: thus you will obtain an exceedingly beautiful copper that has regained its proper color.

### §. 3.

If you wish to calcine and powder it once more in order to consume the sulfur, you will have a beautiful copper crocus <term>Copper Crocus: <note>original: *Kupffer-Crocum* or *Crocus Veneris*; a reddish-brown powder consisting of copper oxide, highly valued by early modern chemists for its drying and caustic properties</note></term>, which dries exceedingly well and bites away <note>effectively cauterizing or chemically removing</note> the pus and proud flesh <note>original: *wilde Fleisch*, a historical term for excessive granulation tissue that prevents a wound from healing correctly</note> of wounds and ulcers.

# D. On *Vitriol of Venus* or Copper Vitriol.
<note>original: *Vitriolo Veneris*; in alchemy, Venus is the planetary association for copper, so "Vitriol of Venus" refers to a salt derived from copper, typically copper nitrate in this specific nitric acid process.</note>

->§. 1.<-

This operation involves copper that has been dissolved by *spirit of nitre* <note>original: *Salpeter-Spiritu*; a historical term for nitric acid</note> and transformed into *vitriol* <note>a term used by early chemists for various crystalline metal salts</note>.

<margin>§. 2. Copper Crystals.</margin>
§. 2. Dissolve two ounces of copper, which has been beaten into small pieces, in 5 or 6 ounces of *spirit of nitre*; let the *dissolution* <note>the resulting liquid mixture</note> flow into a glass *cucurbit* <note>original: *Cucurbitam*; a gourd-shaped vessel used for boiling or distilling</note> and *evaporate* it in a sand bath <note>original: *Sand-Feuer*; a method of heating a vessel evenly by nesting it in warm sand</note> until approximately a fourth part of the moisture has evaporated. Let the remainder stand undisturbed for 5 or 6 hours, and blue crystals will settle together. Once you have set these aside, continue with the *evaporation* and *crystallization* of the *liquor* <note>original: *liqvoris*; the remaining liquid</note> until it is all used up. Let these crystals dry and keep them in a well-sealed vial; they are *caustic* <note>substances that burn or corrode organic tissue</note> and corrosive *remedies* <note>original: *Remedia*</note> used to remove "pus-cores" <note>original: *Eiter-Stöcke*; the hard, necrotic centers of boils or abscesses</note> and whatever growths may break out upon the skin.

<margin>§. 3. Liquor of Venus.</margin>
§. 3. If one allows these crystals to stand in an open vessel in a cellar, they will dissolve into a *liquor* <note>original: *liqvore*; this process, called deliquescence, occurs when salts absorb enough moisture from the air to turn into liquid</note>, which has the same benefits and uses as the crystals.

# E. Remarks.

### §. 1.

One places the copper in a large *matrass* <note>original: *Matras*; a long-necked glass chemistry flask</note> under the *smoke-hole* <note>original: *Rauch-Loch*; a ventilation flue to carry away dangerous fumes</note> and gradually pours *spirit of nitre* <note>original: *Spiritum nitri*; nitric acid</note> upon it. At first, a violent *effervescence* <note>bubbling and fizzing</note> and a red smoke <note>nitrogen dioxide, a toxic gas produced when copper reacts with nitric acid</note> arise, which pass through the neck of the vessel; if any part of this smoke is inhaled, it severely affects the chest. The vessel becomes so hot that one cannot bear to touch it with a hand, and the heat persists until the dissolution is complete. Then the *liquid* <note>original: *liquor*</note> remains clear and has a beautiful blue color.

<margin>§. 1. Dissolution of Copper.</margin>

### §. 2.

The strong *effervescence* triggered at the beginning occurs because the *spirit of saltpeter* <note>nitric acid</note> finds excessively large *pores* <note>original: *poros*; microscopic gaps in the metal's structure</note> in the copper, which correspond so well to the size of its "spikes" <note>original: *Spitzen*; early chemists often imagined acid particles as sharp needles that mechanically wedged into substances</note> that they can lodge themselves there and carry out their attacks. For as soon as these spikes, which previously swam freely in a *liquid* <note>original: *liquido*</note>, are caught within the body of this metal, they use force to tear themselves loose through their motion, and they drive all the small particles of the copper apart. This violent dispersal causes the boiling and the heat, as the spikes of the *acid* <note>original: *acidi*</note> strike roughly against the solid parts of the copper,
