# Remarks.

### §. 5.

The **acid** <note>original: *acidum*</note> is drawn from the copper by the fire, and yet its sharp points are not broken, because the **Spirit of Venus** <note>original: *Spiritus Veneris*; a concentrated acetic acid produced by distilling verdigris (copper acetate)</note> is noticeably sour, which is not found with other metals. The reason for this can be given as follows: since copper contains much <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: *Schwefel*; in alchemical theory, sulfur represents the principle of oiliness, color, and combustibility</note>, it only binds the acids with its branched particles during its <term>dissolution</term> <note>original: *Dissolution*; the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid</note>. Therefore, when the force of the fire drives them out, these sharp points emerge completely intact: they find no resistance from a sufficiently dense **body** <note>original: *Cörpers*</note> that could destroy or even break them. Moreover, they carry away some of the most <term>volatile</term> <note>easily evaporated</note> copper particles with them, as they are inseparably united.

### §. 6.

One must **rectify** <note>original: *rectificiren*; the process of purifying a liquid by redistilling it to remove impurities</note> this spirit, because the fire constantly drives out more and more of its impurities, which were introduced during its **reduction** to **verdigris** <note>original: *Grünspan*; a green crust formed on copper, often used as a pigment or medicinal base</note> through the use of wine dregs <note>original: *Wein-Drüsen*; the sediment or skins left over from winemaking, used here to provide the acetic acid needed to create the copper acetate</note>.

### §. 7.

It has indeed been claimed that even if one were to dissolve corals or pearls with this spirit, it would lose none of its power; and that one could use the same spirit, already used once, to dissolve other materials of this kind again as before. However, experience agrees with

If one wishes to make steel, one <term>stratifies</term> <note>original: *stratificiret*; the process of layering different materials on top of one another</note> iron plates and horn or animal hooves with one another in a large furnace; a great fire is made beneath it, so that the hooves ignite and <term>calcine</term> <note>original: *calciniren*; heating a substance to a high temperature to change its chemical or physical properties, often to drive off volatile substances</note> the iron. I answer: One would indeed have cause to think that more salt should be found in steel than in iron, if, during the process of <term>steel-making<gloss>original: Stahlmache</gloss></term>, the iron were <term>calcined<gloss>original: calcinirte; a process of heating metal to high temperatures to change its properties</gloss></term> on its own without the addition of animal claws or horn. For then one could say that since the <term>sulfur<gloss>original: Schwefel; in early chemistry, this referred to the "oily" or combustible principle of a substance</gloss></term> had partly flown away from the iron, its salt would be that much easier to dissolve. 

However, one should consider that the <term>volatile salts<gloss>original: flüchtigen Saltze</gloss></term> that come out of these animal claws and horns are <term>penetrating alkalis<gloss>original: penetrante Alkali</gloss></term>. Consequently, they "kill" <note>This is a historical chemical term meaning to neutralize or stabilize a reactive substance.</note> most of the salt in the iron—which is acidic—and thus pack the steel particles together very densely. This prevents them from rusting so easily, because the salts, which would otherwise loosen the metal through their movement, are "fixed" and, as it were, dead—or at least in a state where they can no longer move as they did before. This is exactly the reason why a steel plate soaked in water does not produce as much of an "iron taste" as an iron plate of equal weight does when it is quenched in water.

In that process, one labels as <term>slag<gloss>original: Schlacken</gloss></term> or "foam" that which...

## E. *Martis Crocus adstringens*, Astringent Saffron of Mars.

->§. 1.<-

This preparation <note>Original: *præparation*</note> is iron dust that has been stripped and bared of its salty part.

Take as much as you please of the previous opening Saffron of Mars <note>Referring to the *Crocus Martis aperiens* mentioned in preceding sections, which was intended to "open" the body's channels.</note>, wash it five or six times in strong wine vinegar, and let it steep <term>steep<note>Original German: *beitzen*. ## H. The Iron Tincture with Tartar: **Tincture of Tartarized Iron.** <note>original: *Tinctura Martis tartarizata*</note>

-> §. 1. <-

This **preparation** <note>original: *præparation*</note> is a type of **dissolution** <note>original: *Dissolution*</note> of iron of the kind brought about by the **acid of tartar**. <note>original: *acido tartari*. Tartaric acid, naturally occurring in grapes and found as a crust in wine barrels.</note>

<margin>§. 2, Weight.</margin>
§. 2: Powder and mix together 12 ounces of iron rust and 32 ounces of fine white **tartar** <note>original: *tartarum*</note>; boil the mixture together in a large iron cauldron with 12 or 15 pounds of rainwater for 12 hours. Stir the material gradually with an iron spatula and immediately pour more boiling-hot water into the cauldron as soon as the first portion boils away. Finally, let everything stand still, and a black **liquid** <note>original: *liqvor*</note> will appear on top. Filter it and let it evaporate in a furnace over a **sand bath** <note>represented by the symbol <image-desc>alchemical symbol for sand bath (hourglass shape)</image-desc>. A method of heating a vessel evenly by nesting it in warm sand.</note> until it becomes as thick as a syrup; you will then obtain 44 ounces from it.

## Remarks.

§. 4.
Water alone could not sufficiently penetrate the iron or produce such a **tincture** <note>original: *Tinctur*</note> as the one described above, even if one were to let it boil therein for a month. However, if the water is filled with **tartar** <note>original: *tartaro*. Potassium bitartrate, a substance that forms in wine barrels.</note>, the water dissolves the tartar and becomes saturated with it. Yet, one should not think that this tincture is prepared through a very precise or complete dissolution of the iron. For even if it were perfectly dissolved, no more tincture would result than the **dissolution** <note>original: *Dissolution*</note> produced by treating this metal with **spirit of vitriol** <note>original: *Spiritum vitrioli*. Dilute sulfuric acid.</note> and water. It is only because the soluble part of the tartar, which acts here, is nothing other than an impure **acid salt** <note>original: *Sal acidum*</note> that it can only dissolve the iron coarsely; once it has mixed with the iron, it can keep it suspended in the water.

Filter the clear liquid while it is still quite warm through a white cloth, and let the moisture evaporate over a **sand bath** <note>original: *Sand-Feuer*; a container of sand heated to provide even, gentle warmth</note> in a **metal basin** <note>original: *Ertz-Becken*; likely made of bronze or brass</note> or glass vessel until it becomes a thick **extract** <term>extract: a concentrated substance obtained by evaporating a solvent</term>.

This is then a magnificent **opening medicine** <term>aperiens: a substance used to "open" the passages of the body and relieve obstructions, particularly in the digestive system</term> and has the same potency as the **tincture** <note>referring to the Tincture of Tartarized Iron described on the previous page</note> for obstructions of the **liver**, the **spleen**, and the **mesentery** <term>mesenterii: the fold of membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</term>. It incomparably cleanses the **lymphatic vessels** <term>vasa lymphatica</term> of all impurities that might hinder the flow of the **serum** <term>Seri: the clear, watery part of bodily fluids</term>. The **dosage** <term>Dosis</term> ranges from 10 **grains** <note>a small unit of weight, approximately 0.06 grams</note> up to 2 **scruples** <term>Scrupel: an apothecary weight equal to 20 grains</term>. One takes it either in the form of **pills** or lets it dissolve in a suitable **liquid** <term>liquore</term>.

§. 3. What remains at the bottom of the iron pot is the most **earthly matter** of the iron, which is of no use.

# 50. Sweat-Inducing Iron. <note>original: *Mars Diaphoreticus*; "Mars" is the alchemical name for iron, and "Diaphoreticus" refers to a substance that induces sweating.</note>

## §. 1.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' containing floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>This **Sweat-Inducing Iron** is nothing other than **iron particles** that have been "larded" <note>original: *ausgespicket*; a culinary term used here to describe the iron being infused or "pierced" with salts</note> with **volatile salts** <note>original: *flüchtigen salibus*</note>.

## §. 2.

Take equal parts **iron rust** and **sal ammoniac** <note>original: *Salarmoniac*; ammonium chloride</note>. Put this mixture into an earthen **cucurbit** <note>a gourd-shaped vessel used in distillation</note>, place it in a small furnace, and seal it at the bottom with clay and bricks so that the fire only shines through several registers or holes at the top. Attach a **blind head** <note>original: *blinden Helm*; an alembic cap without a spout, used when the goal is sublimation (collecting solids) rather than distilling liquids</note> to your cucurbit and start with a gentle fire. Gradually increase the heat until the bottom of the cucurbit becomes glowing red, and maintain this level of heat until it no longer produces any smoke. <margin>§. 2. Sublimation. Precipitate.</margin> Afterwards, let the vessels cool, remove the head, and collect the **flowers** <note>original: *Blumen*; in early chemistry, this refers to the powdery solid formed by sublimation</note> that have gathered there. Let these dissolve in as much water as is necessary, filter the **solution** <note>original: *Dissolution*</note> through **blotting paper**, and drop **Oil of Tartar** <note>potassium carbonate solution</note> or **Spirit of Sal Ammoniac** <note>ammonia solution</note> into it <note>original: *per descensum*; added drop-by-drop</note>; a **precipitate** will then remain at the bottom of the vessel. Pour off the **liquid** <note>original: *liqvorem*</note> floating on top by tilting the vessel and let this precipitate dry.

## §. 3.

It drives out sweat and is used for all illnesses arising from the corruption of the moistures <note>The German text ends with the catchword *Feuch-*, likely for *Feuchtigkeiten* (humors or bodily fluids), which continues on the next page.</note>

### §. 4.

This preparation is a **sweat-inducer** <note>original: *Sudoriferum*</note> and drives out sweat because it contains some particles of **sal ammoniac** <note>original: *Salarmoniac*; ammonium chloride</note> that remained in the **pores** <note>original: *Lufft-Löchern*, literally "air-holes"</note> of the **precipitated iron** <note>original: *præcipitirten Martis*; in alchemy, "Mars" represents iron</note>. For when these salt particles are activated by the heat of a body—as they are very volatile—they prefer to distribute themselves imperceptibly into the pores of the whole body, rather than taking their way through the urine along with the **fixed salts** <note>salts that remain stable and do not evaporate when heated</note>. Thereupon, sweating or sometimes only an imperceptible evaporation occurs, because these salt particles loosen many moistures and create a free passage for them, which they previously lacked due to their **sliminess** <note>referring to the viscous or "sticky" nature of the bodily humors that can cause blockages</note>. However, because they sometimes find the pores to be too narrow, they must become fixed and seek the common path through the urine: there they open the **lymphatic vessels** <note>original: *vasa lymphatica*</note> and carry out many substances that were held back within them.

## B. On Artificial Cinnabar.

### §. 1.

**Cinnabar** <note>original: *Zinnober*</note> is a mixture of **sublimated** <note>The alchemical process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then cooled back into a solid form to purify it</note> sulfur and mercury.

§. 2. Take one part **sulfur**, which you allow to melt in a large earthenware basin; then gradually mix in three parts of flowing **mercury** <note>original: *Mercurium*</note>; stir and keep the material in a molten state until no more mercury can be seen. Then pulverize your mixture and let it **sublimate** in pots over an open and graded fire; in this way, you will obtain a hard and bright red mass. If any other metal happened to be present in the mercury, it will remain at the bottom of the pots.

§. 3. Besides the convenience—that mercury is easily transported once it has been sublimated into cinnabar—it is also of great use in **painting**. It is also added to ointments for the **itch** <note>original: *Kräze*; likely referring to scabies or other parasitic skin conditions</note>. One also uses it for fumigation when one wishes to induce **salivation** <note>original: *Salivation*; a common medical practice in the 17th and 18th centuries where mercury was used to cause excessive drooling, believed to purge "poisonous humors" from the body, particularly when treating syphilis</note>.

# Remarks.

### §. 4.

**O**ne pound of melted **sulfur** <note>original: *Schwefel*</note> can bind three pounds of **mercury** <note>original: *Mercurium*</note> and make a **mass** out of it.

§. 5. If the mercury were alone, however, or in a material that did not hold it captive, it would evaporate entirely.

Its red color perhaps comes from the sulfur, which carries such a color when it is well loosened <note>original: *auseinander-gelockert*; meaning the particles are dispersed or chemically broken down</note>.

Some women mix it into pomade and paint their cheeks with it; they do not consider what a dangerous consequence <note>original: *Zufall*</note> could arise for them from this makeup, such as **salivation** <note>the excessive production of saliva, a classic sign of mercury poisoning which was often dangerously mistaken for a healing process in this era</note>.

§. 9. **Fumigation** <note>a treatment where the patient inhales medicinal vapors</note> is performed by allowing the sick person to catch the cinnabar smoke that is produced when the substance is thrown into the fire.

## C. The Revivification of Cinnabar into a Flowing or Living Mercury.

§. 1.

This process is undertaken to separate the **sulfur** from the **cinnabar**.

§. 2. Take one pound of **artificial cinnabar**, powder it, and mix it well with three pounds of likewise powdered but **unslaked lime** <note>original: *ungelöschten Kalck*; calcium oxide, a caustic alkaline substance</note>. Then pour the mixture into a well-luted <note>original: *verlutirten*; sealed with an airtight paste or clay to prevent vapors from escaping</note> stoneware or glass flask, leaving at least a third of it empty. Place it in a **reverberatory furnace** <note>a furnace designed to reflect or "reverberate" heat onto the vessel from the roof</note> and attach a receiver vessel filled with water. Let

Apply fire from below and eventually increase it to the highest intensity; then the **mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius*</note> will fall down into the **receiver vessel** <note>original: *Recipienten*</note> as white drops. Maintain the fire until nothing more passes over, as the operation is commonly completed in 6 to 7 hours. Pour off the water from the receiver, wash the mercury to remove the small amount of **earthy residue** <note>original: *Erde*; impurities left over from the chemical reaction</note> it might have picked up, dry it with linen cloths or bread crumbs, and store it away.

<margin>§. 3. Weight</margin>
§. 3. From every pound of **artificial cinnabar** <note>mercury sulfide created in a laboratory rather than mined from the earth</note>, one must obtain 13 ounces of **living mercury** <note>original: *lebendig Quecksilber*; liquid, elemental mercury</note>.

§. 4. One can also further **revivify** <note>return a chemical compound to its pure metallic state</note> the cinnabar by adding an equal amount of **iron filings** <note>original: *Eisen-Späne*</note> to it and proceeding in the same manner as described above.

**§. 28.** Perhaps one might object to me: that **Mercury** <term>Mercurius</term> also excites **salivation** <term>Speichel-Fluß</term> in people who have never had the **French disease** <term>Franzosen</term> <note>a common historical name for syphilis</note>, and who have no boils on their bodies wherein **sour salt** might be found. But to that, it is easy to answer. For no one is found, however healthy they may be, who does not have salty or sour moisture. The **serum** <term>Serum</term> <note>original: *Serum*; the clear component of blood</note>, which flows everywhere in the body, is indeed full of salt; and all **ferments** <term>Fermente</term> <note>substances believed by early modern doctors to drive chemical transformations and digestion in the body</note> that serve to maintain the structure of the body in good health can indeed be formed from nothing else but **salts** <term>Salibus</term> and **acids** <term>acidis</term> <note>original Latin: *Salibus* and *acidis*</note>. Thus, it can be understood just as easily that **Mercury** is united with the **acids** found in the body of a completely healthy person, as it is to believe that it binds with the **salts** or **acids** of the syphilitic boils. For I do not claim that **Mercury** immediately and directly seeks out only the **acid** <term>acidum</term> in the boils of a **syphilitic body** <term>Französigten Leibes</term>—which would attribute to it an intelligence it does not possess. Rather, this is my opinion: because it is loosened and driven about by the heat of the body, it runs everywhere until it encounters a salt that, in a manner of speaking, "kills" it <note>this refers to the chemical process where liquid mercury reacts with another substance to form a stable compound, "killing" its fluid, quicksilver state</note> and causes its movement to stall.

<margin>First Objection.</margin>

<margin>Answer.</margin>
I answer: a.) It is just as false that **mercury** is **volatilized** <note>turned into a vapor or made mobile</note> by the acidic fluids of the **French disease**, as it is untrue that **mercury**—which one places into acidic **spirits** <note>concentrated liquid distillates</note> to make them **corrosive**—has been **volatilized** by one of them. It seems to me that I have explained myself clearly enough when I suggested that if **mercury** sometimes does not find enough **acid salts** <note>original: "Salia acida"</note> for its **arrest** <note>its binding or fixation</note> in a **body**, it is sweated out.

## F. Dulcified Mercury Sublimate, otherwise known as *White Eagle* <note>original: "aqvila alba"; a common alchemical name for calomel (mercurous chloride), considered a "sweetened" form of mercury</note>.

### §. I.

Dulcified sublimate is a **mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> that has been reduced to a white mass by having some of its acidic "spikes" <note>Early modern chemists believed that corrosive substances were composed of sharp, needle-like particles or "spikes" that physically tore at human tissue; "dulcification" was the process of removing or "breaking" these spikes to make the substance safe for internal use</note> broken off.

§. 2. Pulverize 16 ounces of **corrosive sublimate** <term>corrosivisch Sublimat</term> <note>mercuric chloride, a highly toxic and caustic salt</note> in a marble or glass mortar. Gradually add 12 ounces of **revivified cinnabar-mercury** <term>revivificierten Zinnober-Mercurium</term> <note>liquid mercury that has been recovered or "revived" from cinnabar (mercury sulfide)</note> to it. Stir the mixture <term>Mengsal</term> with a wooden pestle <term>Stöpsel</term> <note>literally "stopper" or "plug", here used for the stirring tool</note> until no more quicksilver <term>Qvecksilber</term> remains visible. Then pour this grey-colored powder into several vials <term>Phiolen</term> or a **matrass** <term>Matras</term> <note>a long-necked glass laboratory flask</note>, of which two-thirds must remain empty. Place your vessel in sand <note>a sand-bath, which allowed for even, indirect heat distribution</note>; give it a very weak fire at first, and then strengthen it up to the third degree <note>in historical chemistry, the 'third degree' referred to a strong heat, usually used for sublimation or distillation</note>. Continue in this state for 5 hours to **sublimate** <term>sublimiren</term> and **dulcify** <term>abzusüßen</term> <note>literally "to sweeten"; to remove the harsh, corrosive qualities of a chemical</note> the material. Then allow your vessels to cool, break them, and discard a little bit of earth at the bottom as something useless. Also separate that which has gathered <note>original: "angeflogene"; referring to the matter that rose as vapor and condensed</note> in the neck of the vials and the matrass, and save it for ointments for the sca— <note>The text likely cuts off at "Krätze," the German word for scabies or similar itchy skin conditions</note>

### §. 3.

One must **NB.** <note>Latin "nota bene"; note well</note> never pound the **corrosive sublimate** <term>Corrosivische Sublimat</term> in a metal mortar, because it would corrode <note>original: "benagen", literally "gnaw at"</note> it and strip away a portion that would harm the operation; glass, marble, and stone mortars are far better suited, as they cannot leave any harmful impression on the matter.

...take **mercury sublimate** <term>mercurium sublimatum</term> <note>original: "curium sublimatum"; a toxic compound of mercury and chlorine</note>; and if we have added almost a little more of it than we intended, the remainder will stay behind unmixed.

### §. 5.

If one uses a **matrass** <term>Matras</term> <note>a long-necked glass laboratory flask</note> for the operation, one must first remove half of the neck. If it were made in a common matrass, much of the soot would not be able to rise so high and would fall back onto the **sublimate** <term>Sublimat</term> in the middle, preventing it from being properly **sweetened** <note>original: "absüssen"; the alchemical process of removing "sharp" corrosive properties to make a substance safe for medicine</note>, because this soot contains the sharpest elements. Conversely, this soot rises very easily in matrasses with short necks. Two-thirds of every vessel must remain empty, otherwise the **mercury** <term>Mercurius</term>, which is rarefied like a spirit, would burst them. Because that which settles on the neck of the **vials** <term>Phiolen</term> is far too sharp to be taken internally, it can be added to ointments for **mange** <term>Räude</term> or **skin rashes** <term>Zitter-Mähler</term> <note>likely referring to shingles or tetter; skin conditions involving eruptions or "trembling" sensations</note>.

### §. 6.

The sweetened **sublimate** <term>Sublimat</term> is driven upward by the fire far more easily than the **corrosive** <term>corrisivische</term> kind, because it contains fewer **acids** <term>acida</term>. For the sublimation itself, one would not need to fire for more than approximately three hours; however, the process is not finished with the **sublimation** <term>Sublimation</term> alone. Instead, the matter must circulate for several hours in **matrasses** <term>Matras</term> or vials, so that the acidic spikes of the corrosive sublimate strike against the small mercurial spheres quite firmly and break them <note>The author uses a mechanical metaphor here, imagining the "sharp" acid particles being physically blunted by contact with the mercury</note>.

### §. 14.

If, instead of the 12 ounces of **mercury** <term>Quecksilber</term> that I commanded to be mixed with 16 ounces of **corrosive sublimate** <term>corrosivischen Sublimat</term> in this operation, one takes no more than 10: then the **sublimate**, after the required three-fold **sublimation** <term>Sublimation</term> <note>the process of heating a substance until it becomes vapor and then collecting the cooled solid</note>, will be far more **crystalline** <term>Chrystallinern</term> and more **purging** than it usually is. Therefore, I maintain that the **sweet sublimate** <term>Sublimatum dulce</term> <note>a milder, less toxic form of mercury, known today as calomel</note> made according to my given **description** (where one adds 12 ounces of raw **mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> to 16 ounces of **corrosive sublimate**) is much better—even if it does not purge—than the version where no more than 10 ounces of raw **mercury** are added to 16 ounces of **corrosive sublimate**.

### §. 16.

I hold the same opinion regarding the **sweet sublimate** <note>original: "Sublimato dulci"</note> that has only been **sublimated** <note>refined through heating into vapor and cooling back into a solid</note> twice: while the **acids** <note>original: "acida"</note> have indeed found enough space in it, they have not been sufficiently broken down. Consequently, this **sublimate** has far more **purging power** <note>original: "Purgir-Krafft"</note> than if it had been sublimated three times. Many **recommend** <note>original: "recommendiren"</note> it exceedingly for **venereal diseases** <term>Venerische Kranckheiten</term> <note>specifically syphilis</note> for this reason. However, if it must indeed be purged in such cases, we do not lack for such [remedies]...

§. 1.

It was so well-distributed within the **sublimates** that not the slightest trace of it could be noticed; however, as soon as they were rarefied by the fire, the earth was separated from them and **precipitated** <note>settled or fell out of the vapor</note> onto the bottom of the **matrass**. §. 13. If, however, deeply rooted pox <note>original: *Pocken*; here referring to syphilitic sores or pustules</note> are present, which have already spread their <term>malignancy</term> <note>original: *malignitæt*</note> into many parts of the body; if there are swellings, pustules covered with a skin, poisonous and disgusting ulcers; if the hair falls out; if one feels great pains in the head and limbs; if one is melancholy, heavy, and quite stiff; if one has <term>malignant hemorrhoids</term> <note>original: *hæmorrhoides malignas*</note>; and if <term>chancres</term> <note>original: *Scheeren*; sores or hard ulcers</note> and swollen glands are to be found in several places: in a word, if it is certain that it is the "formal" French disease <note>syphilis in its advanced or secondary stage</note>, because <term>gonorrhea</term> <note>original: *Gonorrhée*; at the time, gonorrhea and syphilis were often thought to be different stages of the same disease</note> or swollen glands are present, or pustules on the genitals spread far without much discharge or oozing: then I know from long and extensive experience, having sought to cure this illness in all sorts of ways, that there is no better remedy for it than to induce a good and strong <term>salivation</term> <note>original: *Speichel-Fluß*; a treatment where mercury was used to make the patient produce massive amounts of saliva to "purge" the disease</note> through smearing and rubbing <note>original: *frictionibus*; the application of mercury ointments to the skin</note>, as is customary; after the patient has been well <term>prepared</term> <note>original: *præpariret*</note> beforehand with bloodletting, <term>purging</term> <note>original: *Purgiren*</note>, and baths. For one often sees that those who, in such cases, are satisfied with the <term>Panacea</term> <note>the milder mercurial medicine mentioned on the previous page</note> only half-recover and must seek medical treatment anew; either because they were not given a sufficiently strong or long salivation, or because the <term>Panacea</term>—whose "air-holes" <note>the author uses a physical metaphor for the medicine's capacity</note> are already half-full—is not powerful enough to remove the <term>acidic salts</term> <note>original: *sauren Saltze*; according to the medical theory of the time, diseases were caused by an imbalance of salts and acids in the blood</note> which are the primary source of the French disease.

<margin>§. 2. Use. Dosage.</margin>

§. 2. Dissolve 16 ounces of **revived mercury from cinnabar** <note>mercury extracted from its ore, cinnabar (mercuric sulfide), which was considered purer for medicinal use than common quicksilver</note> in a glass **cucurbit** <term>Cucurbit; a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</term> with 18 to 20 ounces of **spirit of nitre** <note>original: *Spiritu nitri*; known today as nitric acid</note>. Once the dissolution is complete, pour filtered salt water over it, in which 10 ounces of **sea salt** have been dissolved in two **small measures** <note>original: *Mäßlein*; a regional liquid measure roughly equivalent to a pint</note> of water. To all of this, add half an ounce of **volatile spirit of sal ammoniac** <note>original: *Spiritum volatilem von Salarmoniac*; a solution of ammonium carbonate/ammonia</note>; this will produce a very white **precipitate** <note>original: *Präcipitat*; a solid substance that "falls out" of a liquid solution during a chemical reaction</note>, which must be allowed to settle sufficiently. Once the water has been poured off by tilting the vessel, wash it several times with spring water and let it dry in the shade. It is used to induce **salivation** <note>original: *Speichel-Fluß*; the intentional induction of excessive drooling was a standard, albeit grueling, treatment for syphilis and other "blood" diseases</note>; it causes a little vomiting; one administers 14 to 15 **grains** <note>a unit of weight, approximately 0.06 grams</note> in pills. It is also added to **ointments** <note>original: *Pomade*</note> for **shingles** <note>original: *Zittermähler*; skin eruptions or rashes</note> and **scabies** <note>original: *Kräze*; the "itch," caused by skin mites</note>, specifically half to 2 **drachms** <note>approximately 3.9 grams each</note> mixed into one ounce of ointment.

<margin>Note Well</margin>

§. 9. If, out of curiosity, one throws **spirit of vitriol** <term>spirit of vitriol: sulfuric acid</term> onto the common red precipitate that we have just described, a dissolution will occur. This is because the spirit of vitriol, when it is combined with the **spirit of nitre** <term>spirit of nitre: nitric acid</term> left behind in the precipitate, becomes **aqua fortis** <term>aqua fortis: literally "strong water," a potent acid capable of dissolving most metals</term>, which can invisibly dissolve the mercury particles. However, no **ebullition** <term>ebullition: the bubbling or effervescence seen during a chemical reaction</term> will occur during this dissolution, because the **mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> has already been so rarefied <note>original: "rarificirt"; made less dense or more porous</note> by an acid that the spirit of vitriol merely makes it fluid and does it no further "violence" <note>original: "Gewalt"; a term used to describe the aggressive action of a solvent on a solid</note>. The dissolution is as clear as any other solution of mercury, except that it looks somewhat red; and one can apply the same preparations here that are performed with the dissolution of **quicksilver** <note>original: "Qvecksilber"</note> in aqua fortis.

### §. 18. Usage. <margin>§. 18. Usage.</margin>

The green precipitate <note>original: "præcipitat"</note> is used especially for seminal discharge <note>original: "Saamen-Fluß"; in this period, this often referred to symptoms of gonorrhea or spermatorrhea</note>. Many also give it at the onset of strangury <note>original: "Strangurie," a condition characterized by painful, frequent, and sparse urination</note>, and they continue with it every second or third day until the condition is driven away. However, I am of the opinion that one should rather wait to administer it until the discharge has flowed for at least 15 days, because the remedy causes blockages too quickly if taken right at the start. Moreover, an emetic <note>original: "Vomitiv," a substance that induces vomiting</note> given so many times exhausts the patient too much and sometimes ruins their stomach. Like all other mercurial preparations <note>original: "Mercurialische præparationes"</note>, it must be taken in pills or morsels <note>small pieces of food used to disguise medicine</note>, and never in a drink; otherwise, it would stick to the teeth, causing them to either become loose or resulting in a slight flow of saliva <note>original: "Speichel-Fluß," a reference to salivation, a common side effect of mercury treatment</note>. One can also place it in a suitable conserve <note>a medicinal preserve made with sugar</note>, or a purging electuary <note>original: "Purgir-Latwerge," a paste made of medicinal powders mixed with honey or syrup</note> (such as the *confection Hamech* <note>a traditional purgative formula originating from Arabic medicine</note>), or in pills. The purging power tempers its vomiting power and gives it more of a tendency toward downward evacuation. However, since the primary effect stems from the vomiting produced,

# P. Another Mercurial Oil.

->§. 1.<-

This preparation is nothing other than **corrosive sublimate** <note>mercuric chloride, a highly toxic and caustic mercury salt</note>, which has been dissolved by **spirit of wine** <note>original: "Spiritu vini"; ethanol or high-proof alcohol</note>.

§. 2. Finely powder one ounce of **corrosive sublimate** and pour it into a **matrass** <term>matrass</term> <note>a round-bottomed glass flask with a long neck, used in distillation and digestion</note>. # R. Remarks.

->§. 1.<-

Because the **sublimate** is a **mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> stuffed with **acids** <note>Latin: "acidis"</note>, a portion of it is dissolved in common water: because these acids loosen it apart and turn it into something like a salt. However, because it does not have enough acid to allow this mercury to be brought to a complete **dissolution** <note>Latin: "Dissolution"</note>, the densest part remains at the bottom. One filters the **liquid** <note>original: "liqvorem"</note> so that it becomes quite pure, as it must then be as clear and bright as spring water.

If, out of curiosity, you pour **spirit of sal ammoniac** <term>spirit of sal ammoniac</term><note>an aqueous solution of ammonia</note> into the **vial** <note>original: "Phiol"</note> of red **precipitate** which we just mentioned, and stir the liquid slightly, it will immediately turn white, and you will have a white precipitate. §. 3. Because the oil of tartar <term>oil of tartar</term><note>a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</note> is a dissolved alkali <note>original: "alkali"</note>, it breaks the sharp points of the acid <note>original: "acidi"</note> which previously held the mercury <note>original: "Mercurium"</note> aloft unnoticed, serving as its metaphorical float. Because the mercury now has nothing left to keep it suspended, it falls to the bottom by its own weight. The same thing happens if one pours spirit of sal ammoniac <term>spirit of sal ammoniac</term><note>an aqueous solution of ammonia</note> onto another portion of the dissolution <note>original: "Dissolution"</note> of corrosive sublimate <note>original: "corrosivischen Sublimat"</note>: For because this spirit is likewise an alkali, it has exactly the same effect as that possessed by the oil of tartar.

§. 4. Although all alkalis agree in that they break and destroy acids <note>original: "acida"</note>, their actions always maintain a certain distinction. This is observed in these many-colored precipitates <note>original: "præcipitaten"</note>: the difference in their colors can be attributed to nothing else but the fact that, as the acids are broken in different ways by the alkalis, they arrange, order, and shape <note>original: "figuriren"</note> the particles of the precipitated body in such a way that they create entirely different reflections of light.

§. 5. # Notes.

->§. 5.<-

**The** word Regulus means as much as "Kingly" / and this name is given to the densest and hardest materials of many minerals and metals. <note>The term "Regulus" comes from the Latin for "Little King," so named by alchemists because it represents the "pure" metallic heart of an ore, sitting beneath the slag like a king on a throne.</note>

->§. 6.<-

<margin><image-desc>stylized decorative mark or manicule</image-desc></margin>One’s intention with this preparation is to open the <term>Antimony|A brittle, silvery-white metalloid used in medicine and metallurgy</term> and to purify it of the many coarse sulfurs with which it is stuffed. For this reason, one calcines it <note>Heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its chemical structure or remove impurities.</note> with tartar and saltpeter, which burn easily / and carry away a large portion of this sulfur with them. The remainder stays in the slag / which we intend to prove in the following process.

->§. 7.<-

One pours the mixture into the **melting crucible** bit by bit / because one fears / that if everything were put in at once / the detonation would strike far too violently / the matter would expand <note>original: "rarificirte," meaning the substance would rapidly increase in volume or "thin out" as it turns to gas.</note> / and therefore overflow from the **melting crucible**.

->§. 8.<-

The detonation arises from the bond / where the volatile particles of the saltpeter and the sulfur of the antimony and salt of tartar have been united with one another: But because there is little saltpeter compared to so much sulfurous matter / only a very slight ignition results.

### C. Another Process for Making the Antimonial King.

#### §. 1.

## Observations.

### Section 3.

One must use this method when one wishes to produce a great deal of **regulus of antimony** <term>the metallic form of antimony, separated from its mineral ore</term> at once. Because the **tartar** <term>potassium bitartrate, used here as a flux to aid melting</term> and **saltpeter** <term>potassium nitrate, a powerful oxidizer</term> are combined with the **antimony** in a much larger dose than occurred in the previously described process, the **detonation** <note>the rapid, energetic combustion and sparking that occurs when these chemicals react</note> must be much stronger; this is because the amount of **saltpeter** more closely matches the amount of its **sulfur** <note>original: "Schwefels seiner"; referring to the sulfur naturally present in the antimony ore</note> than in the first process.

Section 4. The mortar or pot must be large, because the material becomes very loosened and expanded during the **detonation**. Therefore, I allow it to burn so that while a large portion of the volatile essence is dispersed, the remainder takes up less space and can fit into a moderately sized **melting crucible**.

Section 5. One must take great care that the material is entirely melted together before removing the fire from the **melting crucible**. When one purifies it with iron, not only are many sulfurous parts—which are the greatest hindrance to its crystallization—removed, but a very hard and dense portion of iron remains within it. This makes the *antimony* much firmer and more enclosed than it was before. In this way, the purification unfolds the natural crystals of the *antimony*, which are shaped like a star; the iron, however, keeps them stretched out because of its hardness. This is why the <term>Martial Regulus of Antimony</term> <note>A metallic form of antimony produced by using iron ("Mars" in alchemy) to strip away impurities</note> is far harder than the other varieties.

§. 12. In short: The crystals appear in the shape of a star upon the <term>Martial Regulus of Antimony</term> <note>original: "Martialischen Regulo Antimonii"</note> because they exist with this very shape within the *antimony* itself. This star does not look quite the same in the common <term>Regulus of Antimony</term>, even if it is purified just as well, because its particles do not have the same extension and attraction as those in this version.

§. 13. Little cups and small bowls are made much more easily from the <term>Martial Regulus of Antimony</term> than from other <term>reguli</term>, and that is for the sake of the portion of iron contained within it. For since this metal is joined with the hardest part of the *antimony*, it does not make it so <term>brittle</term> <note>original: "sauer." ## F. Poterius’s Stomachic.
<note>Stomachicum Poterii: A famous medicinal preparation named after the 17th-century French physician Pierre Potier. It was used as a tonic for the stomach and to treat fevers.</note>

->§. 1.<-

This operation produces a <term>fixed</term> <note>In alchemy, "fixed" refers to a substance that has been made resistant to the transformative power of fire or made non-volatile</note> <term>Martial Regulus of Antimony</term> <note>A metallic form of antimony purified using iron ("Mars")</note> blended with gold.

->§. 2.<-

Take 4 ounces of the <term>Martial Regulus of Antimony</term>, half an ounce of finely powdered gold, and 12 ounces of <term>Saltpeter</term> <note>Potassium nitrate, a common oxidizing agent in early chemistry</note>. Powder the <term>Regulus</term> and saltpeter and mix them very thoroughly with the gold. Let the <term>crucible</term> <note>original: "Schmelz-Tiegel"; a ceramic container used for high-heat reactions</note> become glowing hot over burning coals in a furnace. Throw in one spoonful of the mixture, and a small <term>detonation</term> <note>A rapid, crackling combustion or "puffing" reaction common when saltpeter reacts with minerals</note> will occur. Once that has passed, throw in another spoonful, and continue in this manner until the entire material is in the crucible. Let it <term>calcine</term> <note>Heat a substance to a high temperature to change its physical or chemical state, typically through oxidation</note> for one hour. Afterward, pour it into plenty of warm water and let it soak for some time so that the saltpeter within it is dissolved. Pour off the water by tilting the vessel, and wash the powder remaining at the bottom many more times. Then, dry it in the sun or in the shade. Calcine it again in a new crucible for one hour, stirring it with an iron <term>spatula</term>. The operation will then be complete. Keep this material; it is the **Stomachicum Poterii**.

## Observations.

### §. 4.

One must calcine <note>To heat a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile components or change its physical state.</note> the antimony under a small forge-hood in order to avoid the fumes escaping from it, as they are very harmful to the chest <note>The respiratory system; the vapors produced when roasting antimony contain toxic arsenic and sulfur oxides.</note>.

§. 5. This calcination is undertaken so that one may free the antimony from its coarse sulfur, which would prevent its <term>vitrification <note>original: "Bergläserung"; the process of turning a substance into a glass-like material.</note></term>. Some add borax <note>original: "Borris"</note> to this gray powder, others raw antimony, and still others sulfur; however, all this is done so that it may be turned into glass more easily.

§. 6. Vitrification does not occur until the antimonial particles have become denser and stiffer than they were before, so that the <term>fire-particles <note>original: "Feuer-Theilgen"; a reference to early chemical theories (like the corpuscular or phlogiston theories) which held that fire was a physical substance made of tiny particles that could enter and change a material.</note></term> moving back and forth within the matter form straight air-pores <note>original: "Lufft-Löcher"</note>, which then remain in that state when the antimony has cooled again. This shape of the air-pores is precisely what causes transparency, because it creates a free path for the light to pass through.

§. 7. Sulfur and antimony help with melting; for this reason, some add them to the matter, though in very small

This difference in weight comes from the nature of the saltpeter: For the more <term>volatile <note>Easily evaporated; in alchemy, volatile parts "flee" the fire, while "fixed" parts remain.</note></term> particles this mineral salt contains, the more antimonial particles it can lift up; but now, the refined 
<margin>Saltpeter:</margin> **Sulfur** is far more volatile than the common kind; therefore, the amount of the Liver of Antimony produced from it is much smaller.

§. 12. The Liver of Antimony made from common saltpeter is far redder, and comes closer to the color of an animal’s liver than that which is made from refined 
<margin>Saltpeter:</margin> **Sulfur**. This must certainly arise from the <term>fixed salt <note>original: "fixes Saltz"; the solid, non-evaporating residue of a substance after heating.</note></term>, of which there is more in the former than in the latter, because common saltpeter—as we will report in its proper place—carries much fixed salt, which moreover makes the material heavy in weight.

§. 13. As far as the power of these Livers of Antimony is concerned, they are not so very noticeably different from one another: Yet the one made from refined saltpeter is more <term>emetic <note>original: "vomitivisch"; inducing vomiting.</note></term> than the other.

§. 14. §. 15. §. 16. Take note of this: if you pour 4 ounces of prepared <term>antimony <note>A metallic element that, in this era, was frequently used in medicine to purge the body.</note></term> into a <term>measure <note>original: "Maßlein"; a historical unit of liquid volume, roughly equivalent to a quart or a liter depending on the region.</note></term> of wine, the wine will not draw out more emetic power than if you only used one ounce; because the wine draws in only as much substance as it is capable of holding, while the rest remains sitting at the bottom, and nothing of it dissolves until one pours fresh wine onto it.

<margin>NB. <note>An abbreviation for the Latin "nota bene," meaning "note well."</note></margin>
Thus, experience teaches us that one ounce of *Crocus Metallorum* <note>Latin: "Saffron of Metals," a chemical preparation of antimony.</note> or *Liver of Antimony* is capable of flavoring more than just a single measure of wine; rather, one need only pour an equal amount of fresh wine onto the remaining material after the liquid has been poured off <gloss>by tilting the vessel</gloss>, and let it <gloss>steep</gloss> for two to three days. In this way, one obtains an infusion just as emetic as the first one was.

§. 17. One can pour fresh wine over a single batch of *Saffron of Metals* nine times, and it will still always become emetic.

<margin>NB.</margin>
If one then <term>calcines <note>Heating a substance to high temperatures in the air to change its chemical properties or reduce it to powder.</note></term> the material for a quarter of an hour in an unglazed earthenware bowl over a small fire, and stirs the material constantly with an iron spatula, one can bring it back into a <gloss>molten state</gloss> as before and prepare an emetic wine with it.

[It never loses] its strength; therefore, they always use the same [substance] and pour new wine onto the old material as soon as they have used up their <term>emetic wine <note>A medicinal wine infused with antimony, intended to induce vomiting to "purge" the body of ill humors.</note></term>, even up to 70 times if they think it necessary. However, they deceive themselves: for one only needs to pour 8 to 9 <term>infusions <note>original: "infuſiones"; the process of extracting chemical properties by soaking a substance in a liquid like wine.</note></term> onto the same material from this process, and if it is tried more times thereafter, the emetic wine will already have less strength, and it will keep decreasing more and more. This is because the most soluble <term>salt and sulfur particles <note>In the chemistry of this era, "salt" and "sulfur" were seen as fundamental building blocks of matter representing stability and flammability/potency.</note></term> have already been so thoroughly dissolved in the first <term>solvents <note>original: "Menstruis"; the liquids used to extract the active medicinal properties.</note></term> that those which follow do not find much more soluble matter, and one is left with a wine that carries very little emetic power. This has often been the reason why one had to give some patients up to 6 <term>ounces <note>A standard unit of pharmaceutical weight, roughly 31 grams.</note></term> of emetic wine if they were meant to vomit; from this, it appears that the blame is often placed on a strong and hardy <term>constitution <note>original: "Temperament"; the physical makeup and internal balance of a patient's body.</note></term> when the fault actually lies in the medicine itself.

§. 19. This circumstance has given rise to the belief in some that a strong <term>dose <note>original: "Doſis"; the specific amount of medicine given at one time.</note></term> works neither more strongly nor longer than a lighter one, because one would vomit up everything taken at the start of the <term>operation <note>In this context, the "operation" refers to the medical process or the body's reaction to the drug.</note></term>. However, experience always teaches us the opposite, and one has often had to observe very dangerous incidents that arose because people based their actions on this <term>proposition <note>original: "Lehr-Satz"; a formal rule or theory of medical practice.</note></term>.

Pour your white liquid little by little into a funnel lined with **blotting paper** <note>original: "Lösch-Papier"</note>; the water will strain through, leaving a white powder behind in the **filter** <note>original: "filtro"</note>. §. 3. The reason / that one can give for this / is this: because the air-holes <note>pores</note> of the **Antimony** <note>original: "Antimonii"</note> are large / the matter is soft because of the much sulfur contained within / and the spikes of the **spirit of nitre** <note>original: "Salpeter-Spiritu"; nitric acid</note> are all too hard / and cannot <gloss>indeed</gloss> cut and divide its particles as required; therefore, one needs far coarser knives for it / than the fine spikes of **aqua regia** <note>original: "aquæ regiæ"; "royal water," a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids</note> are <gloss>than</gloss>.

<margin>§. 6. Instant aqua regia <note>original: "Aqua regia extemporanea."</note></margin>
§. 6. If one has not made a regular **aqua regia**, one only needs to mix approximately a 6th part of good **spirit of salt** <note>original: "Spiritu Salis"; hydrochloric acid</note> and this matter with **spirit of nitre** or **aqua fortis** <note>nitric acid</note> / thus one will obtain an **aqua regia** / that will act just as well as the other.

§. 7. The **matrass** <term>Matrass: A long-necked glass flask used in early chemistry for boiling and distillation.</term> must be large enough / so that the matter, which is significantly **rarefied** <note>original: "rarificiret"; expanded or made less dense through chemical reaction</note> / does not escape through the neck. The **dissolution** <note>the process of dissolving or breaking down</note> would also proceed without fire, but very slowly: and one must avoid its vapors / as they are very harmful to the chest / as much as possible.

§. 8. However, there is no actual dissolution occurring here / but only a separation of the antimonial particles: **Aqua regia** cannot keep them suspended / because the **molecules** <note>original: "moleculæ"; small particles or clusters of matter</note> are all too large: It only holds very little at the top / which is **precipitated** <note>original: "præcipitiret"; forced out of the solution to settle at the bottom</note> / when one pours water into the **matrass**.

§. 9. The white color comes from the order and arrangement which the **acids** <note>original: "acida"</note> have given to the particles of the matter / and [from which they] reflect the light back on all sides: whereas by contrast the raw **antimony** <note>original: "Antimonium"</note> is black / namely because its air-holes <note>pores</note> are suited to capture the light / so it is lost inside / and does not return back to our eyes: as many times as the **antimony** is **rarefied** <note>original: "rarificirt"; expanded or thinned</note> by the **acids** to the greatest extent possible / it becomes white / as can be seen in many of the following **operations** <note>original: "Operationibus"; chemical procedures</note>.

->§. 5.<-

In this preparation, one uses 3 pounds of <term>saltpeter</term> <note>Nitre or potassium nitrate, used here as an oxidizing agent</note> to one pound of <term>antimony</term> <note>A brittle, silvery-white metalloid used to create various medicinal compounds</note>, so that after the volatile parts have risen, much fixed saltpeter remains / which binds the antimony / and prevents it / from being an <term>emetic</term> <note>original: *Vomitiv*; a substance that causes vomiting. By "binding" the antimony, the chemist ensures it acts on the skin rather than the stomach</note>.

§. 6. Three parts saltpeter to one part <term>antimony</term> <note>original: *Antimonio*</note> do not cause such a strong <term>detonation</term> <note>A rapid chemical reaction or "flash" that occurs when these substances are heated together</note> nor such a strong decrease of the antimonial parts / as when one uses the parts in equal weight. The reason for this is / that there is too little antimonial <term>sulfur</term> <note>In early modern chemistry, "sulfur" referred to the flammable principle or "soul" of a mineral</note> for this quantity of saltpeter / and that a part of this sulfur is held back in the fixed saltpeter / which does not burn: For the <term>volatile</term> <note>The parts of a substance that easily evaporate or turn into vapor when heated</note> part of the saltpeter burns only in proportion to the sulfur / with which it has been mixed. As proof of this, the following can serve: if one <margin>horizontal ink mark with hook</margin> throws onto burning coals a little saltpeter / which has been extracted from the washings of the <term>Diaphoretic Antimony</term> <note>original: *Antimonii Diaphoretici*; a preparation intended to induce sweating</note> / it will burn once more / because it has found new sulfur in the coal / and has united with its <margin>stylized ink flourish</margin> remaining volatile part. We shall have more to say at length regarding the ignition of saltpeter in the chapter on this salt.

# O. Butter or Ice-Oil of Antimony.

->§. 2.<-

Powder and mix 6 ounces of **regulus of antimony** <term>the metallic form of the element antimony</term> with 16 ounces of **corrosive sublimate** <term>mercury(II) chloride, a highly toxic and corrosive compound</term>. Put this mixture into a glass **flask** <note>original: *Kolben*</note> and leave half of it empty. Place your flask in sand, and once you have attached a **receiver** <note>original: *Recipienten*; a second vessel to collect the distillate</note> and **luted** <term>sealed the joints with a special clay or paste to make them airtight</term> the joints well, one must initially start a small fire beneath it to heat the flask, and afterwards increase it to the second degree. In this way, a **liquid** <note>original: *liquor*</note> will come out, which is delivered into the receiver. Continue with that same degree of fire until nothing...

## Remarks.

### §. 4.*

**A** few days after the two ingredients have been mixed together, the material becomes quite noticeably heated. This is because the **acidic spikes** <note>The author uses the "corpuscular" theory of the time, which imagined acids as tiny particles with sharp points that physically pierced other substances</note> of the **corrosive sublimate** <term>mercury(II) chloride</term> forcefully penetrate and drive apart the particles of the **antimonial regulus** <term>the metallic form of antimony</term>. Thus, the same kind of heat is produced as naturally occurs when an **acid** <note>original: *acidum*</note> penetrates an **alkali** <note>original: *alkali*</note>, or when two dense bodies sharply strike and rub against one another.

## Recipe for Mineral Bezoar.
<note>original: "R. Bezoardicum Minerale"; "R." stands for "Recipe" (take), and Mineral Bezoar was a popular 17th-century chemical medicine made from antimony, named after the bezoar stone for its supposed alexipharmic or poison-neutralizing properties.</note>

### §. 1.

Melt two ounces of **Butter of Antimony** <term>Butter Antimonii</term> <note>antimony trichloride, a thick, oily, and highly corrosive substance</note> in hot ashes, pour it into a **vial** <term>Phiole</term> or **matrass** <term>Matras</term> <note>a long-necked glass flask</note>, and pour good **Spirit of Nitre** <term>Spiritum nitri</term> <note>nitric acid</note> upon it drop by drop until the material is completely dissolved. Usually, one requires just as much **Spirit of Nitre** as **Butter of Antimony**. During the **dissolution** <term>Dissolution</term> <note>the process of dissolving the solid into liquid</note>, such vapors will rise that one must avoid them with the greatest possible diligence; for this reason, the vessel should be placed under the chimney. Pour your **dissolution** into a glass **cucurbit** <term>Cucurbit</term> <note>the lower, gourd-shaped part of a still</note> or into a flat basin, and let it evaporate to dryness there in a very gentle sand-bath <note>a container of sand heated by a fire to provide even, moderate heat to a glass vessel</note>. A white mass will remain; let this cool, then pour two ounces of **Spirit of Nitre** upon it. Place the vessel back in the sand and let the moisture evaporate as before. For the last time, pour two ounces of **Spirit of Nitre** onto the white mass and let the moisture evaporate. Then increase the fire slightly and **calcine** <term>calcinirt</term> <note>to heat a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile components and reduce it to a powder</note> the material for half an hour. Afterward, remove it from the fire, and you will obtain two ounces of white powder, which must be kept in a well-sealed **vial**.

### §. 2. 

It is a good sweat-inducing agent <note>original Latin: "Sudoriferum"</note>, and serves the same purpose for which diaporetic antimony <term>Antimonium Diaphoreticum: a preparation used in early medicine to induce perspiration and "purge" the body of disease</term> is useful. The dose <note>original: "Dosis"</note> is administered from 6 to 20 grains in broth or another suitable liquid <note>original Latin: "liquore"</note>.

## Remarks.

### §. 3.

The spirit of nitre <term>Spiritus nitri: nitric acid</term>, when it is added to the salty and vitriolic acids of the butter of antimony <term>Butter Antimonii: antimony trichloride, a thick, oily substance</term>, creates a kind of royal water <note>original Latin: "aquae regiae," a highly corrosive mixture of acids</note> that effectively dissolves the metallic antimony <note>original: "Regulum Antimonii," the pure metal separated from its ore</note>.

### §. 4.

The spirits of vitriol and salt <note>sulfuric and hydrochloric acids</note> alone would be neither strong nor plentiful enough to completely dissolve the antimony; instead, they would only settle into it if they were not combined with the spirit of nitre, through which they then act much more forcefully. For they penetrate and push all the small particles of the mineral aside, making them entirely unsuited and unreceptive to achieving the fullest dissolution. Since a great effervescence <note>original: "Effervescenz," a bubbling chemical reaction</note> occurs during this penetration, much like in the dissolution of mercury; therefore, let it be said that one should always pour the spirit of nitre on little by little, because otherwise the material might boil over the glass. §. 2. Pour 6 ounces of very finely powdered *antimony* into a glass retort: pour 4 ounces of good spirit of salt <term>Salz-Spiritum: hydrochloric acid</term> and an equal amount of corrosive oil of vitriol <term>Vitriol-Oel: concentrated sulfuric acid</term> over it; stir them together; seal the retort; and place it in sand in such a way that the beak points upward. <margin><unclear>ink scribbles</unclear></margin> Maintain a small digestion-fire <term>Digestion: a process of gentle heating to encourage chemical breakdown</term> beneath it for 24 hours; after this, let the beak of your retort hang down; open it, and attach a glass receiver <term>Recipient: a vessel used to collect the products of distillation</term>; seal the joint with a wet bladder; create a small fire beneath it; let the heat rise from below until it reaches the second degree <note>in early chemistry, the "second degree" of heat was roughly the temperature of a warm sand bath, stronger than a water bath but not yet glowing hot</note>, and thus a white *liquid* <note>original Latin: "liquor"</note> will pass over. It is applied using a quill.

## Chapter 10.
# A. Concerning Arsenic.

->§. 1.<-

<margin><image-desc>Handwritten symbol in the margin resembling a stylized cursive 'M' with a descending flourish.</image-desc></margin>
**Arsenic** <note>original: *Arsenicum*</note> is a **mineral matter** <note>In early chemistry, minerals were categorized by their "principles."</note> that consists of much **sulfur** <note>original: *Schwefel*; refers to the oily, combustible principle in alchemy</note> and a **caustic salt** <note>original: *ätzenden Saltze*; a corrosive or "eating" chemical component</note>. There are three kinds: **White**, which retains the name **arsenic**; **yellow**, which is called **orpiment** <note>original: *Auripigmentum*; used as a pigment and in medicine despite its toxicity</note>; and **red**, which is called **realgar** <note>original: *Realgal*</note> or **sandarach**. The whitest is the strongest among them all and sometimes glitters like **crystal**. Some identify a fourth type of arsenic as a "yellow arsenic" that is otherwise an **orpiment**, maintaining only this distinction: that it is not as shiny or light-colored.

# C. Arsenical Sublimate.

## §. 1.

This process involves arsenic from which its "worst" sulfur <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" often refers to the combustible or impure principle of a substance rather than just the element sulfur.</note> is removed, and which is raised to the top of a matrass <term>matrass: a long-necked glass flask used in chemistry for distillation or sublimation</term> by means of fire.

## §. 2.

Pour as much coarsely powdered arsenic as you wish into a melting crucible, which you must place over a small fire under the chimney <note>original: Feuer-Esse; a hearth or forge equipped with a flue</note>; let it calcine <term>calcine: to heat a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile impurities or to change its physical state</term>, and let approximately one-third of the matter smoke away. However, take care as best as you can to guard against these evil fumes <note>arsenic fumes are highly toxic; the author is providing a safety warning</note>. Pour the powdered residue into a mortar, weigh it, and add an equal amount of decrepitated salt <term>decrepitated salt: common salt (sodium chloride) that has been heated until it stops crackling, which removes its internal moisture</term> to it. Put this mixture into a matrass, and leave two-thirds of it empty. Place it on warm sand in a small furnace, starting with a small fire underneath at first, but gradually increasing it to the third degree <note>the "third degree" of fire refers to a strong heat, typically used to drive off vapors but below the temperature needed to melt the glass or the metals</note>, and let the arsenic sublimate <term>sublimate: the process where a solid turns into vapor and then solidifies again on a cooler surface, effectively purifying it</term>. Continue with this until nothing more rises; the process will be completed within 5 to 6 hours. Let the vessel cool, then break it and collect what has deposited itself at the top of the matrass and save it. What remains at the bottom must be thrown away as useless matter.

If one repeats this sublimation 4 to 5 times, adding [fresh] salt each time, then

# E. The Corrosive Oil of Arsenic

-> §. 1. <-

This liquid <term>liquor|A general term for a liquid or fluid substance</term> is an arsenic that has been permeated by the <term>acids|Latin: acidis</term> of <term>corrosive sublimate|Mercuric chloride, a highly toxic chemical used here to react with the arsenic</term> and has been made into a thick butter.

-> §. 2. <-

Take equal parts arsenic and corrosive sublimate, powder them, mix them together, and pour the mixture into a glass <term>retort|A glass vessel with a long, curved neck used for distilling substances</term>. Place it in sand <note>A sand bath, used to provide even, controlled heat to the glass vessel</note>, attach a <term>receiver|A vessel used to collect the products of distillation</term>, seal the joints well with <term>lute|A paste used to make the apparatus airtight</term>, and distill over a gentle fire a buttery liquid <note>Arsenic trichloride</note> that corresponds to the Butter of Antimony <note>Antimony trichloride, a similar chemical compound known to early chemists</note>. When nothing more comes over, remove the receiver and attach another filled with water; increase the fire, and you will see the <term>mercury|mercurius</term> fall into the water drop by drop. Continue the distillation until nothing more flows out.

-> §. 3. <-

You can use this mercury at any time like any other, though you must have washed and dried it well beforehand.

-> §. 4. <-

The <term>Butter of Arsenic|Arsenic trichloride</term> is a very strong caustic agent and forms a crust <note>German: *Rinden*; referring to an eschar or scab formed by a chemical burn</note> much faster than the Butter of Antimony.

## Remarks.

-> §. 5. <-

In this process, the same thing occurs as happens during the preparation of the Butter of Antimony <note>Antimony trichloride</note> mentioned above: namely, the <term>spirits|In this context, the acidic vapors or "spirit of salt" (hydrochloric acid) contained within the salt</term> of the corrosive sublimate leave the mercury and instead attach themselves to the arsenic, which they draw out into a gummy <term>liquor|liquid</term>. Thereupon the mercury, because it has been set free and finds no <term>sulfur|schwefel; used here as a chemical principle of stability</term> with which it might be fixed <note>made solid or stable</note>, turns into vapors and is condensed in the water.

§. 2. When the stone from which one makes <term>lime</term> has become glowing hot in the kiln, the workers must take care that the fire is maintained at a constant intensity until the stone is completely <term>calcined|calcinirt; burned or reduced to a friable powder by heat</term>. For if the flame—which has begun to travel back and forth between the stones—subsides slightly, and the heat settles before the process has come to an end: they will never again obtain <term>lime</term> from these stones, even if they were to burn a hundred times as much wood as is normally required. This is because, during the fluctuation of the stone's heat, the <term>air-holes|pores or passages within the stone</term>—which a great fire had begun to form—close up again, and the matter sinks down in such a way that it throws everything into confusion. Moreover, the flame cannot rise up within it again, because it no longer finds any <term>interstices|interstitia; small gaps or spaces</term> <note>original: "interstitia"</note> between the stones as there were before. At that point, the matter becomes unfit to mark itself with the <term>fire-particles</term>, because all the small cells in which they could otherwise remain have been broken and destroyed during this confusion.

<margin>§. 10. Objection.</margin>
§. 10. One might perhaps say to me in opposition that the <term>fire-particles|microscopic corpuscles of heat</term> <note>original: "Feuer-Theilgen"</note> which I have lodged in the <term>lime|calcium oxide or quicklime</term> <note>original: "Kalck"</note> are just as unproven as the <term>salt|mineral residue</term> <note>original: "Saltz"</note>: And if I were to allow no salt at all in this <term>calcined stone|stone treated with high heat</term> <note>original: "calcinirten Stein"</note> because I find none within it, then I could just as little establish the presence of these <term>fiery corpuscles|tiny bodies of fire</term> <note>original: "feurigen Cörpergen"</note> for so long as I have not brought them to sight.

<margin>§. 11. Answer.</margin>
§. 11. I answer: There is a great distinction to be noted here: For salt is a matter that allows itself to be packed densely together, and therefore presents itself quite easily to our senses; it can be seen, touched, and tasted. But this is not the case with the fire-particles; these are <term>corpuscles|tiny bodies</term> far too <term>subtle|fine and microscopic</term>, far too rarefied, and far too much in motion to be shown outside of coarse matter. One knows them only by their effects; and if one were to find a means by which they could be specifically packed densely together, they would already cease to be fire-particles, because they would have lost their movement—which is their essential part and absolutely necessary to their nature.

## B. Phagedenic Water or Ulcer Water. <note>original: "Aqua Phagedenica oder ulceraria"; a medicinal lotion used to "eat away" dead tissue in ulcers, from the Greek "phagedaina," meaning a canker</note>

->§. 1.<-

This water is a mixture of **corrosive sublimate** <note>original: "corrosivisches Sublimat"; mercuric chloride, a highly toxic substance used here as an antiseptic and caustic</note> and lime-water.

§. 2. Pour one pound of lime into a large earthenware basin and slake it with 7 to 8 pounds of warm water; after you have allowed the lime to steep for 5 to 6 hours and settle again to the bottom, pour off the water by tilting the vessel; this is now called **lime-water** <note>original: "Kalck-Wasser"; a saturated solution of calcium hydroxide</note>.

<margin>36.</margin>
§. 3. For every pound of such water, one pours 15 to 20 **grains** <note>original: "Gran"; a historical unit of weight approximately equal to 65 milligrams</note> of powdered corrosive sublimate: This initially turns it yellow; afterward, one stirs it together for a long time in a glass or marble **mortar** <note>original: "Mörsel"</note> and uses this **liquid** <note>original: "liquorem"</note> to heal old wounds: It eats away the superfluous flesh; it is also used for **gangrene** <note>original: "kalten Brand"; literally "cold burn," referring to tissue death where the flesh turns black and cold</note>, where one adds wine or sometimes **spirit of vitriol** <note>original: "Vitriol-Spiritum"; an archaic name for sulfuric acid</note> to it.

# Notes.

<margin>§. 4. What is gravel-ash?</margin>
->§. 4.<-

<term>Gravel-ash</term> <note>original: "Grieß-Asche"; a high-quality potash made from the sediment of wine.</note> is nothing other than a <term>calcined tartar</term> <note>Potassium carbonate produced by heating cream of tartar to a high temperature.</note>. It is made by burning wine lees; however, because these lees have fermented more than common tartar due to their fluidity, the extracted salt is also far more penetrating than other salts of tartar, and consequently, it is very well suited for the making of <term>caustics</term> <note>original: "Causticorum"</note>. The lime also contributes much to making them stronger, because the <term>fire particles</term> <note>A historical theory that heat consisted of physical particles that could be trapped in a substance during heating.</note> contained within it mix with this salt and make it even more active and sharp.

§. 5. One must not powder the lime, for one would only drive out the small <term>fire-particles</term> <note>Based on the historical theory that heat consisted of physical particles trapped within a substance.</note> before it even reached the water.

§. 9. But one might ask me: why does the blackness disappear once the **dissolution** <note>The process of a solid being dissolved into a liquid.</note> has occurred?

§. 10. §. 13. Thus, the visible ink disappears because the particles that made it black are dissolved; and the invisible ink, by contrast, appears because the dissolved particles have been revivified.

->§. 1.<-

Flint stones, like other stones, are formed by salts and acidic **liquids** <note>original Latin: "liqvoribus."</note> which penetrate the earth (which is an **alkali** <term>Alkali: A substance that reacts with and neutralizes acids; in this historical context, it refers to the "base" material of the soil.</term>), and combine with it in such a way that from this **mixture** <note>original: "Mengsal."</note> a **mass** <note>original: "Lob." and quench them in common cold water:
Let them become glowing anew and
quench them again, three to four times, or as long
as is required until they allow themselves to be rubbed down
and become an impalpable powder once they have dried.

§. 3. Crystal is **calcined** in the same way,
yet it becomes far more brittle than the flint stones.
One can also extract the <term>liquor</term> <note>A liquid extract or solution of the mineral's essence.</note> and the <term>tincture</term> <note>A medicinal or alchemical infusion containing the "soul" or color of the stone.</note>
from it, which we shall demonstrate immediately
hereafter with the flint stones. They possess
the same virtues.

## Notes.

### §. 4.

The flint stones found in rivers that have differently colored veins are considered the best, because they are said to yield the most **tincture**. <note>In alchemy, a tincture is a concentrated extract or essence believed to contain the medicinal or transformative properties of a substance.</note>

### §. 5.

Flint stones and crystal are far too hard to be powdered in the common way; instead, one must seek means and ways to make these stones soft so that they may then be easily ground down. Cold water makes them brittle if one throws them in while they are completely glowing-hot. This is because the cold of the water—after the <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to remove impurities or make it easier to pulverize.</note> has opened its air-holes [pores]—suddenly closes them again. At that moment, the tiny **fire-particles** <note>original: "Feuer-Cörpergen." This reflects an early "corpuscular" theory where fire was thought to consist of physical particles that could be trapped within the pores of a mineral.</note> swarm to and fro and, like prisoners, attempt to rush out with a great storm and break their small prisons. Because of this, the matter is loosened and becomes crumbly. One repeats this heating to a glow and quenching in water three to four times so that the stones are penetrated in all their small parts and made soft. Some even use wine vinegar instead of water and quench the flint stones or crystal in it.

# C. The Tincture of Flint Stones.

## Section 1.

This operation is an elevation of several particles of flint stones and salt of tartar <note>An alchemical term for potassium carbonate, often derived from the residue in wine barrels.</note> in spirit of wine <note>original: "Spiritu vini," refers to high-proof distilled alcohol.</note>.

## Section 2.

Mix 4 ounces of calcined flint stones, which have been ground into an impalpable <note>A powder so fine that individual grains cannot be felt between the fingers.</note> powder, with 24 ounces of potash <term>potash</term> <note>original: "Grieß-Asche." This refers to crude potassium carbonate, a vital flux used to lower the melting point of minerals.</note>; stir them well together and place this mixture into a large melting crucible; cover it, and set it in a blast furnace. Gradually rake the fire around it, heating it slowly and gently, and finally give it the strongest fire: continue this for 5 hours until the matter has completely melted into a flux. Insert a spatula, pull it out again, and see if the matter has begun to become as transparent as glass. If it is so, pour it into a pre-warmed iron mortar; it will immediately congeal into a hard mass which, while it is still warm, must be powdered, and half of it poured into a very dry and well-warmed <term>matrass</term> <note>A glass flask with a long neck used for chemical reactions.</note>. Pour enough of the best rectified spirit of wine over it so that it stands four fingers high above the substance. Seal your matrass well with another <note>This describes a "double vessel" or circulatory setup where one flask is inverted over another.</note>, whose neck must fit into the one holding the matter: lute <term>lute</term> <note>original: "Berlutirt." To seal a vessel's joints with a paste or bladder to make it airtight.</note> the joints as well as possible with a wet bladder; and place it in

<margin>§. 7. Why it is called the Oil of the Philosophers <note>original: "oleum philosophorum"</note>.</margin>
§. 8. The old chemists <note>alchemists</note> named all preparations involving bricks "philosophical." For, just as they call themselves the true Philosophers <note>original: "Philosophos"</note> above all others (*par excellence*), they believed they must also bestow this fine name upon the Oil of Bricks. This is because bricks normally serve as the construction materials for the furnaces in which they work toward the "Great Work" or the Philosopher’s Stone <term>lapidem philosophicum: the legendary substance alchemists sought to create to transform base metals into gold</term>. For they claim that through this work, they arrive at the true philosophy.
