Then pour the solutions <note>original: "Dissolutions"</note> together, pour them into a glass cucurbit <note>a gourd-shaped chemical vessel</note> or into a Gretz-basin <note>an evaporating dish or wide pan</note>, and let two-thirds of the moisture evaporate over a sand-fire <note>a sand bath used to provide steady, indirect heat</note>, until a very loose little skin <note>a pellicle, which forms on the surface of a liquid when it reaches the point of saturation</note> can be seen upon it. Filter this impregnation and save it for the salt-making and for a <term>Magistery</term> <note>a "magistery" is a refined medicinal substance or precipitate prepared from raw materials with minimal alteration of its internal essence</note>, which we shall treat hereafter.

[cool] place to crystallize. For one will find the purest salt at the bottom of the vessel, which must be separated from the moisture and dried. One then allows a portion of the salty moisture to evaporate <note>original: "verrauchen"; literally "to smoke away" or turn to vapor</note> and the other part to crystallize in a vessel in a cellar. Continue with this evaporating and crystallizing until you have finally evaporated all the moisture, because no more crystals will want to form in it. For the remaining salt is filled with a resinous fat which almost cannot be separated from it; and this is exactly what prevents the crystallization. By all appearances, this fat comes from the earth of the aforementioned **salt-ponds** <note>original: "Salz-Lachen"</note>.

§. 13. If one throws the salt that crystallized first into **oil of tartar** <term>oil of tartar: a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate, used here as a standard alkaline reagent</term>, or another liquid <note>original: "liquorem"</note> that carries a dissolved alkaline salt, its mixing nevertheless causes no disturbance or **effervescence** <note>original: "Ebullition"; the bubbling or "boiling" seen during a chemical reaction</note>. For although sea salt is an **acid** <note>original: "acidum"</note>, its "points" are far too coarse and have too little movement to push the alkaline particles aside and drive them out. <note>In 17th-century chemistry, it was believed that acids had sharp, needle-like structures or "points" that physically interacted with the pores of alkaline substances.</note>

§. 14. ## B. Calcination or Incineration of Common Salt.
<term>Calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in an open vessel to change its properties or reduce it to powder.</term>

->§. 1.<-

<margin>§. 1. Decrepitation.</margin>
<note>Decrepitation is the loud crackling or snapping sound salt makes when heated, caused by the sudden expansion and escape of water trapped inside the crystals.</note>
Heat an unglazed pot until it is red-hot between burning coals: throw approximately one **ounce** <note>original: "Untze"</note> of sea salt into it and cover it; it will then make a loud crackling sound and turn into powder.

...until it glows. This crackling sound is called **decrepitation** <term>decrepitation: the sharp, snapping sound produced when certain minerals or salts are heated, caused by the sudden expansion and escape of water trapped within the crystals</term>. Once it has ceased, pour just as much salt into the pot once more, and continue doing this until you have enough.

§. 2. The pot must always remain glowing hot; once the popping stops, remove it from the fire. After it has cooled again, pour the powder into a well-sealed bottle so that the air does not moisten it once more. People hang it, while warm, in small pouches around the neck, and thereby dry up <note>original: "verzehret"; literally "consumes" or "eats away"</note> the excessive dampness of the brain, as it opens the air-passages <note>early modern medical theory believed that vapors or moisture in the brain could be cleared through the pores of the skin or by opening the "channels" of the head</note>. It is also used in various **chemical processes** <term>chemical processes: laboratory operations or experiments involving the transformation of substances</term>.

# Remarks.

->§. 3.<-

The crackling of the salt when it is in the fire is caused by the moisture that is constantly hidden within it: because as it is **rarefied** <term>rarefied: the process by which a substance becomes less dense, such as when water expands into steam</term>, it bursts forth with all its might. Finding the air-passages <note>the tiny pores within the salt crystal</note> too narrow, it drives the salt particles aside and thus opens a free passage for itself. Many other things that have very narrow air-passages make a similar noise during **calcination** <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the open air to remove volatile components or to make it brittle and powdery</term>, such as glass and seashell fragments.

§. 4. If you have had 12 **ounces** <term>ounce: a historical unit of weight; 12 ounces would be approximately 340-370 grams depending on the local standard</term> of salt **calcined**, you will get ten and a half <note>original: "eilffthalbe"; an archaic German fraction meaning "half-eleven," or 10.5</note> **ounces** out of it.

# C. Spirit of Salt. <note>original: "Spiritus Salis, Saltz-Spiritus"</note>

## §. 1.

This **spirit** is an acidic **liquid** <term>liquor: in this context, a concentrated liquid substance</term> that is **distilled** <term>distilled: the process of heating a substance to capture its purified vapors as a liquid</term> out of the salt.

## §. 2.

Dry the **salt** over a small fire or in the sun; make 2 pounds into a very fine powder; mix it well with 6 pounds of powdered clay or **bole** <term>bolum: a type of fine, earthy clay used in alchemy and medicine as a base or binder</term>. From this mixture, make a hard dough with as much rainwater as is necessary; form small pellets about the size of a nut from it, and place them in the sun for a long time. Once they are perfectly dry, put them into a large, glazed earthenware <note>original: "Gretz-"; likely referring to a type of ceramic from Graz or a specific refractory clay</note> or glass **retort** <term>retort: a spherical vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck, used for distilling substances that require high heat</term>, of which one third must remain empty. # Chapter 16.

## A. Concerning Nitrum or Saltpeter.

->§. 1.<-

It seems as if the *Nitrum* <note>A Latin term used historically for various salts; the author clarifies its shifting meaning below.</note> of the ancients was either Egyptian **natron** <note>original: "Natron"; a natural mixture of sodium carbonate decahydrate and sodium bicarbonate.</note>, or a salt that was lifted from the earth in grey, dense lumps, or natural **borax** <note>original: "Borris"; likely referring to crude borate minerals.</note>, or the salt that was drawn from the water of the **Nile** <note>original: "Nili"</note> and many other rivers. It may also well be that all these salts made up certain classes of their *Nitrum*; however, modern *Nitrum* is nothing other than **saltpeter** <note>Potassium nitrate, a key ingredient in gunpowder.</note>, and it is of this that <margin>Here the</margin> discussion precisely falls.

->§. 2.<-

Saltpeter is a salt full of **air-spirits** <note>original: "Lufft-Spirituum"; in early chemistry, these were the volatile, gaseous essences believed to be trapped within solids.</note>, which make it volatile, and it is found on the stones and earth of old buildings. One also encounters it in cellars and many other damp places, because the air in these places condenses and very easily combines with the stones.

# B. Purification of Saltpeter:
## purification of nitre <note>original: "purificatio nitri"</note>.
### §. 1.

To purify **saltpeter** means as much as to remove a portion of its **fixed salt** <note>original: "fixen Saltz"; the stable, non-volatile residue</note> and a small amount of **resinous earth** <note>original: "harzigte Erde"; referring to organic or oily impurities found in raw nitre</note> which it carries. <margin><unclear>signify</unclear></margin>

§. 2. Dissolve 10 to 12 pounds of **saltpeter** in as much water as is required for it: Let the **solution** <note>original: "Dissolution"</note> stand, filter it, and let it **evaporate** <note>original: "verrauchen"; literally 'to smoke away'</note> in a glass or earthenware vessel until half is gone, or a small **film** <note>original: "Häutlein"; a thin layer of crystals forming on the surface, indicating saturation</note> settles on top: Afterward, move your vessel to a cold place as gently as you can, and let it stand until the next day; then you will find **crystals**, which you must pick out from the **liquid** <note>original: "liquore"</note>: Let the liquid evaporate again until a film forms, and set the vessel back in a cold place; new crystals will form; repeat the **evaporations** and **crystallizations** until all your **saltpeter** is used up.

<margin>§. 3. Fixed salt of nitre.</margin>
§. 3. Here it should be noted that in the final crystallizations, one obtains a salt that is completely similar to **sea-salt** or **rock salt** <note>original: "Saltz gemmæ"; Sal gemmae, or mineral halite</note>: One must save it separately, and can season and prepare food with it.

Once the *liquid* <note>original: "liqvore"</note> has been poured over the ashes and strained off several times, it is finally allowed to evaporate and *crystallize*.

## Observations.

### §. 4.

This preparation is called **Prunella Salt**, or stone, either because the **essential salt** <note>original: "Sal essentiale"; in early chemistry, this referred to a salt extracted from plant matter</note> extracted from **sloes** <note>original: "Prunellen"; the small, tart fruit of the blackthorn tree</note> has nearly the same virtue <note>medicinal power or efficacy</note> and shape as the mineral crystal; or because it is administered in high fevers, the heat of which corresponds to the heat of burning coals, which are called **pruna** <note>Latin for "burning coal" or "live ember"</note>. The Germans give it the shape of a sloe after they have previously dyed it red with roses.

### §. 5.

**Saltpeter** flows <note>reaches a liquid, molten state</note> much more easily than sea salt because it contains less **earth** <note>In the chemistry of this era, "earth" referred to the solid, non-volatile impurities or the elemental base of a substance.</note>.

### §. 6.

The ancients believed that one must throw **flowers of sulfur** <note>original: "Schwefel-Bluhmen"; a fine powder produced by sublimating sulfur</note> onto the molten saltpeter if it were to truly become an **aperient** <note>original: "aperiens"; a medicine used to "open" the body's channels, often acting as a mild laxative or diuretic</note>. But in this way, it is robbed of its most penetrating **spirits** <note>original: "Spirituum"; the volatile, active components believed to give a medicine its potency</note>, which the sulfur carries away with it as it burns; thus, one would deprive it of its best qualities if one sought to make it more "open" and potent in such a manner.

->§. 1.<-

This operation produces a **saltpeter** that has been "fixed" <note>In alchemy, "fixing" refers to making a volatile substance stable under heat</note> by **sulfur** and fire.

§. 2. Powder and mix together equal parts of **saltpeter** and **common salt** <note>While the previous paragraph mentions sulfur, the recipe here calls for common salt (sodium chloride); this variation may reflect a specific regional or personal recipe for this "salt of many uses."</note>; pour about one ounce of this mixture into a good **crucible** that has been previously made red-hot, and a large flame will flare up. Once the material has cooled down, powder it and dissolve <note>original: "zerschmeltzt," used here in the sense of dissolving into a liquid</note> it in a sufficient quantity of water, filter the **solution**, and let it evaporate to dryness in a metal basin or glass vessel over a **sand bath** <term>sand-fire: a method of heating a vessel evenly by nesting it in a container of heated sand</term>.

# E. Spirit of Nitre [Nitric Acid]

## §. 1.

Spirit of nitre <note>original: "Spiritus nitri"; known today as nitric acid.</note> is a very sour and corrosive <term>liquid|original: liqvor; a fluid substance</term> that is <term>distilled|original: distillirt; the process of heating a substance to collect its essence through evaporation and condensation</term> from saltpeter.

## §. 2.

Powder and mix well together two pounds of crude saltpeter <note>original: "Salpeter de houfflage"; likely referring to unrefined saltpeter collected from the walls of buildings or cellars.</note> and 6 pounds of dry clay. Pour this mixture into a large glazed glass or <term>stoneware retort|original: Gretz-Retorte; a heat-resistant vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</term>. Place it in a closed <term>reverberatory furnace|original: Reverberir-Ofen; a furnace designed to reflect or "reverberate" heat from the roof onto the material being heated</term>. Attach a large <term>balloon|original: Balon; a large spherical glass vessel</term> or <term>receiver|original: Recipient; the flask used to collect the condensed distillate</term> to it. Kindle a very small fire under it for 4 to 5 hours, so that all the <term>phlegma|original: phlegma; the watery, non-medicinal part of a distillate</term> is <term>distilled</term> out drop by drop. When you see that nothing more will come over, discard the contents of the <term>receiver</term> as something useless. Reattach it and <term>lute|original: verlutirt; sealing the joints of chemical apparatus with a paste or "lute" to make them airtight</term> the joints well. Gradually increase the fire to the second <term>degree|original: Grad; early chemists categorized heat into four levels of intensity</term>, and the <term>spirits|original: Spiritus; the volatile vapors</term> will come over and fill the <term>balloon</term> with white clouds. Maintain the fire at this same <term>degree</term> for two hours. Then increase it to the utmost power; even when the red vapors <note>Nitrogen dioxide gas, which gives nitric acid its characteristic reddish-orange fumes during high-heat distillation.</note> appear, continue to drive the fire until nothing more will come out. The <term>operation|original: Operation; the chemical procedure</term> will be finished within 14 hours. Once the vessels have cooled and the joints are op-

<margin>S. 5: Salamander's blood.</margin>
Vapors come from the **volatile saltpeter part** <term>volatile saltpeter part|original: volatilischen Salpe-ter-Theil; the portion of the substance that vaporizes more easily at lower temperatures.</term> and produce a very weak **spirit** <note>original: "Spiritum"; here referring to a diluted acid.</note>. For otherwise these **spirits**, as they rush out with great violence, might burst everything in their search for space.

# F. *Sweetened spirit of nitre*, sweetened Saltpeter-Spirit.

->§. 1.<-

This operation produces a **spirit** <note>original: "Spiritus"</note> of saltpeter from which the sharpest points have been broken off or evaporated away <note>The author uses the metaphor of "breaking the points" to describe neutralizing the harsh, corrosive nature of the acid through a chemical reaction.</note>.

§. 2. Put 8 ounces of good **spirit of nitre** <term>spirit of nitre|original: Spiritum nitri; nitric acid.</term> into a **matrass** <term>matrass|original: Matras; a long-necked glass chemical flask.</term>, and just as much well-**dephlegmated** <term>dephlegmated|original: dephlegmirten; distilled to remove excess water, thereby concentrating the substance.</term> **spirit of wine** <term>spirit of wine|original: Spiritum vini; high-proof alcohol.</term>. Place your matrass on a straw ring <note>original: "Stroh-Hut"; literally "straw hat," but here referring to a woven ring used to stabilize round-bottomed glassware.</note> under the chimney flue; the **liquid** <note>original: "liqvor"</note> will become hot even if the vessel is not placed over a fire, and in half an hour or an hour, it will begin to boil violently. Take care to avoid the red vapors <note>These red vapors are nitrogen oxides, which are toxic if inhaled.</note> that will rush out of the neck of the matrass in great abundance. Once the **boiling** <note>original: "Ebullition"</note> is over, you will find your liquid standing quite bright and clear at the bottom; although it has decreased by half, pour it into a vial and keep it, for this is precisely the sweetened spirit of nitre.

§. 3. It is good for **windy colic** <note>original: "Colicam ventosam"; abdominal pain caused by gas.</note> and **kidney pain** <note>original: "nephriticam"</note>, **uterine complaints** <term>uterine complaints|original: Mutter-Beschwerungen; historically called "suffocation of the mother," a term for various physical and emotional symptoms believed to originate in the womb.</term>, and all blockages. One administers 4 to 8 drops in broth or another **liquid** <note>original: "liqvore"</note> suitable for the illness.

§. 2. Great **boiling** <note>original: "Ebullition"</note>.

# Notes.

## §. 4.

One must leave the **matrass** <term>matrass|original: Matras; a long-necked glass chemical flask.</term> open. Otherwise, the vapors will either blow out the stopper (if one is used) or burst the vessel; during the **boiling** <note>original: "Ebullition"</note>, the matrass becomes so hot that one cannot bear to touch it with a hand.

## §. 5.

The heat and boiling begin either slower or faster depending on whether the **spirits** <note>original: "Spiritus"; referring to the nitric acid and the alcohol.</note> used for it are more or less **dephlegmated** <term>dephlegmated|original: dephlegmiret; distilled to remove water, thereby increasing concentration.</term>, or whether the weather is colder or warmer. In winter, one must heat the **liquid** <note>original: "liqvorem"</note> over a small **sand-heat** <term>sand-heat|original: Sand-Feuer; a sand bath used to distribute heat evenly to a glass vessel.</term>; but when it has become somewhat warm, remove it from the fire and shake it, and it will begin to boil up.

## §. 6.

Therefore, this is a quite strange thing: because the **spirit of nitre** <term>spirit of nitre|original: Salpeter-Spiritus; nitric acid.</term> is very acidic, and the **spirit of wine** <term>spirit of wine|original: Spiritus des Weins; alcohol.</term> is a **sulfur** <note>In alchemical theory, "sulfur" referred to the principle of flammability and oiliness, not just the mineral sulfur.</note>, one cannot imagine any **alkali** <note>original: "Alkali"; a base.</note> being present here that would cause a boiling with the **acid** <note>original: "acido"</note> according to the common course of nature. This operation demonstrates very well that one cannot explain everything by **acid and alkali** <note>original: "acido und alkali"</note> alone, though some would wish to do so. <note>The author is critiquing the "acid-alkali" theory of the late 17th century, which attempted to explain all chemical reactions as the neutralization of these two opposites.</note>

§. 17. Some chemists have called the **liquor of fixed nitre** <note>original: "liquorem nitri fixi"; a solution of potassium carbonate made from saltpeter</note> **Alkahest** <note>original: "Alkaest"</note>; this signifies a universal solvent, because they believed that the sulfurous substance could be extracted from all mixtures <note>original: "mixtis"</note> with it.

§. 18. If one calcines <note>original: "Calcinirt"; to heat a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile parts</note> 32 ounces of common saltpeter without any additives over a strong fire for 8 hours, it will neither burn nor crackle or burst, for there is no sulfur within it. However, the saltpeter will decrease significantly, and no more than two and a half <note>original: "drittehalbe"; an archaic German numerical expression where "the third is half," meaning 2.5</note> ounces of it will remain. Nevertheless, this salt calcined in this manner will still burn a little over glowing coals, from which it appears that not every single volatile <note>original: "volatile"</note> part of the saltpeter has been elevated. Nonetheless, it is an **alkali**, because as the fire particles were drawn in and out of the air-pores <note>original: "Lufft-Löcher"; 17th-century chemistry often explained reactions through the physical movement of particles into microscopic pores</note>, they turned it into a **calx** <note>original: "Kalck"; the powdery metallic or mineral residue remaining after calcination</note>.

§. 19. If one allows this salt to dissolve in a cellar <note>this refers to the process of deliquescence, where a salt absorbs enough moisture from the humid cellar air to turn into a liquid solution</note>, one obtains a **liquor of fixed nitre**, which is used like the previous one; however, it is considered even better for cleansing the face <note>original: "Ausputz des Angesichts"; likely a cosmetic or dermatological use for treating skin blemishes</note>.

# Chapter 17.

## A. On *Sal Armoniacum*, *Sal Ammoniac*. <note>original: "Sal Armoniacum, Salarmoniac"; historically known as ammonium chloride, a salt used extensively in alchemy and early chemistry for soldering, dyeing, and as a reagent</note>

->§. 1.<-

The *Sal Armoniacum* is either a natural or an artificial salt. The natural kind is formed in hot countries / such as many places in *Africa* / that lie toward the *torrid zone* <note>original: "Zonam torridam"; the region of the Earth between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, known for intense heat</note>. It is also found in the earth / which animals have soaked with their urine / where the sun *sublimates* <note>original: "sublimiret"; the chemical process where a solid substance transitions directly into a vapor and then back to a solid upon cooling, used to purify salts</note> the volatile salt from this urine / and that is the *Sal Armoniacum*.

### D. Aqua Regia <note>Latin: "Royal Water"; a powerful acidic mixture capable of dissolving noble metals like gold</note>

->§. 1.<-

§. 7. It is difficult enough to comprehend how **royal water** <note>original: *aqua regia*</note> dissolves gold—which is a very solid metal—and yet cannot **dissolve** <note>original: *solviren*</note> silver, which is by far not as dense.

§. 8. When some **chemists** <note>original: *Chymisten*</note> wish to resolve this difficulty, they have said that because gold is a metal that contains more **sulfur** <note>In early chemistry, "sulfur" referred to the "principle of inflammability" rather than just the element we know today</note> than silver, it requires a similarly sulfurous **solvent** <note>original: *Dissolvens*</note> like **royal water**, which consists of the **volatile** sulfurous salts of **sal ammoniac** <note>original: *Sal-armoniacs*; ammonium chloride</note>. However, this explanation refutes itself; for if gold contained more sulfur than silver, it would consequently not be so heavy, since sulfur is indeed one of the lightest chemical **principles** <note>original: *Principia*; the fundamental building blocks of matter</note>.

§. 9. I know very well that the **alchemists** <note>original: *Alchymisten*</note> will say their sulfur is far different from common sulfur, and that one must imagine a **fixed** <note>stable or non-volatile</note> and therefore heavy sulfur within the gold.

§. 10. But besides the fact that "fixed sulfur" exists only in the imagination, it could never be as heavy as the other **principles** which, according to their opinion, are supposed to be in gold, and which they must consider to be just as fixed as the sulfur in proportion.

§. 11. If we furthermore examine what occurs with the composition of the gold-**solvent** <note>original: *Menstrui*; a substance used to dissolve a solid</note>, we will easily be able to contradict this opinion. For we see that as soon as the **spirit** <note>original: *Spiritus*</note> of saltpeter <note>nitric acid</note> begins to penetrate the **sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride</note>, the acidic salt becomes combined with it, and it releases the **volatile** salts. Because these salts, acting as **alkalis** <note>original: *alkali*</note>, encounter some **acids** <note>original: *acida*</note> from the **spirit of nitre** <note>original: *Spiritu nitri*; nitric acid</note> during their passage, a great **effervescence** <note>original: *Efferveſcenz*; a bubbling or fizzing reaction</note> occurs, which always happens when alkaline salts and **acids** meet. §. 7. It is difficult enough to understand why **royal water** <note>original: *aqua regia*; a highly corrosive mixture of acids</note> dissolves gold—which is a very solid metal—and yet cannot dissolve silver, which is by far not as dense.

§. 8. When some **chemists** <note>original: *Chymiſten*</note> wish to resolve this difficulty, they have said that because gold is a metal containing more **sulfur** <note>original: *Schwefel*</note> than silver, it therefore requires such a sulfurous **solvent** <note>original: *Diſſolvens*</note> as **royal water** is, which consists of the volatile sulfurous salts of **sal ammoniac** <note>original: *Sal-armoniacs*; ammonium chloride</note>. §. 9. I know very well that the **alchemists** <note>original: *Alchymiſten*</note> will say their sulfur is widely different from common sulfur, and that one must imagine a **fixed** <note>original: *fixen*; stable and non-evaporating</note> and therefore heavy sulfur within the gold.

§. 10. But besides the fact that this fixed sulfur exists only in the imagination, it could also never be as heavy as the other **principles** which, according to their opinion, are supposed to be in gold, and which they must hold to be just as fixed as the sulfur in proportion.

# E. The Volatile Spirit of Sal Ammoniac

->§. 1.<-

This preparation is a <term>volatile salt<note>original: *volatilisches Saltz*; a salt that evaporates easily at room temperature, in this case, ammonium carbonate or aqueous ammonia</note></term> that has been released from <term>sal ammoniac<note>ammonium chloride</note></term> by <term>lime<note>original: *Kalck*; calcium oxide, used here to react with the salt</note></term> and dissolved into a liquid through a watery moisture.

->§. 2.<-

Take 8 ounces of sal ammoniac and 24 ounces of <term>unslaked lime<note>quicklime; calcium oxide that has not yet reacted with water</note></term>; powder them separately and put them together in a mortar. Place it in the furnace over sand and immediately attach a large <term>balloon<note>original: *Balon*; a large, round glass receiving vessel</note></term> or receiver to it. <term>Lute<note>original: *Verlutirt*; to seal joints with a paste (lute) to make them airtight</note></term> the joints with all diligence. The first <term>spirits<note>the chemical vapors being released</note></term> will distill within a quarter of an hour without any fire. Thereafter, throw 2 to 3 burning coals under the retort and increase the fire to the <term>second degree<note>a moderate heat; early chemists categorized heat into four degrees, from the warmth of a water bath to the intense heat of a smelting furnace</note></term>; maintain this until nothing more will come over. The operation comes to an end in 3 hours. Cool the vessels and open them. Take away your receiver and pour the spirit contained therein...

# F. Another Preparation of the Volatile Spirit of Sal Ammoniac, which is Accomplished by the same Means: The Flowers and the Fixed Fever-Reducing Salt <note>original: "Sal fixum febrifugum"; 'fixed' refers to a substance that does not evaporate when heated, and 'febrifugum' indicates its use in treating fevers</note>.

## §. 1.

Pulverize and mix together 8 ounces of sal ammoniac <term>sal ammoniac: ammonium chloride, a salt used historically in chemistry and medicine</term> and an equal amount of salt of tartar <term>salt of tartar: potassium carbonate, often used as a reagent to react with ammonium salts to release volatile ammonia</term>.

## §. 2.

Put this mixture quickly into a glass cucurbit <term>cucurbit: a gourd-shaped glass vessel used as the bottom part of a distillation apparatus</term> and moisten it with 5 ounces of common water; place a helm <term>helm: also called an alembic or 'head,' this sits atop the cucurbit to collect and direct vapors</term> upon it, attach a receiver <term>receiver: a glass vessel designed to collect the liquid condensed during distillation</term> to it, and seal the joints as well as possible with a wet bladder <note>animal bladders were commonly used as a flexible, airtight 'lute' or sealant in early laboratories</note>: place your vessel in a sand bath, give it a small fire at first so that the cucurbit gradually becomes hot and the spirit falls over drop by drop: but if you see that nothing more will come over, then remove the receiver and seal it as well as possible: increase the fire to the third degree <note>the 'third degree' of heat typically refers to a strong heat where the sand bath is very hot to the touch, but not yet a direct flame</note> and maintain it for about two hours; by doing so, white flowers of sal ammoniac <note>original: "Salarmoniac-Blumen"; in alchemy, 'flowers' refers to the fine powder formed when a substance is heated into a gas and then cools directly back into a solid</note> will be sublimated, which will settle as a meal <note>a fine, flour-like powder</note> at the bottom of the helm.

## §. 3.

## I. *Volatile Oily Aromatic Salt.* <note>original: "Sal volatile oleosum aromaticum"</note>

### §. 1.

This operation results in a <term>volatile sal ammoniac</term> <note>a salt based on ammonia that evaporates easily; often ammonium carbonate</note> that is filled with aromatic essences.

### §. 2.

Powder and mix together equal parts <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note> and <term>salt of tartar</term> <note>potassium carbonate</note>. Place this mixture into a glass or earthenware <term>cucurbit</term> <note>a gourd-shaped vessel used in distillation; the term "Gretz" likely refers to a specific type of clay vessel</note>; pour enough high-quality <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>concentrated alcohol or ethanol</note> over it until it covers the mixture by the height of one finger. Chapter 18.

# A. Concerning Vitriol.

-> §. 1. <-

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'D' intricately patterned with foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>Vitriol <term>Vitriol: a historical name for sulfate minerals, named for their glassy or "vitreous" appearance</term> is a mineral that consists of an acidic salt and a sulfurous earth. There are four kinds: blue, green, white, and red vitriol.

§. 2. The blue variety is found around copper veins in Hungary and the island of Cyprus, from where it is brought to us in beautiful crystals; because of their place of origin, these are called Hungarian or Cyprian vitriol. It contains a great deal of the essence of copper, which makes it somewhat corrosive. It is used only externally, such as for compresses and for the removal of "wild flesh" <note>original: "wilden Fleisches"; referring to "proud flesh," an overgrowth of granulation tissue that can form during the healing of a wound</note>.

§. 3. There are three kinds of green vitriol: German, English, and Roman. The German variety has a bluish tint and contains a little copper; it is better suited for the production of **Aquafortis** <term>Aquafortis: literally "strong water," the historical name for nitric acid</term> than the others. The English variety contains some iron and is good for making **Spirit of Vitriol** <term>Spirit of Vitriol: a concentrated sulfuric acid produced by distilling green vitriol</term>. The Roman variety otherwise matches the English, except that it does not melt as easily.

<margin>§. 4. White Vitriol.</margin>
§. 4. White vitriol is a salt that is extracted through **evaporation** <term>Evaporation: the process of heating a liquid to turn it into vapor, leaving behind solid minerals</term> from vitriolic well waters, or it is a green vitriol that has been calcined <term>Calcined: heated to a high temperature to remove volatile substances and reduce a mineral to a dry powder</term> until white, then dissolved in water, filtered, and dried over a fire. Whichever type it may be, it is nevertheless purified from metallic substances more than the others. It can be taken internally to induce vomiting, and used externally in **eye washes** <note>original: "collyria"; medicinal lotions for the eyes</note>.

<margin>§. 5. Red **Colcothar** <term>Colcothar: a reddish-brown iron oxide residue produced from the calcination of vitriol</term> or **Chalcitis**.</margin>
§. 5. Red vitriol has been brought from Germany for some years now and is called natural **Colcothar** or **Chalcitis** <term>Chalcitis: a historical name for various copper or iron-based minerals found in oxidized zones</term>. It is believed that it is a green vitriol that has been calcined by an underground fire. It is the rarest among all vitriols; it stills bleeding when it is applied to the bleeding areas.

<margin>§. 6. **Vitriolum**, a mysterious name.</margin>
§. 6. Vitriol in general is a very useful **substance** <note>original: "Species"</note> in **medicine**, and many magnificent **remedies** drawn from it. It is called **Vitriolum** in Latin. # C. Calcination of Vitriol.

### §. 1.
Pour as much as you like of green vitriol <note>Iron(II) sulfate; often called copperas</note> into an unglazed earthenware pot: place it in the fire, and the vitriol will melt into a liquid <note>original: "Wasser"; literally "water," referring to the substance dissolving in its own water of crystallization upon heating</note>; let it boil until the moisture is consumed, or until the matter has become a white-gray lump. Move it away from the fire then; it will have decreased by almost half [in weight], and this is called white-calcined vitriol.

### §. 2.
If you calcine <term>Calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to remove volatile components or change its chemical state</term> the gray vitriol for a somewhat long time over the fire, it becomes blood-red: It is called Colcothar <term>Colcothar: a reddish-brown iron oxide residue produced by heating iron sulfate; used as a pigment, a polishing powder, or as a medicinal astringent</term>, and it stanches bleeding when it is applied to a wound.

## Observations <note>original: "Anmerckungen"</note>.

### §. 3.
One must not calcine the vitriol in a glazed pot at all, so that no glaze <term>Litharge: original "Glätte"; a lead-based coating used on ceramics</term> chips off and alters <note>original: "alterire"; meaning to chemically contaminate or change</note> the vitriol.

### §. 4.
One can let it calcine—or rather dry—in the sun until it is white; which method of calcination is better than the first, but also more tedious.

## D. The Distillation of Vitriol.

### §. 1.

This spirit <term>Spirit: In early chemistry, a "spirit" referred to a volatile liquid obtained through distillation, usually an acid or alcohol</term> is an acidic salt of vitriol which has been dissolved into a liquid <note>original: "liquorem"</note> by intense fire.

### §. 2.

Fill two-thirds of a large earthen <note>original: "Ertz-", likely referring to stoneware or ceramic capable of withstanding high heat</note> or glass retort that is glazed with white calcined vitriol <term>Calcination: The process of heating a substance to a high temperature to drive off water or volatile matter, reducing it to a dry powder</term>: place it in an open reverberatory furnace <note>A furnace that reflects heat from the roof onto the material being treated, preventing direct contact with the fuel</note>, attach a large balloon or receiver to it, warm it with a very small fire, and thus let the remaining watery moisture in the vitriol pass over drop by drop. When nothing more comes forth, pour the contents of the receiver into a bottle; this is called vitriol phlegm <note>original: "phlegma vitrioli"; the watery, non-acidic portion of the distillate</note>, and one washes the eyes with it for eye ailments.

<margin>Section 25. Oil of vitriol turns red with rose tincture.</margin>
Section 25. If one pours a few drops of spirit of vitriol or oil of vitriol <note>original: "Vitriol-Spiritum oder Oel"; these are early names for sulfuric acid</note> into a small measure of warm water in which a few dried red roses have been soaked, the liquid <note>original: "liquor"</note> will in a short time become as red as wine. One must not attribute this effect solely to the spirit of vitriol making the water acidic and thereby making it more powerful in pulling the tincture out of the roses. Rather, it is more due to the fact that this acid <note>original: "acidum"</note> rarefies <note>thins out or expands</note> and spreads apart the rose particles that were dissolved by the water, allowing them to be seen better than before. For if you strain your infusion <note>original: "infusion"</note> and remove the roses from it before pouring the spirit of vitriol into it, the strained liquid <note>original: "Colatur"</note>—even if it has little color at first—will become just as red when you pour the spirit in as if the roses were still inside. The same also applies to other tinctures which are extracted by means of acids, as well as to those which are brought out by an alkaline salt.

This operation produces a very **stable** <note>original: "fixes" — in early chemistry, a 'fixed' substance is one that resists the heat of fire and does not evaporate</note> vitriol salt that remains after distillation.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial D</image-desc>This salt is a part of the vitriol that the fire was unable to thin <note>original: "rarificiren" — to rarify or turn into a gaseous state</note> into a **spirit** <note>original: "Spiritu" — in early chemistry, a volatile, distilled vapor or essence</note>. I truly believe that a **fixed** <note>original: "fixes" — a substance that is stable in heat and does not evaporate</note> vitriol salt, from which no sulfur has been removed, moves downward <note>acting as a laxative</note> rather than upward <note>acting as an emetic</note>. For vomiting is only triggered by the salty sulfur that is in the stomach and pinches the fibers, whereby a **convulsion** <note>a muscle contraction or spasm</note> occurs there.

### Chapter 19.
# A. On Rock Alum, and its Purification.

§. 1.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter A, decorated with flowing leaf and vine patterns.</image-desc>Rock alum <note>original: "Alun de Roche"</note> or stone alum is a very firm mineral salt and is found in the veins of the earth in many European locations. It makes the teeth white and acts effectively as a **diuretic** <note>original: "treibet durch den Urin wohl aus" — promotes the discharge of urine</note>. # B. Distillation of Alum.

->§. 1.<-

Pour 5 pounds of crushed alum into a large glass or stoneware **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit: a gourd-shaped vessel used in distillation</term>; attach a **helm** <term>helm: the "head" or cap of a still that directs vapors downward</term> and a **receiver** <term>recipient: a vessel used to collect the condensed liquid</term> to it. Distill over a **sand bath** <note>original: "Sand-Feuer" — a method of heating a vessel evenly by nesting it in a container of sand</note> until whatever can rise has risen. In this way, you will obtain an **alum phlegm** <note>original: "Allaun-Phlegma" — the watery, less potent first liquid to come over during distillation</note>, which is used for eye complaints, for "throat-sickness" <note>original: "Kehlsucht" — historically referring to laryngeal ailments or croup</note>, for **quinsy** <term>Bräune: an old term for severe throat inflammation or tonsillitis</term>, and for the cleaning of wounds. 

Open the vessels, break the cucurbit, and grind the remaining white mass into a powder. Place it into a stoneware **retort** <term>retort: a glass or earthenware vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances at high heat</term>, leaving half of it empty. Set your retort in an open **reverberatory furnace** <term>Reverberir-Ofen: a furnace that reflects heat back onto the vessel</term> and attach a large **balloon flask** <note>original: "Balon" — a large, round glass receiver</note>. **Lute** <note>original: "verlutirt" — to seal the joints of the apparatus with a paste to prevent vapors from escaping</note> the joints well. Maintain a very small fire for three hours to warm the retort; then, increase the heat hour by hour to the highest degree. The **spirits** <note>original: "Spiritus" — the volatile, acidic essence of the mineral</note> will then cross over and fill the balloon flask with white clouds. 

Maintain the fire for three days, then allow the vessels to cool. You will find 8 ounces of acid **spirit** <note>original: "Spiritum"</note> in the receiver. This you can **rectify** <note>to purify a liquid by redistilling it</note> and distill over a sand bath in a glass **alembic** <term>alembic: a traditional distillation apparatus</term> so that it becomes all the clearer.

§. 1. <term>Alum water</term> <note>original: "Aqua aluminis"</note>. <term>Spirit of alum</term> <note>original: "Spiritus aluminis"</note>.

# B. Distillation of Alum.

### §. I.

Pour 5 pounds of crushed alum into a large glass or stoneware **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit: a gourd-shaped vessel used in distillation, often called a "body"</term>; attach a **head** <term>head: also known as an alembic or helm, used to collect vapors</term> and a **receiver** <term>receiver: a vessel that collects the distilled liquid</term> to it. Distill over a sand bath, allowing whatever is able to rise to ascend; in this way, you will obtain an **alum-phlegma** <term>phlegma: an early chemical term for a watery, tasteless distillate</term>, which is used for eye complaints, for **croup** <note>original: "Kehlsucht"</note> and **tonsillitis** <note>original: "Bräune"</note>, and for the cleansing of wounds. 

Open the vessels, break the cucurbit, powder the remaining white mass, and put it into a stoneware **retort** <term>retort: a glass or earthenware vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances at high heat</term>, leaving half of it empty. Place your retort in an open **reverberatory furnace** <term>reverberatory furnace: a furnace that reflects heat from the roof onto the material being heated</term> and attach a large **balloon** <note>original: "Balon" — a large, round glass receiver</note> to it. Seal the joints well with **lute** <term>lute: a clay or paste used to make airtight seals on chemical apparatus</term>. Maintain a very small fire beneath it for three hours to warm the retort. Increase the heat hour by hour until the highest degree, and the **spirits** <note>original: "Spiritus" — here referring to the volatile acidic vapors</note> will pass over and fill the balloon with white clouds. 

Continue with the fire for 3 days, and then let the vessels cool. You will find 8 ounces of **acidic spirit** <note>original: "sauern Spiritum"</note> in the receiver, which you can **rectify** <term>rectify: to purify a liquid by repeated distillation</term> and distill over a sand bath in a glass **alembic** so that it becomes all the clearer.

## Balsam of Sulfur <note>original: "Balsamus Sulphuris"</note>

### §. 1.

This operation is a dissolution of the oily particles of common sulfur, which is carried out in oil of turpentine.

<margin>§. 2. Efficacy, Dosage.</margin>

### §. 2.
Pour an ounce and a half of **Flowers of Sulfur** <note>original: "Schwefel-Blumen"; a fine yellow powder produced by heating sulfur until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies.</note> into a small <term>matrass</term> <note>original: "Matras"; a long-necked glass flask used by early chemists and pharmacists for boiling or distilling.</note>; pour 8 ounces of **oil of turpentine** over it. Place your matrass in sand <note>A "sand bath" was used to provide even, indirect heat to glass vessels to prevent them from cracking.</note> and maintain a small <term>digestion fire</term> <note>original: "Digestions-Feuer"; a gentle, steady heat meant to encourage a substance to break down or "digest" into a solvent.</note> beneath it for one hour. Afterward, increase the heat slightly and continue for 2 to 3 hours, until the oil takes on a red color. Let the vessels cool down again, and then pour off the clear balsam from the undissolved sulfur.

### §. 3.
This balsam is excellently suited for ulcers of the lungs and chest; one to six drops of it are administered in a helpful liquid.

If one wishes to make aniseed balsam of sulfur <note>original: "balsamum sulphuris anisatum"</note>, one takes aniseed oil instead of oil of turpentine and proceeds in the manner described above. It is far more pleasant but not as sharp <note>That is, less acrid or potent in its chemical action.</note> as the previous one.

## Notes

->§. 6.<-

No great heat is required for this operation: for because sulfur is fatty <note>Early chemists classified sulfur as "fatty" because it is combustible and oil-soluble, similar to fats.</note>, it is very easily united with the oils and naturally imparts a red color to them. If one wishes to take this balsam in a drink, one must dissolve it in a little egg yolk so that it can be mixed into water or broth <note>The egg yolk acts as an emulsifier, allowing the oil-based medicine to blend with water-based liquids.</note>.

§. 8. One can make a sulfur balsam with linseed oil instead of oil of turpentine and use it for treating wounds.

## E. Spirit of Sulfur.

### §. 1.

This spirit is an acidic portion of sulfur that has been separated and turned into a liquid <term>liquor</term> by the action of fire.

### §. 2. 
Take a large stoneware basin <note>original: "Gretz-Becken"; likely referring to heat-resistant earthenware from regions like Greußen, commonly used for chemical apparatus.</note>; place a small bowl made of the same earth inside it, but turned upside down, and place another bowl full of melted sulfur on top of it. Close off these two bowls with a large glass funnel, which you have had specially made with a neck as long as that of a <term>matrass</term> <note>A long-necked glass flask used for boiling or distilling.</note>, and it must be about a thumb or an inch wide. Light a fire under the sulfur; do not plug the hole of the funnel so that it always has air to burn, otherwise the flame would be extinguished. Once your sulfur is consumed, put more under it, and continue this until you find as much "spirit" <note>In early chemistry, a "spirit" was a volatile liquid obtained by distillation or combustion; here, it refers to the acidic condensate (sulfuric/sulfurous acid) created by the burning sulfur.</note> under the inverted bowl as is necessary, and store it in a phial.

<margin>MB</margin>
### §. 3. 
One pours enough of this into juleps <note>A sweet, syrupy medicinal drink used as a base for other medicines.</note> until they have acquired a pleasant sharpness, if one wishes to use it to drive away everyday fevers and to promote the flow of urine. Some prescribe it for lung complaints; however, because acids <note>original: "acida"</note> cause coughing, it can do more harm than good to this part of the body.

-> §. 4. <-

A great many machines have been invented for the production of spirit of sulfur: the most common is a glass bell jar, under which one allows the sulfur to burn; the emerging spirits <note>Vapors or gases that condense into liquid.</note> then settle on its walls in a condensed state and, in the same manner as we suggested in the description of our machine, distill into a stoneware basin <note>original: "Gretz-Becken"; heat-resistant earthenware.</note> placed underneath.

## Chapter 21.

# A. Concerning Succinum, or Karabé, or Amber <note>original: "Agtstein," an archaic German name for amber</note>.

§. 1.
<margin>§. 1. The various names for amber.</margin>
In the streams and rivers by the sea in the Duchy of Prussia, and nowhere else, one finds a certain coagulated resin or bitumen <term>bitumen: a historical term for various natural flammable substances, including mineral resins and asphalt</term> that is called *Succinum* <note>Latin for amber</note> because it appears to be an "earth-juice" <note>original: "Erd-Safft"; a reference to the belief that amber was a liquid from the earth that hardened</note>. It is likewise called *Karabé* because it draws straw to itself; for this word in the Persian language means as much as "straw-puller" <note>original: "tirepaille" (French) or "Stroh-halm-Zug" (German)</note>. Furthermore, it is called *electrum* <note>the Greek-derived term from which we get the word "electricity," due to amber’s static properties</note>, *glesum* <note>an ancient Germanic term mentioned by Roman historians</note>, *citrine amber* <note>original: "ambra citrina"</note>, and in French *ambre jaune*, or yellow amber.

§. 2. Because this resin is soft and slimy [when first formed], many small animals are trapped within it and, as it were, buried.

§. 3.
<margin>§. 3. The various types of amber.</margin>
One finds differently colored amber, such as white, yellow, and black.

<summary>This page concludes a discussion on the medicinal properties of sulfur and introduces Chapter 21 on amber, detailing its various historical names and its origin as a soft resin that traps insects.</summary>
<keywords>amber, Succinum, Karabé, Prussia, bitumen, natural history, etymology, resin, fossilized insects</keywords>

--- Page 767 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Chapter 21 regarding amber (Agtstein). The previous page established the names and origins of amber in Prussia and its tendency to trap small animals.</meta>

§. 4. The white variety is held in high esteem above all others in medicine, even though it is opaque <note>original: "dunckel," here meaning cloudy or non-transparent rather than dark-colored</note>. It emits a pleasant scent when rubbed vigorously against an object. From this kind, one extracts a greater amount of volatile salt <term>Sal volatile: an early chemical term for ammonium carbonate, used as smelling salts or a stimulant</term> than from the others.

§. 5. The yellow variety is transparent and exceptionally lovely to behold. It is worn around the neck [as jewelry] and crafted into small curiosities <note>original: "Cabinetgen," referring to small decorative items or miniatures for a "cabinet of curiosities"</note>. It is also highly valued in medicine, as a significant amount of oil can be obtained from it. The black variety possesses the least medicinal power.

§. 6. <margin>§. 6. Power, Dosage.</margin> Amber <note>original: "Agtstein"</note> arrests the spitting of blood <note>original: "Blutausspeyen," likely referring to coughing up blood or hemoptysis</note>, the "red flux" <term>rothe Ruhr: an old term for dysentery, specifically when accompanied by blood</term>, the bleeding of hemorrhoids <note>original: "hæmorrhoidum"</note>, excessive menstruation, and seminal discharge. The dosage is ten grains to half a drachm <term>drachmam: an apothecary weight, approximately 3.9 grams</term>. It also provides some relief for the common cold <note>original: "Schnuppen"</note> and moderates various "fluxes" <note>In humoral medicine, a "flux" was an abnormal discharge of bodily fluids</note> when the smoke from burning it is inhaled through the nose.

§. 7. <margin>§. 7. Rock oil.</margin> Some scholars believe that rock oil <note>original: "petroleum"</note> is nothing more than a liquid <note>original: "liqvor"</note> drawn from amber by the heat of subterranean fires, effectively distilling it underground. §. 8. This theory would seem plausible enough if the locations from which these substances <note>original: "Species"</note> are taken were not so far apart. ## B. Oil of Amber

### §. 1.

This procedure consists of the dissolution of certain oil particles from the amber, which is performed in spirit of wine <term>Spirit of wine: high-proof distilled alcohol, the precursor to modern ethanol</term>.

§. 2. Take five to six ounces of yellow amber and grind it into an impalpable powder <note>original: "ungreifflichen Pulver," a powder so fine it cannot be felt between the fingers</note>; pour it into a <term>matrass</term> <note>a glass flask with a round belly and a long neck</note>, and pour spirit of wine over it to a height of four fingers. Place another flask upside down over the first so that it becomes a <term>joined vessel</term> <note>original: "vaisseau de rencontre," a setup where two flasks are joined at the neck to allow vapors to circulate and fall back down</note>. Seal the joints well with a wet bladder <note>Animal bladders were commonly used as a flexible, airtight seal in early chemistry</note>, set it for <term>digestion</term> <note>the process of extracting substances using gentle, steady heat</note> in hot sand, and let it stand for five to six days, or until the spirit of wine has taken on the yellow color of the amber. Pour off this <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "Tinctur," a medicinal extract dissolved in alcohol</note> by decanting it carefully, and pour fresh spirit of wine over the remaining material. Allow it to digest as before, separating one infusion <note>original: "imprægnation"</note> after another. Mix these together, filter them, and through <term>distillation</term> in an <term>alembic</term> <note>a classic distillation apparatus consisting of a boiling vessel and a cooling cap</note> over a very gentle fire, draw off approximately half of the spirit of wine (which can be reused as before). Keep the tincture remaining at the bottom of the alembic in a well-sealed vial.

-> §. 8. <-

**Jet-stone** <term>Aststein: a type of bituminous wood or fossilized branch, often used interchangeably with jet</term> and **jet-oil** <term>Gagatstein-Oel: oil distilled from jet (a type of lignite), known for its pungent odor</term> are particularly effective for **uterine complaints** <term>Mutter-Beschwerungen: historically known as "hysteria," a range of symptoms once attributed to the womb's movement</term> due to their foul smell. # D. Volatile Salt of Amber: The 
## Volatile Amber-

->§. 5.<-

Pour 32 ounces of powdered **amber** <note>original: "Agtstein," an archaic German name for amber, literally "burning stone"</note> into a fairly large glass or **Grätz-style distillation flask** <note>original: "Gretz-Cucurbit"; likely a heat-resistant vessel from the town of Grätz, known for its glassware</note>, so that only one-fourth of it is filled. Place this **flask** <term>Cucurbit: the bottom vessel of a distillation apparatus, often gourd-shaped</term> in a sand bath, set a **still-head** <term>Helm: the top part of a still where vapors condense</term> upon it, and attach a **receiving vessel** <note>original: "Recipienten"</note>. Once the flask is heated through, gradually increase the heat to the **third degree** <note>In historical chemistry, the "third degree" of heat is a strong fire, typically used for distilling heavy oils or salts in a sand bath</note>. Finally, first a white oil and then a red, clear oil will distill. When no more vapors rise, let the fire go out and allow the vessels to cool. Open them and brush off the **volatile salt** <note>original: "Sal volatile"</note> with a feather. ## Chapter 22.
# On Ambergris.

->§. 1.<-

Ambergris is a <term>mineral pitch <note>original Latin: 'bitumen'; a term used historically for various natural flammable substances like asphalt or naphtha</note></term> or resin that is found in many places along the sea-coasts.

->§. 2.<-

It is believed that it comes only from the Eastern <note>Oriental</note> seas, even though it is occasionally gathered on the English sea-coasts and in many other places in Europe; however, it is most frequently found on the Malindi coast <note>the coast of modern-day Kenya</note>, especially at the mouth of the river called Rio di Sena <note>the Zambezi River in modern-day Mozambique</note>.

->§. 3.<-

This resin is hardened by the rays of the sun. The best ambergris is the grey, well-dried variety, and that which softens easily from heat: if it is moist, it appears black.

->§. 4.<-

Ambergris is an excellent <term>strengthening agent <note>original Latin: 'corroborans'</note></term>, and it is administered in a <term>liquid <note>original Latin: 'liqvore'</note></term> or <term>medicinal paste <note>original Latin: 'opiato'; a semi-solid preparation often used as a carrier for drugs</note></term> to awaken the seed <note>to stimulate libido or fertility</note>: the <term>dosage <note>original: 'Dosis'</note></term> consists of one to four grains <note>a small unit of measurement, roughly 65 milligrams per grain</note>.

§. 3. ### Concerning Vegetables or Plants in General.

->§ I.<-

<image-desc>Large decorative initial letter 'A' serving as a drop cap, intricately detailed with botanical motifs including winding vines, large serrated leaves, and clusters of berries or small round fruits.</image-desc>All plants, whether they be large or small, spring from seeds: which are therein enclosed for a time in a <term>concise form <note>original: 'kurtzen Begriff'; implying that the entire potential of the plant is summarized or contained within the seed</note></term>, as if within a mother, until the salty moisture of the earth has dissolved and softened the shell of the seed. Thereupon, the moisture introduces itself into the <term>pores <note>original: 'Poros'</note></term> of the tiny plant, allowing it to shed its casing: it is then that one first comes to see its distinct parts in an orderly manner, which previously appeared altogether too disorderly. The apple and pear tree lie enclosed within their kernels just as surely as the very smallest plant does in its seed. A plant, however, is primarily nourished through its root, whose <term>air-holes <note>original: 'Lufftlöcher'; early botanical term for the pores or channels in roots and stems</note></term> are so arranged that they can catch the <term>sap <note>original: 'Safft'; referring to the nutrient-rich fluids drawn from the soil</note></term> of the earth. This sap, driven forth by the heat of the sun—

§. 2. Plants / whose sap is resinous / oily or gummy / generally grow less than others: because these fatty substances clog the <term>pores <note>original: 'Poros'</note></term> of a plant and prevent the sap from being easily distributed for its nourishment. For this reason / in warm countries / where the sun draws many oily particles from the earth into the plants / one sees trees become <term>stunted <note>original: 'verbutten'; meaning the tree's growth is choked or arrested by its own internal density.</note></term> by their own fatness / unless one performs / so to speak / a <term>bloodletting <note>original: 'Aderlasen'; a medical metaphor for tapping the tree's fluids.</note></term> on them / and makes several cuts in the lower bark / from which turpentine then flows. Resins are distinguished from gums in this / that the former are much oilier / and allow themselves to be dissolved and broken down in oil more easily than gums.

# On Jalap / or Jalappa and its Resin.

§. 1.
Jalap is a gray root, cut into pieces and dried, as it is brought from America. Its plant is a type of <term>nightshade <note>original: 'Solano'</note></term>, which some call *night beauty* <note>original: 'belle de nuit' (French) or 'Nachtschöne' (German); known today as the four-o'clock flower.</note>. It grows in the province of <term>Michoacán <note>original: 'Mechoacam'; a region in Mexico famous for this medicinal export.</note></term> and in other places as well. The best variety is the firmest, which has many fine resinous veins. It purges the <term>waters <note>original: 'Wasser'; referring to excess bodily fluids or humors.</note></term> very well, which is why it is commonly prescribed to those with <term>dropsy <note>original: 'Wassersüchtigen'; edema or swelling.</note></term> and <term>venereal diseases <note>original: 'Ziprianern'; a term referencing 'Cyprians' or followers of Venus, used here for those with syphilis or similar conditions.</note></term>. The <term>dose <note>original: 'Dosis'</note></term> starts at 10 grains and reaches up to one <term>drachm <note>original: 'Drachmam'; an ancient unit of weight.</note></term>; it is taken in a soup or white wine.

Put one pound of coarsely powdered good <term>Jalap <note>original: 'Jalappa'</note></term> into a large <term>matrass <note>original: 'Matras'; a round-bottomed glass flask with a long neck.</note></term>: pour enough <term>rectified spirit of wine <note>original: 'Spiritum vini Alkolifatum'; essentially pure alcohol.</note></term> over it so that it stands four fingers high above the material: invert another matrass over it, so that its neck fits into the first one, and when you have sealed the joints well with a wet bladder <note>A common technique in early chemistry where a piece of animal bladder was used as a pressure-resistant sealant for glassware.</note>, let the material <term>digest <note>original: 'digeriren'; the process of softening or extracting substances through gentle, steady heat.</note></term> for three days in a <term>sand bath <note>original: 'Sandfeuer'; a container of sand heated by a furnace to provide a stable, even temperature for glass vessels.</note></term>, and the spirit of wine will take on a yellowish color: pour it off by <term>decanting <note>original: 'Neigungs-weise'; literally 'by way of tilting,' pouring off liquid while leaving sediment behind.</note></term>, and pour fresh spirit in its place onto the <term>Jalap <note>original: 'Galappa'</note></term>; proceed as before, then mix your <term>solutions <note>original: 'Dissolutiones'</note></term> together, and filter them through <term>blotting paper <note>original: 'Lösch-Pappier'</note></term>: pour the filtered liquid into a glass <term>alembic <note>original: 'Alembic'; a specialized apparatus used for distillation.</note></term> and distill two-thirds of the spirit of wine in a <term>steam bath <note>original: 'Balneo vaporum'</note></term>, which can be used again another time for this same process. ## B. Remarks.

### § I.

Because the *spirit of wine* is a sulfur <note>In early modern chemistry, "sulfur" was one of the three primary principles of matter, representing the oily, flammable, or fatty parts of a substance. Because alcohol is flammable, it was classified as a highly refined sulfur.</note>, it is also a very convenient *solvent* <note>original: 'Menstruum'; an alchemical term for a liquid used to dissolve a solid.</note> for extracting *resins*, which are also considered a coarse sulfur: one must take as much of it as is enough to dissolve the *resin* of the *jalap*, and give it time so that it can penetrate the entire *body* <note>original: 'corpus'; the physical mass of the plant material.</note> of the jalap: after which one sets aside a good *portion* <note>original: 'Partie'</note> of *spirit of wine*, which can be used just as well as before, provided it has been distilled over a very gentle fire. For if one makes the fire too strong, it will carry a part of the *resin* away with it.

§. 2. One pours plenty of water onto the *remains* <note>original: 'Reliqvien'; the residue or sediment left over after the distillation process.</note> of the distillation so that the *spirit of wine*, which holds the *resin* in solution, is weakened: then, as soon as it [the spirit] withdraws and its *particles* fall back together, a kind of milk forms, which becomes clear as soon as the *resin precipitates* <note>original: 'præcipitiret'; the chemical process where a solid settles out of a liquid solution.</note>.

§. 3. If the pound of *jalap* used for this contains 16 *ounces*: you will obtain one *ounce* and 6 *drachms* <note>original: 'Drachmas'; a unit of weight equal to one-eighth of an ounce.</note> of well-washed and dried *resin*.

§. 4. If one has 6 *ounces* of good *scammony*, one extracts 5 *ounces* of *resin* through a similar *preparation*.

## B. Notes.

### §. I.

Although the name <term>Extract</term> <note>A concentrated medicinal substance made by dissolving the active parts of a plant in a solvent and then evaporating the liquid.</note> is very widely used in medicine, it is specifically applied to a certain preparation that has been brought to the consistency and firmness of an <term>electuary</term> <note>original: 'Electuarii'; a medicinal paste or conserve, often made with honey or sugar.</note>. This is nothing other than a purification which is achieved when one frees a <term>mixed substance</term> <note>original: 'mixtum'.</note> from its earthy particles, so that it can work with all the more power the more it has been opened and the freer it has become. Therefore, this <term>operation</term> is useful for <term>mixed substances</term> <note>original: 'mixta'.</note> that give off no scent, but not for those that do smell: because through <term>evaporation</term> one would drive out the best part, which consists of a <term>volatile substance</term> <note>original: 'Volatili'; a substance that evaporates readily at normal temperatures, often carrying the fragrance.</note>. Thus, I would advise no one to make an extract of spices, because the nature of the <term>worker</term> <note>original: 'Laborantens'; personifying Nature as the chemist within the human body.</note> is sufficient to do the same in our bodies when the <term>principles</term> <note>original: 'Principia'; the fundamental chemical components or 'spirits' of a substance.</note> can be separated as easily as they are in this kind of <term>mixed substance</term>.

§. 2. **The Distillation of Guaiacum Wood.** This operation is a separation of the liquid parts of the <term>Guaiacum</term> <note>A heavy, medicinal wood from the Americas, often called *Lignum vitae*.</note> from its earthy part.

§. 3. Take <term>French-wood</term> <note>A common name for Guaiacum, as it was the primary treatment for the "French Disease" (syphilis).</note> that has been rasped or sawn into small pieces, and fill three-quarters of a large <term>retort</term> <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids.</note> with it. Place it in a <term>reverberatory furnace</term> <note>A furnace designed to reflect heat onto the vessel from all sides.</note> and attach a large balloon-shaped <term>receiver</term> <note>original: 'Recipient'; the vessel that catches the distilled vapors.</note> to it. Begin the distillation with a "fire of the first degree" <note>The lowest level of heat, intended to gently warm the substance without scorching it.</note> so that the retort becomes hot very slowly, and the watery moisture or <term>phlegm</term> <note>In early chemistry, 'phlegm' was the inactive, watery component of a substance, one of the five primary principles.</note> passes over. Continue this until it no longer drips, which is a sign that all the phlegm has passed over. Pour off what is in the receiver as useless material. After you have reinserted the receiver into the neck of the flask, seal the joints with <term>lute</term> <note>original: 'verlutirt'; a paste or clay used to make the connections between glass vessels airtight.</note> with all diligence. Then increase the fire degree by degree, and the <term>spirits</term> and the oil will pass over like white clouds. Maintain the fire until nothing more will pass over. Let the vessels cool, open them, and pour the contents of the receiver into a funnel lined with <term>blotting paper</term>. Set this over a bottle or another vessel; the spirit will flow through, leaving a thick, very foul-smelling black oil in the funnel. Pour it into a vial and keep it, for it is <gloss>a</gloss> <note>original: 'Krafft'; referring to the medicinal power or virtue of the substance.</note> a very excellent remedy for <term>mouth-rot</term> <note>original: 'Mundfäule'; likely scurvy or severe oral ulcers.</note>, for toothache, and for the cleansing of old wounds.

<margin>§. 4. How it helps for toothache.</margin>
§. 4. These types of oils are very good for toothache, because with their branch-like particles they close up the nerves <note>original: *Spann-Adern*; literally "tension-veins," a term historically used for nerves, tendons, or ligaments</note> and prevent any air from entering. §. 6. The fixed salt <note>original: *Sal fixum*; the salt that remains stable and does not vaporize even under high heat</note> is an alkali <term>original: *Alkali*; a basic salt that reacts with acids</term>, which acts much like others of its kind: however, it is likely enough that the fixed salts of plants—no matter how thoroughly they have been calcined <term>original: *calcinirt*; reduced to ash through intense heat to remove all organic matter</term>—always retain some power from the plant from which they were extracted.

§. 7. If one wishes to calcine the remaining earth further, one can still extract some salt, although very little.

## The Fourth Chapter.
### A. On Paper, its Oil and Spirit.

->§. 1.<-

The Papyrus of the ancients, from which our paper takes its name, was a tree <note>The author refers to the papyrus plant (*Cyperus papyrus*) as a tree, a common historical classification for large aquatic plants</note> that grew in Egypt near the Nile: its bark was prepared in a certain way and used for writing upon. However, our paper is made from collected old rags and scraps, which are pounded in special mills and turned into a very fine material: this is then moistened with enough water and finally placed under a press to make paper from it.

->§. 2.<-

Now, this paper also has some use in medicines, such as when several small pieces are lit together to create a smoke which women burdened with hysterical vapors <note>original: *vaporibus hystericis*; a historical medical term for a wide range of physical and emotional symptoms once believed to be caused by the womb</note> inhale: as they are commonly comforted by such an unpleasant smell, as well as by many other similar things.

# Chapter 6.

## Regarding the Bark of the Cinchona tree in General.

§. 1.

**Quinquina** or **Cinchona bark** <note>original: "China de China"</note> is a bark that has been brought to us from Peru for several years now. It retains the name of the tree from which it is peeled, which is as large as a cherry tree and is called **Fever-wood** <note>original: "Palo de Calenturas" (Spanish) and "Fieber-Holz" (German)</note> by the Spaniards. It is available in two varieties, either cultivated or wild: a) The cultivated is far better than the other; the best **Quinquina** is the bark which is grown most densely together, has a bitter taste, and a red color.

§. 2. This is the most certain remedy that has been found to date for restraining the *agitation of intermittent fevers* <term>fermentation of Febrium intermittentium</term> <note>The author refers to the "fermentation" of the blood or humors that was once believed to cause the recurring cycles of "intermittent fevers," such as malaria.</note> and alternating fevers. For a long time, it was used in this way: the patient was made to take half a *drachm* to 2 *drachms* <term>drachmas</term> <note>A drachm (or dram) is a historical unit of weight; 2 drachms would be roughly 7.8 grams or about 1.5 teaspoons of powder.</note> of its fine powder in warm wine right at the onset of the *fever fit* <term>paroxismi</term> <note>A paroxysm is the sudden attack or peak of a disease's symptoms, in this case, the shaking chills and high heat of a fever.</note>. However, in our time, the method has changed, such as when one [extracts] an ounce in 2 pounds of wine for twice twenty-four hours in a *water bath* <term>Balneo Mariæ</term> <note>Literally a "Mary's Bath" or bain-marie; a vessel of water used to heat another container gently to a fixed temperature.</note>

That is: it holds the moisture bound and turns it into a kind of sediment <note>original: "Loß"; likely referring to a neutralized, thickened mass that has ceased to "ferment" or flow.</note>. After this, the moisture usually remains still for 15 days, and the patient feels somewhat bloated and heavy, especially if they have not yet been sufficiently **purged** <note>Given laxatives to clear out "corrupt" fluids.</note>. Then the fever returns because the moisture is stirred up by the **spirits** <term>spiritus</term> <note>In early medicine, these were vital, volatile fluids believed to circulate and power the body's functions.</note> of the body; it then unites with other similar moistures that have collected over the 15 days, breaks free from the **Cinchona bark**, and ferments just as before.

## B Tincture of Cinchona Bark.

->§. 1.<-

This process is an extraction of the most oily and pure components from the <term>Cinchona bark</term> <note>original: "Chinæ de China"</note>, which is achieved by using <term>spirit of wine</term> <note>original: "Spiritus Vini"; a high-proof distilled alcohol used as a solvent</note>.

->§. 2.<-

Pour four ounces of good and coarsely powdered Cinchona into a <term>cucurbit</term> <note>original: "Cucurbit"; a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation and extraction</note>. Pour spirit of wine over it until it reaches four fingers' height above the material. Place another cucurbit on top of it so that a <term>double vessel</term> <note>original: "vaisseau de rencontre"; a French term for two vessels joined at the mouth to allow vapors to circulate and condense</note> is formed. Seal the joints with great care and place your vessel for four days in <term>manure</term> <note>original: "Mist"; composting manure was used as a source of gentle, steady heat in early chemistry</note> or a <term>steam bath</term> <note>original: "Balneum vaporum"</note>. Stir it from time to time, and the spirit of wine will take on a red color. Open the vessels, filter the tincture through <term>blotting paper</term> <note>original: "Lösch-Pappier"; used here as a filter</note>, and store it in a well-sealed bottle.

### Chapter 7.
## A. Concerning Cloves in General.

->§. 1.<-

<margin>§. 1. Description of the Clove tree.</margin>
A clove is the fruit of a tree that is as large as a <term>laurel tree</term> <note>original: "Lorbeer-Baum"</note> and grows without cultivation on the <term>Molucca Islands</term> <note>the "Spice Islands" in modern-day Indonesia</note>. Its bark looks like <term>cinnamon bark</term> but tastes like cloves. This tree has very many branches; its leaves resemble those of the willow; they smell and taste strongly of its fruit. Its blossoms, which it bears in great quantity, are first white, then green and strongly scented, and finally they turn red from the heat of the sun. At that point, they reveal the clove, which is like the bud or the beginning of a fruit; it has the shape of a nail. Therefore, they are called *clou de giroffle* <note>French for "nail of clove"</note> or "spice-nails" <note>original: "Gewürtz-Nägelein"</note>; they are always found at the very tips of the tree's branches.

§. 2. No herb is seen growing beneath the clove tree, and this is without doubt due to its many...

# B. Observations.

### §. 1.

The acorns are allowed to dry for this reason: to drive out a watery moisture that otherwise prevents the acorn oil from binding easily with the hazelnut oil. They are also peeled so that only the oiliest part of the acorn remains. They are powdered very finely so that the hazelnut oil can more easily penetrate all their small particles and dissolve the oil out of them all the better.

<margin>§. 2. Pressing alone yields no acorn oil.</margin>

### §. 2.

Acorn oil cannot be extracted by pressing alone because it is stuck in too much earthy matter and is, as it were, swallowed up and held by it. It is true that if one distills the acorn through a <term>retort</term> <note>original: "Kolben"; a glass or metal vessel with a long neck used for distilling liquids</note>, just as one does with <term>guaiacum wood</term> <note>original: "Frantzofen-Holtz," literally "Frenchman's wood." This resinous wood from the Caribbean was famously used in the early modern period to treat "the French disease" (syphilis).</note>, one forces an oil out: however, it is black and stinking, as all oils extracted in this manner tend to be, and it is not suitable for the purposes for which acorn oil is normally used.

### §. 3.

There would indeed be another way to make acorn oil if one wanted to use a <term>still</term> <note>original: "Blaſe"; the boiler or copper pot of a distilling apparatus</note> along with its <term>condenser</term> <note>original: "refrigeranten"; the cooling part of the still where vapors turn back into liquid</note> (both of which must be tin-lined) for that purpose; the acorn powder would be poured into a large amount of water and distilled like cinnamon oil. However, even if one had distilled for a very long time, one would still not get more than a few...

### §. 4.
Therefore, it seems most sensible to me to prepare a blended oil that carries as much of the acorn's potency as possible, rather than making one without additives that completely lacks the desired effect. Moreover, hazelnut oil is exceptionally well-suited to the properties of acorn oil.

<margin>§. 5. Nut Oil.</margin>

### §. 5.
When one wishes to make hazelnut oil, one must select the finest, largest hazelnuts—which are called **filberts** <note>original: "avelines" or "abelines" in French and "avellanæ nuces" in Latin; specifically referring to the large, cultivated variety of hazelnuts.</note>. Take a generous quantity of their kernels, crush them in a marble mortar until they become a paste, and then place them in the press between heated wooden plates. An oil will be squeezed out, which should be collected in a bowl.

### §. 6.
This oil is good for **stabbing chest pains** <note>original: "Brust-stechen"; a term often used in historical medicine for pleurisy or sharp respiratory discomfort.</note>. One administers a dose of two **drams** <note>original: "drachmas"; an apothecary weight approximately equal to 3.9 grams.</note> up to one **ounce**. Externally, it is used to make the skin clean and soft, as it strengthens it.

§. 6. If one only requires the <term>fixed salt</term> <note>original: sal fixum; the stable alkaline salts, such as potassium carbonate, that remain after a plant is burned to ash and processed</note> from a plant, regardless of which type it may be, one does not necessarily need to undertake the entire distillation of the plant.
