After letting it steep therein, one then filters the <term>infusion</term> and allows the moisture to evaporate in a basin; what remains is a brownish salt. This is then <term>calcined</term> <note>original: calcinirt; a chemical process where a substance is heated to high temperatures in a crucible to remove impurities</note> in a melting-pot for as long as it takes to turn white. One then dissolves it in clear water, filters the **solution** <note>original: dissolution</note>, and allows the moisture to evaporate in an earthenware basin. In this way, one obtains a very pure and white salt, which must be stored in a very well-sealed glass bottle.

<margin>§. 6. Adulterated Salt.</margin>
§. 7. Just as one extracts only a small amount of <term>fixed salt</term> from a great many herbs—and indeed only with considerable effort and loss of time—people have not been idle in adulterating it, so that they might sell it at a low price. §. 7. a) Every **fixed salt** <note>original: sal fixum</note> extracted from a plant through **incineration** <note>original: Einäscherung; the process of burning a substance to ash</note> must be **alkaline** and necessarily **effervesce** <note>original: auffsieden; to bubble or hiss, like a modern antacid tablet in water</note> when **acids** <note>original: acida</note> are poured onto it—which those **fixed salts** falsely presented as such do not do.

b) Because the **fixed salt** of a plant has very wide **pores** <note>original: porós</note>, it absorbs water very easily and melts <note>This refers to deliquescence, where a salt absorbs so much atmospheric moisture that it dissolves into a liquid.</note> immediately if it is not kept sealed in a glass bottle with all possible diligence. Yet this does not happen with the salts of the **itinerant sellers** <note>original: Umbträger; traveling peddlers who sold unregulated medicines and chemical preparations</note>, who can keep them in their boxes for several years without them becoming damp; moreover, they even tend to produce a **purified** **saltpeter** <note>original: Salpeter; potassium nitrate, used in gunpowder and medicine</note> or **alum** <note>original: Alaun; a mineral salt used as an astringent</note> [instead of the promised plant salt].

c) Furthermore, the **alkaline salt** of a plant **crystallizes** only with great difficulty, and its **crystals** do not look at all like the salts sold by the itinerant sellers.

d) Since plants do not yield much salt, and its production costs a fair amount, it also cannot be sold as cheaply as they do, for they sell a pound for at most 30 **soles** <note>original: soles; likely referring to the "sou," a coin of relatively low value</note> or 12 **groschen** <note>a common silver coin in German-speaking lands</note>.

## The 13th Chapter.
# A. Of Roses in general.

For when one takes them out / it attaches itself to the fingers and other parts it touches / in such a way that it causes an itching / which one must scratch <note>original: *gratter*</note> for a long time. Their seeds are constipating / and one adds them to the <term>decoctions: liquid medicines made by boiling herbs in water</term>.

§. 5. The simple pale roses smell much stronger and are far better than the full <note>meaning "double" roses with many layers of petals</note> roses, because their medicinal power remains concentrated in fewer petals. They are preferred far more than the others; they purge <note>original: *purgiren*; to cleanse the bowels</note>, thin, and purify the blood <note>original: *Geblüth*</note>, and dispel vapors <note>original: *Dünste*; internal gases or "humors" thought to rise from the stomach and affect the head</note>. Their scent alone sometimes disperses the viscous moisture of the brain which, when it descends into the stomach—as I have often seen—causes vomiting. This mucus <note>original: *Rotz*</note> is also discharged through the nose and saliva, and triggers a cold <note>original: *Schnupffen*</note>. From these roses, one also makes rose syrup and other purgative compounds <note>original: *purgierende Compositiones*</note>.

<margin>§. 6. Musk-Roses <note>original: *Biesem-Rosen*; "Biesem" is an archaic German term for musk</note></margin>
§. 6. The Musk-Roses are named as such because they have a musk-like scent; their color is white; they appear much later than the other roses, only coming forth in the autumn. They have almost the same effect as the pale roses, yet they purge—especially in warm countries—far more strongly than the others. One needs only three or four of them to have a sufficient <term>purgative: a medicine used to encourage the evacuation of the bowels</term>. They are taken in juices or sometimes in <term>preserves: medicinal preparations where plant material is "conserved" with sugar</term>; they often cause vomiting.

<margin>§. 7. Common white roses. §. 8. Provence roses</margin>

§. 7. Common white roses smell very strong and are used only for distillation.

§. 8. Red roses are called <term>Provence roses</term> <note>likely *Rosa gallica* or *Rosa centifolia*, highly valued in early modern pharmacy</note> because many fine specimens come to us from those lands; they have very little scent. One picks them from the buds before they have fully blossomed so that they can be kept in good condition, for when they are open, they lose much of their color and potency. They are <term>astringent</term> <note>original: "stopffen," meaning they bind the bowels or constipate</note>; a rose conserve is made from them, as well as rose honey and many other preparations. They are left to dry for use in various remedies, and they are far more effective at binding the bowels when dried than when fresh. From these same roses, as I have demonstrated in my notes on the distillation of <term>vitriol</term> <note>sulfuric acid or its sulfate salts</note>, one also makes a rose tincture.

§. 9. There are also other kinds of roses, such as blue ones that grow in Italy, and yellow ones. However, it is not necessary to speak of them because they are not used in medicine.

<margin>§. 2. The time to pick roses.</margin>
§. 2. One should pick roses that have just recently bloomed, a little after sunrise; this is so that the goodness and the <term>spirit of the air</term> <note>original: "Lufft-Spiritus"; a contemporary belief in a vital life-force or "spirit" present in the atmosphere and captured by morning dew</note>, which the nightly dew has impressed upon them, might be preserved before the heat of the sun scatters it again. It must also be fair weather, because rain otherwise moistens them and robs them of their strength.

<margin>§. 3. How the rose juice is easily extracted.</margin>
§. 3. To extract the rose juice more effectively, they must be well-stamped <note>crushed or pounded</note>, then left to steep <note>original: "beitzen"</note> for 8 to 10 hours in a bowl <note>original: "Napp"</note> or an earthenware basin, and then pressed out through a linen cloth using a press. This <term>fermentation</term> <note>here referring to a brief maceration process rather than long-term alcohol production</note> makes the slimy parts of the rose subtle, thin, and fluid. They yield far less juice and will tear the linen cloths if one brings them to the press immediately after stamping without this added fermentation.

§. 4. If one wishes to add no moisture at all to the roses, one must distill them in a <term>water bath</term> <note>original: "balneo Mariæ"; a double-boiler method used to ensure gentle, even heating</note> or a <term>steam bath</term> <note>original: "vaporum"</note>. For if the vessel were placed over an open fire, the roses would settle at the bottom and burn; the resulting water would then either taste scorched or, at the very least, smell of the <term>distilling equipment</term> <note>original: "Brenn-Zeug"</note>.

§. 5. # D. Spirit of Roses.

### §. 1.

This operation raises the oily, subtle, and essential parts of the rose into a liquid <note>original: *liquore*</note>.

### §. 2.

Take 14 or 15 pounds of pale, simple, whole, and strongly scented roses together with the buds: crush them well and then place them into a large earthenware pot <note>original: *Gretz-Topff*; likely a ceramic vessel from Graz, known for heat-resistance</note>, of which at least one-third must remain empty. Pour over it 6 pounds of other such rose-juice that has been warmed and in which 8 or 10 ounces of <term>beer yeast</term> <note>brewer's yeast used to trigger fermentation</note> must have been dissolved; stir everything together well and seal the pot with all diligence. Then digest <note>to let sit in gentle heat</note> the matter for 3 or 4 days in warm <term>horse manure</term> <note>a common historical method for providing steady, low fermentation heat</note> until it has taken on a wine-like odor, and then distill it in a <term>steam bath</term> <note>original: *balneo vaporum*</note>. You must <term>seal</term> <note>original: *verlutiren*; to seal the joints of the apparatus with "lute" (a clay or paste) to prevent steam from escaping</note> its vessels well and manage its fire very gently so that only the most spirituous part rises. When you have drawn off about 4 pounds of liquid, extinguish the fire, remove the <term>receiver</term> <note>original: *Recipienten*; the vessel that catches the distillate</note>, and rectify <note>to purify a liquid through repeated distillation</note> its contents through a <term>matrass</term> <note>original: *Matras*; a long-necked glass flask</note>, in the same manner as the Spirit of Cress <note>original: *Kresse-Spiritum*</note> described above is rectified.

§. 2. The pot must be large because of the fermentation, which pushes the material upward. §. 3. One can also make a Spirit of Roses <note>original: *Spiritum rosarum*</note> in the following manner: Crush 20 to 30 pounds of pale roses into a paste; pour it into long beer jugs made of Grætz earth <note>A type of clay from Grätz (modern Hradec), valued for its durability in laboratory work</note>; pour a layer one finger thick of powdered common salt, cork wood <note>original: *Pantoffel-Holtz*; literally "slipper-wood," a historical name for cork because it was used for the soles of slippers</note>, and pitch over it. # Chapter 14.

## On Orange Blossom Water.

->§.I.<-

Take 6 pounds of orange blossoms, while they are still fresh; crush them in a marble mortar and put them into a stoneware jar <note>original: *Gretz-Krug*, referring to high-quality chemical-resistant pottery</note>: mix 6 ounces of bitter, finely chopped orange peels (outermost layer only) among them, and pour 4 pounds of white wine and lemon balm water over it: stir everything well together with a small stick, seal the jar as best as possible, and let the matter <term>digest</term> <note>A process of steeping material in gentle heat to extract its properties</note> for two days in warm manure <note>Manure was commonly used in early chemistry as a source of steady, low heat</note>; open the vessel again, quickly pour the material into a large stoneware or glass flask and fit it with a still-head and <term>receiver</term> <note>original: *Recipienten*; the vessel that collects the distilled liquid</note>: seal the joints with all due diligence <note>original: *verlutirt*; to seal with "lute," a paste of clay or wax</note>, and place the <term>cucurbit</term> <note>The lower part of the distilling apparatus containing the liquid</note> in a <term>Bain-Marie</term> <note>original: *balneum Mariæ*; a water bath</note> or steam bath <note>original: *vaporum*</note>, and let the moisture distill over a strong fire; thus you will have a very precious orange blossom water: keep this in a well-protected bottle: it is otherwise called **Napha water** <note>original: *l'eau de Naphe*</note>.

### §. 4.

The **strawberry** and **raspberry** are far better suited for food than for **medicine** <note>original: "Artzeney"</note>: they refresh the sight, the smell, and the taste when they are truly ripe. They have a wine-like flavor and, like all vinous liquids, they strengthen the heart, the stomach, and the brain. Generally, strawberry and raspberry water is distilled in this way: the fruit is crushed, and the moisture is distilled in a **water bath** <note>original: "Balneo Mariæ"; a vessel of boiling water used to heat another container gently.</note> without prior fermentation; however, this water contains very little **spirit** <note>original: "Spiritus"; the volatile, active essence or alcohol of the plant.</note>.

### §. 5.

Others soak their crushed strawberries for 24 hours in **white wine**, then pour everything together into a glass or **Graz cucurbit** <note>original: "Gretz-cucurbit"; a gourd-shaped distilling vessel, specifically one made of earthenware from the city of Graz, known for its heat resistance.</note>, and allow the moisture to pass over. In this way, they obtain a strawberry water that is very good for internal use. The **spirit of wine** <note>original: "Spiritus vini"; alcohol.</note> combines during distillation with the strawberry water and serves as a **vehicle** <note>original: "vehiculo"; a medium used to carry or deliver the medicinal properties.</note> upon which it may pass over.

### §. 5.

<note>The author repeats the section number "5" in the original text.</note>
Others pour their crushed strawberries into **donkey’s milk** and have such a mixture distilled together; this latter water makes the **skin beautiful**.

### §. 6.

The method described by me is to be preferred over the others because the strawberry parts—

However, I would not be against it if one were to pour a little **white wine** onto the pressed strawberries, so that the matter begins to ferment all the sooner once it has become more fluid.

### §. 7.

One must take very ripe strawberries for this, because they are best suited for fermentation. I leave a third of the jar empty, because the material swells up significantly during fermentation. The warmth of **manure** <note>original: "Miſtes"; horse manure was frequently used in early chemistry to provide a steady, gentle "digestive" heat for laboratory vessels.</note> is very well suited to set the particles in motion, as it provides a true heat for **digestion** <note>original: "digestion"; the process of softening or preparing a substance through gentle heat to extract its essence.</note>.

### §. 9.

The **essential salt** <note>original: "sal essentiale"; a chemical principle believed to contain the plant's unique vital properties.</note> of the strawberry performs the same function in this material as that of grapes does in the **must** <note>original: "Moſt"; freshly pressed fruit juice</note> when it foams. Namely, it **rarefies** <note>original: "rarificirt"; to make something less dense or more volatile.</note> the oil-particles and turns them into **spirits** <note>original: "Spiritibus"; volatile alcohols or essences.</note>. However, because there are far fewer of these **principles** <note>original: "Principien"</note> in strawberries than in grapes, a much weaker fermentation occurs in them, and far less spirit is produced.

### §. 9.

Strawberry and raspberry waters that one buys from **lemonade vendors** <note>original: "Limonade-Wirthen"</note> are merely the pressed juice of these fruits, into which enough water and sugar have been added to prepare a pleasant water: they allow it to clarify and place it in **ice**, and sometimes even add **aromatics** <note>original: "Rauchwerck"; literally "smoke-work," referring here to fragrant substances or spices added to enhance the scent and flavor.</note> to make it even more delightful.

### Chapter 16.
## Nut Water.

§. 1.

Build a gentle fire beneath it and allow approximately half of the liquid to distill. Let the fire go out, strain and press the remainder left in the vessel, and pour the pressed juice back into the vessel, and let approximately two-thirds distill over. Pour these distilled waters together and save them.

## B. Notes.

->§. 1.<-

<margin>§. 1. Why nothing grows around walnut trees</margin>
The walnut <note>original: "Welsche Nuß"</note> is called in Latin <term>nux juglans</term> <note>walnut</note>, as if it were <term>Jovis glans</term> <note>Jupiter's acorn</note> or <term>glans Juvans</term> <note>the helpful acorn</note>, that is / it is called Jupiter’s acorn or the Helping-Acorn / because it is of a particular excellence / and serves many purposes in the arts as well as in food and medicines. It is not necessary to describe its tree / because nothing is more common. Around the walnut tree / much greenery will never grow / either because a certain vapor or <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "Spiritus"; a volatile chemical essence</note> comes from its root which stifles it / or because the tree / being very tall / has widely spreading branches and bears large oily leaves, casting too much shadow / so that neither the sun nor the air-spirit <note>the vital qualities of the atmosphere believed to nourish plants</note> can reach these little plants and allow them to grow.

§. 2. Because walnut blossoms have little juice / one must pour their own <term>decoction</term> <note>original: "decocto"; a concentrated liquor made by boiling the plant material</note> over them: otherwise they might stick to the vessel during distillation / and the water would smell burnt.

§. 3. When the nuts are still only a third of their full size / compared to their usual size at maturity / they are filled with a viscous juice; this part is well-loosened by the <term>digestion</term> <note>a chemical process where a substance is softened or broken down by gentle, consistent heat</note> performed after the crushing / so that the <term>principles</term> <note>original: "principia"; the fundamental chemical or medicinal components believed to be the "spirit" of the plant</note> can become free and volatile. It is also added to **enemas** <note>original: "Clystire"</note>. Furthermore, when freshly extracted without the use of heat, it is used to cleanse the face.

## Chapter 17.

### A. The Wound-Water, which is also
### called Gunshot-Water (*eau d’arquebusade*).

->§. 1.<-

Take the leaves and roots of the Great **Comfrey** <note>original: "Consolida"</note>, leaves of **Sage**, of **Mugwort** <note>original: "Artemisia"</note>, and of **Sanicle** <note>original: "Lorenz-Kraut"; likely *Sanicula europaea*</note>—four handfuls of each. Furthermore, take the leaves of **Betony**, **Wood Sanicle**, **Daisy** <note>original: "Tausendschön"</note>, the **Small Comfrey**, or **Great Figwort** <note>original: "scrophularia"</note>, **Plantain**, **Agrimony**, and **Vervain**.

**Wormwood** and **Fennel**, two handfuls of each: furthermore, leaves of **St. John’s Wort**, **Long Birthwort**, **Spearmint**, **Speedwell**, **Lesser Centaury**, **Yarrow**, **Tobacco**, **Mouse-ear**, **Curled Mint**, and **Hyssop**, one handful of each. Draw off the moisture in the usual manner with a moderate fire, and thus you will have the **Gunshot-Water**, which you must keep in a well-secured bottle.

§. 2. Applied externally, it is good for fractures, sprains, and swellings. It cleanses old injuries, encourages the growth of new flesh, strengthens, protects against **putrefaction** <note>gangrene or rotting</note>, and halts the progress of **cancers** <note>original: "Krebs"; can refer to malignant tumors or spreading ulcers</note>. It can also be used against the **vapors** <note>a historical term for lightheadedness, fainting, or anxiety</note>.

§. 41. <margin>§. 42. Hyssop.</margin>
§. 42. **Hyssop**, which is called *hyssopus* in Latin, is a plant with many stems or splayed-out rods that are somewhat hairy, a **foot** <note>original: *Schuh*; a historical unit of measurement approx. 30cm</note> high, knotty, and branched. It has long and narrow leaves; the blossoms appear like ears of grain and are blue. The root is as thick as a little finger, long, hard, and woody; it grows in gardens and contains much volatile salt and refined oil, but little water and earth.

<margin>§. 43. Power of hyssop.</margin>
§. 43. It is a good **wound-herb** <term>Wund-Kraut: a plant used to heal cuts and external injuries</term>; it removes impurities, opens [blockages], and is used for chest and lung diseases, such as **shortness of breath** <note>original: *Engbrüstigkeit*</note> and **consumption** <term>Schwindsucht: a historical term for wasting diseases, most often tuberculosis</term>.

§. 44. Because most plants that are added to these **waters** <note>Referring to the distilled medicinal "gunshot-wound water" mentioned on the previous page</note> do not have much juice of their own, one must add white wine, as this **liquid** <note>original: *liquor*</note> triggers fermentation and tears the volatile salt and **sulfur particles** <note>original: *Schwefeltheilgen*; in early modern chemistry, "sulfur" was the principle of flammability and oiliness</note> loose from the plant matter.

§. 45. However, during the distillation process, one must not maintain too strong a fire, so that the material does not settle at the bottom and the distilled water does not take on the smell of the distillation vessel or of burning.

§. 46. Once half of the **liquid** <note>original: *liquorem*</note> has been distilled, one must pour the remaining residue out of the **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit: the gourd-shaped glass or ceramic vessel that holds the liquid to be distilled</term> into a linen cloth and squeeze out the juice in a press. This juice is then poured back into the cucurbit and distilled. In this manner, the burnt smell can be prevented. However, if one has a **steam bath** <note>original: *Balneum vaporum*</note> or **water bath** <note>original: *Balneum Mariae*; literally "Mary's bath"</note> that is large enough for the task, it is much safer to distill using that method.

§. 47. If one then dries and burns the **pulp** <note>original: *Drester*; the solid remains after pressing</note> in such a way as to make a lye from its ashes, and extracts a **salt** through evaporation, this salt can then be dissolved into the distilled water. This results in an exceedingly magnificent, cleansing, and dissolving **medicine** <note>original: *Artzeney*</note>.

### §. 4. How it becomes wine.

To explain this matter, one must know that the **must** carries much **essential salt** <term>sal essentiale: in early chemistry, a salt believed to contain the specific "essence" or life-force of the plant</term>: now, when this salt, acting as a volatile salt during **fermentation** <note>original: Fermentation</note>, exerts all its power to tear itself loose from its oily particles—to which it was, as it were, bound—it penetrates, divides, and pushes these aside until, with its subtle and sharp-cutting points, it **rarefies them into spirits** <note>original: Spiritibus rarificirt</note>. This force causes the surging and boiling that occurs with the wine, and simultaneously its purification. For it separates and casts out its coarsest particles into a foam, one part of which attaches to the sides of the barrel and becomes stone, while the other part sinks to the bottom; this is called **tartar** <note>original: tartarum</note> or wine-stone and **lees** <note>original: Heffen; the sediment of yeast and grape debris</note>.

### §. 5. What is the spirit of wine?

## B. The Distillation of Wine into Aquavit.

->§. 1.<-

Fill a large copper <term>still-pot</term> <note>original: "Blase"; literally a "bladder" or "bubble," referring to the rounded base of the distilling apparatus</note> half-full of wine, place its <term>still-head</term> <note>original: "Helm"</note> or <term>condenser</term> <note>original: "refrigeranten"</note> upon it, and attach a <term>receiver</term> <note>original: "Recipienten"; the vessel that collects the distillate</note>: <term>seal</term> <note>original: "verlutirt"; from "lute," a paste used to make joints airtight</note> all the joints well with wet bladders, and distill approximately one fourth of the moisture over a gentle fire; or continue until the distilled <term>liquid</term> <note>original: "liquor"</note> no longer catches fire when held to a flame. What is then found in the <term>receiver</term> is <term>Aquavit</term> <note>original: "Aquavit"; from the Latin "aqua vitae" or "water of life," a high-proof distilled spirit</note>.

->§. 2.<-

§. 3. One can indeed obtain Aquavit from all kinds of wines; however, the wine in one country always yields more than in other places. ### §. 13. Decomposition of the Wine
<note>original: *Aufflosung des VVeins*</note>

If one wishes, out of curiosity, to completely decompose the wine, one must take the residue remaining in the cucurbit <term>cucurbit</term> <note>a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</note> after the brandy <term>Aqvavit</term> <note>literally "water of life," referring to distilled spirits</note> has been drawn off, and distill away all the water. A substance will then remain of the kind that can only come from wine-grapes. Place this into a retort <term>Retorte</term> <note>a glass vessel with a long neck pointing downward, used for distilling liquids</note> and place it in a furnace; draw off even more phlegm <term>phlegma</term> <note>the watery, tasteless part of a distillate</note> over a small fire until the sharp substance begins to arrive. Then, attach a large receiver <term>Recipienten</term> <note>a vessel used to collect the products of distillation</note> to the retort, seal the joints well with lute <note>original: *verlutirt*; a clay or paste used to make laboratory equipment airtight</note>, and increase the fire gradually so that the acidic spirits <term>Spiritus</term> and a stinking oil come out; maintain the fire for as long as it takes until nothing more wishes to distill out.

§. 14. Separate the oil from the spirit <term>Spiritu</term> using a funnel lined with blotting paper <term>Lösch-Pappier</term>, because the spirit will filter through while the oil, which is very thick, will remain on top. However, one must keep in mind that far more oil is drawn from must <term>Most</term> <note>fresh, unfermented grape juice</note> than from wine, which sufficiently confirms the judgment I previously offered regarding the origin of the volatile <term>volatilisch</term> <note>easily evaporated at room temperature</note> spirit of wine. For since a considerable portion of oil from the must has gone into the composition of the volatile spirit of wine, certainly not much of it can have remained in the juice from which the brandy was distilled.

->§. 4.<-

<margin>§. 4. Common way to make Spirit of Wine.</margin>

# C. Hungary Water <note>original: *Hungarisch Wasser*; a famous 14th-century medicinal tonic and perfume, traditionally made by distilling rosemary with high-proof alcohol.</note>

## §. 1.

This operation is nothing other than a **spirit of wine** <note>original: *Spiritus vini*; distilled alcohol</note> that is infused with the most essential and nourishing parts of **rosemary blossoms**.

<margin>§. 2. Efficacy. Dosage.</margin>

## §. 2.

Pluck **rosemary blossoms** when they are at their peak perfection; fill a glass or **Grätz cucurbit** <note>original: *Gretz-Cucurbit*; a gourd-shaped boiling flask likely named for the glassworks in Graz, Austria</note> halfway with them, and pour enough **spirit of wine** over them until the rosemary blossoms are swimming around inside. Place the cucurbit in a **water bath** <note>original: *Balneum Mariæ*; a gentle heating method using a vessel of hot water</note> and provide it with its **helm** <note>original: *Helm*; the still-head or alembic top</note> and **recipient** <note>original: *Recipienten*; the receiving flask</note>. **Lute** <note>original: *verlutirt*; to seal the joints of the apparatus with a paste or clay to prevent steam from escaping</note> all the joints well, and maintain a **digestion-fire** <note>original: *digestions-Feuer*; a low, steady heat used to draw out the properties of a substance without boiling it rapidly</note> under it for three days. After this, you may open your vessels and pour the distilled liquid back into the cucurbit. Set up your flask again and give it a strong fire so that the juice passes over, with one drop following steadily after another. Once you have drawn off approximately two-thirds, let the fire go out, allow the vessels to cool, and open them; you will find a very good **Hungary Water** in the recipient, which you can keep in a well-secured **vial**. It is good for **heart palpitations** and associated weaknesses, for **gout**, for **lethargy** <note>original: *Schlaff-sucht*; literally "sleep-sickness," historically referring to abnormal drowsiness or coma</note>, for **stroke** <note>original: *Schlag*; apoplexy</note>, and for **uterine complaints** <note>original: *Mutter-Beschwerungen*; historical term for "hysteria" or ailments believed to be caused by the womb</note>. The dose ranges from one **drachm**— <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword *ma* indicates the word "drachma" or "drachme."</note>

<margin>§. 5. The phlegm of wine vinegar does not depart through distillation.</margin>
§. 5. Generally, one distills wine vinegar in such a manner that one separates what comes over first and discards it as a <term>phlegm</term> <note>phlegma: in early modern chemistry, this referred to the watery, tasteless, and medically "weak" part of a substance that often distills off first</note>, keeping only that which distills thereafter. However, I have observed that the <term>phlegm</term> of wine vinegar cannot be separated at all like that of many other acidic <term>liquors</term> <note>original: "Liqvoribus"; a general term for liquid chemical substances</note>: what comes over first is just as sour as what follows, no matter how small a fire one starts with. For this reason, I do not extract any <term>phlegm</term> from the wine vinegar at all, but rather take the strongest I can find right away. Furthermore, one does not distill wine vinegar for the purpose of obtaining its water and <term>phlegm</term>, but rather one only wants to rid it of its coarse <term>tartaric</term> <note>tartarischen: relating to "tartar," the potassium bitartrate crystals and sediment found in wine barrels</note> particles, so that it becomes as clear as water and imparts no <term>tincture</term> <note>Tinctur: here meaning an unwanted color or staining quality</note> to the <term>ingredients</term> <note>original: "ingredientibus"</note> dissolved within it.

§. 6. The reason why one cannot pour off the wine vinegar from its <term>phlegm</term> through distillation is because it holds many <term>sulfurous spirits</term> <note>original: "schwefflichte Spiritus"; in the chemistry of the time, "sulfurous" referred to the oily, volatile, or combustible principle of a substance</note> as if bound within itself; these, however, always retain some degree of movement and volatility, which lift the <term>acids</term> <note>original: "acida"</note> and make them just as light as the <term>phlegm</term>.

## D. Crystals of Steel—or Martial Tartar.
<note>"Martial" is an alchemical term referring to the planet Mars, which was traditionally associated with the metal iron.</note>

### §. 1.

This **preparation** <term>preparation: a chemical substance processed for medicinal or laboratory use</term> is a crystalline salt that is filled with the most subtle iron particles <note>original: "Eisentheilgen"</note> that can be most easily dissolved.

### §. 3.

§. 13. If one allows some salt of tartar <note>original: "Tartarsalz"; potassium carbonate.</note> or liquid of tartar to dissolve in fresh water that has been distilled from a green plant, the water becomes completely green; and the greener the <margin>B.</margin> plant was from which this water was drawn, the greener this salt will also become. Sour cherry <note>original: "Morellen-Wasser."</note> water becomes greener than lemon balm water, and lemon balm water greener than the water of small speedwell <note>original: "Veronica-Wasser."</note>, and so on.

§. 14. The cause of this occurrence lies in the fact that the alkaline salt thins <note>original: "rarificirt"; to make less dense or more fluid, allowing trapped particles to expand and become visible.</note> and makes visible many small plant particles that rose with the water during distillation and were previously invisible. However, the water must be distilled by a very strong heat: for if it were drawn over in a **water bath** <note>original: "balneo Mariæ"; a gentle heating method using a container of hot water to ensure the temperature does not exceed boiling.</note> or by a similar heat, nothing green would be seen, even if one added alkaline salt to it.

§. 15. Cherry, rose, and other waters that are distilled from fruits or blossoms do not take on any color, even if one pours salt of tartar into them.

§. I.

This operation is an extraction of certain particles from the salt of tartar, which is accomplished by the **spirit of wine** <note>original: "Spiritu vini"; high-proof distilled alcohol.</note>.

§. 2. Melt 20 ounces of salt of tartar <term>salt of tartar <note>original: "Tartar-Saltz"; potassium carbonate produced from the crusts left in wine barrels.</note></term> in a melting crucible <term>melting crucible <note>original: "Schmeltz-Tiegel"; a ceramic or graphite container used for high-temperature melting.</note></term> with a strong fire: once it is melting, cover it with a tile; stoke the coals all around it, and blow upon them in such a way that an even greater heat is produced than if you were melting gold. Maintain this degree of heat for about 6 hours, or until your salt of tartar has taken on a red-speckled color. This can easily be recognized if you dip the tip of a spatula into the melting crucible, as some of the material will remain hanging on it when you pull it out again. Then, grasp the melting crucible with the fire tongs and place it in a marble mortar; the material will coagulate in a short time. Powder this immediately and place it into a previously warmed <term>matrass <note>original: "Matras"; a glass flask with a round body and a long neck.</note></term>. Pour tartarized spirit of wine <note>original: "Spiritum vini tartarisatum"; highly concentrated alcohol that has been distilled with salt of tartar to remove water.</note> over it until it rises 4 fingers high above the material. Cover it with another <term>matrass</term> so that a meeting vessel <note>original: "vaisseau de rencontre"; a chemical apparatus where two flasks are joined neck-to-neck, allowing vapors to circulate and condense back into the bottom flask.</note> is formed. Seal the joints as well as possible with a wet bladder <note>This refers to using a piece of animal bladder, which shrinks and hardens as it dries, to create an airtight seal.</note>; place your <term>matrass</term> in sand <note>A "sand bath" used to provide even, indirect heat.</note> and keep it warm with a graduated fire so that the spirit of wine boils for seven to eight hours, during which time it will turn red. After this, let the vessels cool, open them, and pour off this tincture—which will have a very pleasant smell—by tilting the vessel, and store it in a well-secured vial <term>vial <note>original: "Phiole"; a small glass container for liquids.</note></term>.

§. 3. One can pour more spirit of wine onto the remaining salt of tartar and proceed as before,

§. 4. The **tincture** of **salt of tartar** is an excellent **opening medicine** <term>aperient <note>original: "Aperiens"; a substance used in historical medicine to "open" the body's channels and promote the elimination of waste.</note></term>; it purifies the blood and removes bad humors <note>original: "böse Feuchtigkeiten"; referring to the theory that health depended on the balance of four vital fluids or "humors" in the body.</note>. §. 5. One must place the **melting crucible** in the **oven** upon a brick, so that the wind blowing through the small door does not cool the bottom, and thus hinder the **melting** of the salt.

§. 6. This **effect** comes solely and entirely from the fact that the fire thins and volatilizes <note>original: "volatilisiret"; the process of turning a solid into a vapor through heat.</note> the particles of this fixed salt, making them capable of rising along with the sulfur of the coal <note>original: "Kohlschwefel"; a historical term for the combustible components found in charcoal or coal.</note>.

It is true that the **spirit of wine** <note>original: "Spirit Vini"; high-proof alcohol, often used as a solvent.</note> takes on the color of a dry leaf; however, it does not come close to the color it must have if it is to be the **tincture of salt of tartar** <note>original: "tinctura salis tartari"</note>. For this must be as red as wine; if it is to become so, one must **calcine** <term>calcine <note>original: "calciniren"; to heat a substance to high temperatures to remove impurities or change its state.</note></term> the salt of tartar in the manner described, and put a great deal of it into a **melting crucible** <note>original: "Schmelztiegel"</note> because it shrinks beyond all measure. One must also 
<margin>Note</margin> observe here that one uses the most highly **rectified spirit** <note>original: "Spiritum vini rectificatissimum"; alcohol that has been repeatedly distilled to achieve maximum purity and strength.</note>: For if even a little **phlegm** <term>phlegm <note>original: "phlegma"; in historical chemistry, the watery, tasteless, and inactive residue left after distillation.</note></term> remains, it will not turn red.

§. 8. This **tincture** therefore does not come from the **fixed sulfur** <note>original: "fix-Schwefel"</note> contained in the salt of tartar, as many would have it; rather, it is nothing other than this salt **exalted** <note>original: "erhöhetes"; in alchemy, to "exalt" a substance meant to raise it to a higher or purer state.</note> in the spirit of wine. For if you only distill the tincture out of curiosity, you will draw out nothing but a spirit of wine, and yet only a little salt of tartar will remain at the bottom, which then has its ordinary whiteness. From this it is sufficiently clear that this color comes solely from the **most secret union** <note>original: "geheimsten Vereinigung"</note> of the spirit of wine with the salt of tartar, because this color disappears again as soon as they are separated from one another.

§. 9. The tincture of this salt of tartar loses its red color over time, namely because the most **subtle** <note>The "subtle" or most volatile parts of a liquid were thought to be the most potent.</note> part of the spirit of wine disperses through the air holes of the glass, and only a spirit remains behind.

This operation is a salt of tartar / which is marked with the acids of the **spirit of vitriol** <term>spirit of vitriol <note>original: "vitriol Spiritus"; a historical name for sulfuric acid.</note></term>.

§.2. Pour into a glass **cucurbit** <term>cucurbit <note>original: "Curcurbit"; a gourd-shaped chemical vessel used in distillation.</note></term> as much **oil of tartar made by deliquescence** <term>deliquescence <note>original: "per-deliquium"; the process of letting a salt sit in a moist place until it absorbs enough water from the air to turn into a liquid "oil."</note></term> as you please / and little by little pour **rectified spirit of vitriol** <note>original: "Spiritum vitrioli rectificatum"; purified sulfuric acid.</note> upon it / then a great **effervescence** <note>original: "Effervescenz"; bubbling or fizzing.</note> will arise therefrom: continue with the pouring / until no more **ebullition** <note>original: "Ebullition"; boiling or bubbling up</note> occurs : then place your cucurbit in the sand <note>A "sand-bath," used to distribute heat evenly from a fire.</note> / and let all moisture evaporate over a small fire / so you will keep a very white salt behind / which you must store in a well-secured **phial** <note>original: "Phiole"; a small glass bottle.</note>.

### §. 4.

One can make vitriolated tartar <note>original: "vitriolirten Weinstein"; potassium sulfate.</note> with salt of tartar <note>potassium carbonate</note> as well as with the oil <note>referring to the "oil of tartar" mentioned on the previous page.</note>: The **boiling** <note>original: "Ebullition"</note> arises from this: that the **acid** <note>original: "acidum"</note> of the vitriol penetrates the alkaline salt of the tartar, separating the particles from one another with force, and granting a free exit to the fire-particles <note>A reference to the early chemical theory that "fire" was a physical substance trapped within matter and released during reactions.</note> locked within. This **effervescence** <note>original: "Effervescenz"</note> happens every time an **alkali** and an **acid** <note>original: "acidum"</note> come together, and it lasts as long as the acid finds nothing left to penetrate in the alkaline salt. A **thickened mass** <note>original: "coagulum"</note> forms, as it were, at the bottom of the vessel; for when the alkali and acid strike against each other and have hooked into one another, their motion is lost, and they **precipitate** <note>original: "præcipitiren"</note> to the bottom due to their weight. Therefore, the **liquid** <note>original: "Liqvor"</note> is by far not as sharp as the oil of tartar was before, even though one has mixed at least as much **spirit of vitriol** <note>original: "Spiritum vitrioli"; sulfuric acid</note> into it: one must let the moisture evaporate gradually, especially toward the end, so that the acid does not rise up.

### §. 5.

### §. 6.
If you have taken two ounces of salt of tartar <note>original: "Tartarsalz"; potassium carbonate</note> for the process, you will extract two and a half ounces of vitriolated tartar <note>original: "tartarum vitriolatum"; potassium sulfate</note>. This addition [of weight] stems from the inherent heaviest and strongest part of the spirit of vitriol <note>original: "Vitriol-Spiritus"; sulfuric acid</note>, because the moisture that evaporated is very phlegmatic <note>original: "Phlegmatisch"; in early chemistry, this refers to a watery, inactive, or weak byproduct of distillation.</note>.

### §. 7.
One can also use rectified oil of vitriol <note>original: "Vitriol-Oel"; a more concentrated form of sulfuric acid than the "spirit."</note> instead of the spirit, but it must be done in smaller quantities because it is exceedingly strong. However, the vitriolated tartar <note>original: "vitriolirte Weinstein"</note> will not be as white as when one uses spirit of vitriol, because some tincture <note>coloration</note> always remains in the oil of vitriol, no matter how well it may have been rectified <note>purified by distillation</note>.

### §. 8.
Some have indeed written that if one puts vitriolated tartar <note>original: "vitriolirten tartarum"</note> into a retort <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids</note> and drives it with fire, one could extract the spirit of vitriol <note>original: "Vitriol-Spiritum"</note> again in almost the same state as it was found during use. But it remains the case that it cannot be as strong, because it has lost its most subtle acid <note>original: "acidum"</note> when it rubbed against the alkali; this can be recognized as much by the taste as by its effects.

§. 19. The same can be said of many other acidic substances that awaken <term>fermentation</term>.

§. 20. At that point, a kind of re-coagulation occurs—that is, the matter returns to its former circumference and volume.

§. 21. There is yet another effect of <term>acids</term> <note>original: "acidorum"</note> which seems distinct from those just discussed: namely, they keep certain bodies that are placed within them fresh, much as salt preserves food. §. 35. What we have established regarding **acids** <note>original: "acidorum"</note> can help us greatly to explain **fevers** and their primary symptoms.

§. 36. First, everyone must admit that when **obstructions** <note>original: "Verstopffungen"</note> occur in our body, the trapped matter **ferments** and becomes **sour**, just as dough, wine, and many other things become sour when they grow old.

§. 37. Yet exactly the opposite occurs, because yeast becomes sour over time. Indeed, vinegar merchants know quite well how to use yeast for this very purpose, letting it ferment heartily with their wine when they wish to quickly produce wine vinegar.

## The 22nd Chapter.

### A. Concerning Opium.

->§. 1.<-

**Opium** <note>original: "Opium," derived from the Greek "opos" for juice</note> is a discharge that runs out of a **poppy head** <note>the seed pod of the poppy plant</note> either naturally or through an incision. Such poppies are commonly found in Greece, the Kingdom of **Cambay** <note>original: "Cambaya," a region in western India</note>, and around **Cairo** <note>original: "Alkair"</note> in Egypt. There are three varieties: black, white, and yellow opium.

§. 2. Although the inhabitants of these countries keep the fine opium for themselves and send us only the **meconium** <note>historically, this referred to the juice pressed from the whole poppy plant, rather than the pure resin harvested from incisions</note>, which is a juice pressed out of these poppy heads. They allow it to become quite thick and wrap it in leaves so that it can be transported more easily. This **medicinal substance** <note>original: "Specerey"; literally "spice," but historically used for exotic drugs</note> is called "opium" in a very broad sense, and we must make do with it because we cannot obtain the genuine kind; however, because it is much less pure than the true opium, it also does not have as much **potency** <note>original: "Krafft"</note>.

§. 3. One can similarly produce a meconium from the poppy heads that grow in Italy and **Languedoc** <note>a historical province in southern France</note>

# B. Extract of Opium, which is simply called Laudanum.

§. 1.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'D' featuring floral and scrollwork ornamentation.</image-desc>This preparation <note>original: "Operation"</note> is the purest part of opium, which has been extracted with **dew** <note>likely May dew, a common solvent in alchemy</note> and **spirit of wine** <term>spirit of wine: high-proof alcohol or ethanol</term> and brought to the consistency and thickness of an extract.

§. 2. Cut 4 ounces of good opium into pieces and put it into a **matrass** <term>matrass: a long-necked glass flask used for boiling and distilling</term>. Pour a small measure of well-filtered rainwater over it, seal your matrass, and place it in a sand bath <note>a container of sand heated to provide even temperature to the glass vessel</note>. Start a small fire beneath it, increasing it gradually, and let the liquid <note>original: "Liqvorem"</note> simmer and boil for two hours; afterwards, strain it while warm and pour it into a bottle.

§. 3. Take the opium that was not dissolved by the rainwater and let it dry in an earthenware basin over a small fire; pour it into a matrass and add **spirit of wine** <note>original: "Spiritum Vini"</note> to the height of four fingers, then seal the flask—

### Observations

->§. 1.<-

**Opium** consists of a **volatile** <note>original: "Spirituösen"</note> part and a coarse, earthy resin. The spiritual part can be very easily dissolved in water; the resinous part, however, must have a sharp <term>solvent <note>original: "Menstruum," a term used by early chemists for a substance that dissolves a solid</note></term>, such as <term>spirit of wine <note>original: "Spiritus Vini," an early term for concentrated alcohol or ethanol</note></term>.

->§. 2.<-

One must let the opium dry after the first dissolution, so that the <term>spirit of wine</term> is not weakened by the watery moisture contained within it, which could prevent the dissolution from proceeding as quickly.

<margin>※</margin>
->§. 3.<-

Distilled wine-vinegar certainly dissolves the opium; however, it can be said that <term>acids <note>original: "acida"</note></term> somewhat weaken its power, as they either destroy or "fix" its volatile part, which otherwise serves as the vehicle <note>literally "wagon"</note> for the other component.

->§. 4.<-

One could indeed use <term>spirit of wine</term> alone to dissolve both parts of the **opium**, but one would have to live in fear that it might allow the volatile part to escape during <term>evaporation <note>original: "Evaporation," the process of heating the liquid to leave behind a concentrated solid</note></term>.

->§. 5.<-

According to our description, one obtains and retains everything that is in the **opium**. Even if the resinous part is dissolved in <term>spirit of wine</term>, it cannot rise up <note>evaporate</note> with it, because it is far too heavy for that: The other part

§ 18. Finally, one can assert that **opium** is one of the greatest remedies we possess, when it is administered in its proper place, at the right time, and in a reasonable **dose** <note>original: "Dosi"</note>. But if one allows too much of it to be taken, it thickens and glues together the fluids in the brain with its sticky particles to such an extent that the arriving **spirits** <note>the vital forces or vapors believed to drive bodily functions</note> are not powerful enough to dissolve this excessive matter; they come to a standstill, gradually **coagulate** <note>thicken or clump together</note>, and finally must lose all their motion. This is why many have died from taking opium.

§ 19. At the same time, however, one can also note that many people have become so accustomed to opium that they eventually no longer become sleepy from its use unless they have taken three to four times more than is normally prescribed. There are people in France who take up to a **drachm** <note>a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams; original: "Drachmam"</note>, and it affects them no more than two **grains** <note>a very small unit of weight, about 65 milligrams; original: "Grane"</note> affects others. The Turks are known to take a piece the size of a hazelnut before they go into battle, in order to make themselves courageous and strong. The reason why no harm comes to them is this: because the opium has already passed through the **brain-tubes** <note>referring to "Hirnröhren," the early modern anatomical belief that nerves and brain passages were hollow tubes for the flow of spirits</note> so often, it has, as it were, made them wide enough. Since it now finds a wide enough passage, nothing at all becomes blocked there,

§. 14. <term>Purgatives (purgantien)</term> <note>original: "Purgantien"; medicines used to cleanse the bowels</note> have been divided into <term>melancholy-expellers (melanogoga)</term>, <term>phlegm-expellers (phlegmagoga)</term>, <term>bile-expellers (cholagoga)</term>, and <term>water-expellers (hydragoga)</term>. §. 17. The <term>phlegm-expelling medicines (phlegmagoga)</term> <note>original: "Phlegmagogischen Artzeneyen"; medicines intended to purge phlegm</note>, such as <term>larch agaric</term> <note>original: "Lerchenschwamm"; a fungus that grows on larch trees, historically used as a potent purgative</note> and <term>colocynth</term> <note>original: "Coloquinten"; also known as bitter apple, a powerful laxative</note>, carry away the <term>phlegm (pituita)</term> <note>original: "Pituite"; one of the four humors, associated with coldness and moisture</note>. This phlegm particularly resides in the brain, which these medicines fill with volatile salts; by means of the body's natural heat, these salts are easily driven upward. When they then <term>condense</term> <note>original: "densificiren"; to make thicker or more solid</note> these <term>humors</term> <note>original: "humores"</note>, they allow them to fall down through the regular purgative channels.

§. 18. The <term>bile-expelling medicines (cholagoga)</term> <note>original: "Cholagogischen"; medicines used to purge yellow bile</note>, such as cinnamon and <term>rhubarb</term> <note>original: "Rhebarbara"</note>, are "sweet" species and do not have as much power to cause fermentation as the others; therefore, they purge only the bile. Because they dissolve most easily and initiate fermentation, they cannot penetrate either the <term>melancholy</term> <note>black bile</note> or the phlegm because of the "filth" <note>viscosity or waste matter</note> of those humors. Thus, one should not be surprised if, in the results of these medicines, one sees a greater evacuation of bile than of other humors.

§. 19. It can be further noted that the remedies which purge phlegm and the <term>melancholic blood</term> remain much longer in the body—leaving their effects behind—than those that purge bile, because they leave behind more solid or <term>fixed salts</term> <note>original: "fester oder Saltze"; in alchemy, "fixed" salts were those that resisted heat and stayed in the body longer</note>. Furthermore, one must not imagine that these phlegm- and melancholy-expelling medicines carry away no bile at all; for they scour out as much as they find. §. 20. The <term>water-expelling medicines (hydragogues)</term> <note>original: "Hydragogischen"</note>, such as the <term>resins</term> <note>original: "resinae"</note> of <term>jalap</term> <note>a Mexican vine root used as a powerful laxative</note> and <term>scammony</term> <note>a purgative resin from a species of bindweed</note>, and <term>polychrest salts</term> <note>original: "salia polychresta"; literally "salts of many uses," usually referring to potassium sulfate</note>, purge the waters [bodily fluids]. However, if one applies oneself even a little bit to <term>medical practice</term> <note>original: "Medicinische Praxin"</note>, one will very quickly observe how purgatives exert different effects on different matters and humors. And even if one could not be entirely convinced of this through medical practice, the <term>rules of chemistry</term> <note>original: "Chymischen Regeln"</note> demonstrate it sufficiently. For just as one has different dissolving agents for the different types of matter one deals with [in a laboratory], why should different purgatives not also be necessary in our bodies to carry away the differently-natured humors?

## Chapter 27.
### On Turpentine.

§. 1.

<margin>§. 1. Turpentine described.</margin> Turpentine is a liquid <term>resin</term> <note>original: "resina"</note> with the consistency of a balsam, which flows out through incisions from many types of trees that grow in great abundance in warm places, such as Italy, Spain, Cyprus, the island of Chios, Provence, and Dauphiné.

It flows from the turpentine tree, which is of moderate height and has elongated, pointed, firm, laurel-green, and very small leaves; its blossoms are shaped like red clusters of grapes, its fruit—

**§. 3.** The turpentine commonly used by us, which is more accurately called mixed turpentine, is an oily, clear, transparent, sticky, bleached white, fragrant, and somewhat sharp-tasting liquid; in the summer, it has the consistency of a syrup, but in the winter, it is as thick as a balsam, and over time it becomes quite dense and firm. It is also tapped through incisions made in spruce, fir, and larch trees in Forest <note>likely Forest-Saint-Julien</note> in Dauphiné <note>a former province in southeastern France</note>, from where it is brought to us. The inhabitants call it *Bijon*, but the only true *Bijon* is that which flows down by itself in summer without any incision, and which very closely resembles the <margin>NB.</margin> true white balsam from Peru.

**§. 4.** Turpentine juices are good <term>diuretics</term> <note>original: "diuretica"; substances that promote the production of urine</note> and expel [waste] through the urine; they are especially good for <term>the stone</term> <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, for <term>nephritic colic</term> <note>original: "nephritische Colica"; severe pain caused by kidney stones</note>, for the retention of urine, for <term>seminal discharge</term> <note>original: "Samenfluß"; often referring to involuntary discharge or gonorrhea</note>, and for ulcers of the kidneys, bladder, and <term>womb</term> <note>original: "Mutter"</note>. 
<margin>pills</margin> 
They are administered in <term>morsels</term> <note>original: "Bißen"; small medicinal balls or pills</note>, or dissolved in a liquid with a bit of egg yolk. They are given in doses from one <term>scruple</term> <note>a small unit of weight, about 1.3 grams</note> up to one <term>drachm</term> <note>original: "drachmäm"; about 3.9 grams</note>. They give the urine an odor that almost resembles that of violets, and they sometimes cause a slight headache during their operation.

**§. 5.** Because it is partly difficult to take pure turpentine in <term>morsels</term> <note>original: "Bißen"; small medicinal balls or boluses</note>, and because it also tastes quite unpleasant when dissolved in drinks, various other convenient <term>methods of ingestion</term> <note>original: "Einnehmungs-Mittel"</note> have been devised. One method is to boil it in water for half an hour, or until it reaches a thick consistency; this is called <term>Colophony</term> <note>original: "Colophonium"; commonly known today as rosin</note> or boiled turpentine. Pills are also made from it before it has cooled, which can be swallowed very easily. However, through the boiling process, the water carries away much of its <term>essential salts</term> <note>original: "sale essenciali"; historical term for the active mineral or chemical essence of a substance</note>, in which its greatest power resides.

<margin>And</margin>
**§. 6.** Others merely wash the turpentine many times in <term>Pellitory-of-the-wall</term> <note>original: "Mauer-Kraut"; Parietaria officinalis, a plant traditionally used for urinary health</note> and turnip water, giving it a consistency that is less fluid. This washing does not take away as much of the <term>essential salts</term> <note>original: "sal essentiale"</note> as boiling does, yet it always carries some of it away nonetheless.

<margin>...</margin>
**§. 7.** Therefore, it is best done when one takes it in its natural state, after giving it the thickness of a morsel by mixing in various suitable powders, such as <term>purified nitre</term> <note>original: "nitri purificati"; saltpeter or potassium nitrate</note>, <term>crystals of tartar</term> <note>original: "Tartar-Chrystallen"; potassium bitartrate</note>, <term>spignel</term> <note>original: "Motten"; likely referring to "Mottenwurz" or Spignel (Meum athamanticum), used in traditional medicine</note>, and <term>liquorice</term> <note>original: "Süßholtz"</note>.

**§. 8.** It is also used for washing, where it is dissolved in oil or egg yolk.

-> §. 1. <-

This operation is a separation of the <term>turpentine oil</term> <note>original: "Terpentin-Oels"</note> from its earthy part.

## Remarks.

->§. 7.<-

The <term>spirit of turpentine</term> <note>original: "Spiritus Terebinthinæ"</note> is actually an ethereal oil mixed with a little <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "phlegmate"; a historical term for the watery, non-active part of a distillation</note> and acidic <term>essential salt</term> <note>original: "sale essentiali"</note>, which is why it becomes an <term>aperient</term> <note>original: "aperiens"; a substance used to "open" the body's systems, acting as a mild laxative or diuretic</note>; and it is this spirit that gives turpentine its specific smell.

# Chapter 28.
## A. On Benzoin.

-> §. 1. <-

Benzoin—which is also called *Assadoux* or *Assand* <note>original: "Assadoux/ Assand"; likely derived from "Asa dulcis," meaning "sweet resin," to distinguish it from the foul-smelling "Asa foetida"</note> by some—is a very aromatic resin that flows out of a foreign tree. Its specific name is not known, although some wish to call it *Laserpitium* <note>original: "Laserpitium"; historically, a plant that produced the ancient medicinal resin "silphium," though the author is applying it here to the benzoin tree</note>. This tree is very common in Samaria and the surrounding places.

§. 2. One should select benzoin that is pure, clear, transparent, reddish, brittle, and studded with white "tears" <note>droplet-shaped resin deposits</note> that look almost like broken almond kernels. For this reason, it is called <term>almond benzoin</term> <note>original: "benzoinum amygdaloides"</note>; it must also have a sweet and pleasant scent.

§. 3. Benzoin is in great use among perfumers; in medicine, it is also used to expel bad <term>humors</term> <note>original: "humores"; in historical medicine, these were the bodily fluids thought to govern health and temperament</note> and to strengthen the heart and brain.

## B. Flowers and Oil of Benzoin.

-> §. 1. <-

This operation is an <term>elevation</term> <note>the process of sublimation, where a substance transitions from solid to vapor and back to solid crystals</note> of the most volatile salts of the benzoin and a separation of its oil through distillation.

## Tincture of Benzoin.

->§. I.<-

Take 3 ounces of Benzoin and half an ounce of Storax <note>a fragrant resin derived from the bark of trees in the *Styrax* genus</note>, powder them coarsely, and put them into a bottle or a <term>matrass</term> <note>a round-bottomed glass flask with a long neck</note> so that half of it remains empty. ### Chapter 23.

# On Camphor.

->§. 1.<-

Camphor is a resin that drips from a tree which looks almost like a walnut tree and is found on the island of <term>Borneo</term>. It is also brought from China in small discs, although it is not as good. The Dutch purify it by <term>subliming <note>original: "sublimiren"; heating a substance so it turns directly from a solid to a vapor and then back to a solid, leaving impurities behind</note></term> it, and separating it from the earth that remains sitting at the bottom of the vessels. One must take the white, transparent, pure, crumbly, and unblemished kind, which is very difficult to set on fire <note>While camphor is flammable, this may refer to the purity required for it to burn without leaving residue or smoke</note>.

§. 2. Camphor consists of a sulfur and a salt <note>In the "Tria Prima" theory of early chemistry, "Sulfur" represented the principle of flammability and "Salt" the principle of fixity or body</note>, which are so volatile that one can only preserve them with great effort and difficulty; and even if it is stored as well as possible, it still continually diminishes <note>Refers to camphor's tendency to evaporate (sublime) at room temperature</note>.

## B. Camphor Oil.

->§. 1.<-

This operation results in a **camphor** that is characterized by the **acids** <note>original: "acidis"</note> of the **spirit of nitre** <note>original: "Spiritus nitri"; a historical term for nitric acid</note>, which turn it into a **liquid** <note>original: "Liquore"</note>.

§. 2. Powder 3 to 4 ounces of good camphor, put it into a **matrass** <note>original: "Matras"; a long-necked glass flask used by chemists for boiling or distilling</note>, and pour twice as much **spirit of nitre** over it: Seal your vessel well and place it in a pot half-filled with somewhat warm water: stir it constantly and help the **dissolution** <note>the process of the solid camphor dissolving into the liquid acid</note> to reach completion within 2 to 3 hours. You will then see how the camphor has been transformed into a clear oil that floats upon the spirit of nitre: separate it from it and keep it in a well-sealed **phial** <note>original: "Phiole"; a small glass bottle</note>.

§. 3. It is used for **mouth rot** <note>original: "Mundfäule"; likely refers to scurvy or ulcerative stomatitis</note>; one brushes the exposed nerves with it and uses it for wounds and toothaches, where one places a little bit of cotton dipped into it upon the area.

## Remark.

### §. 4.

This oil is merely a solution of <term>camphor</term> <note>original: "Kampffers"</note> in <term>spirit of nitre</term> <note>original: "Spiritu nitri"; a historical name for nitric acid</note>. For if one pours water upon it to break the power of the <term>spirit of nitre</term>, it returns to being <term>camphor</term> once more, just as it was before.

§. 5. Of all <term>resins</term> <note>original: "Hartzen"</note>, this is the only one that is dissolved in <term>spirit of nitre</term>; and this occurs without <term>effervescence</term> <note>original: "Ebullition"; the bubbling or "boiling" seen during a chemical reaction</note> or any noticeable heat. Because <term>camphor</term> consists of thin and loosely woven <term>particles</term> <note>original: "Theilgen"</note>, the <term>acids</term> <note>original: "acida"</note> fall into them and separate them quite easily. Furthermore, because the <term>acids</term> are mixed with <term>sulfur</term> <note>original: "Schwefel"; in early chemistry, this often refers to the flammable or oily principle of a substance</note>, they do not naturally excite any <term>effervescence</term>, which only occurs when encountering bodies that fold and yield easily.

§. 6. If you have employed 3 <term>ounces</term> <note>original: "Untzen"</note> of <term>camphor</term> for this <term>operation</term> <note>chemical procedure</note>, you will extract 4 <term>ounces</term> of oil; thus, the <term>spirit of nitre</term> has decreased by one <term>ounce</term> and has lost much of its <term>acridity</term> <note>original: "Schärffe"; the biting or corrosive quality of the acid</note>.

§. 7. Some have criticized this <term>process</term> for the reason that the <term>corrosive spirit</term> <note>the nitric acid</note> does such violence to the <term>camphor</term> during its dissolution, and many of its <term>particles</term> embed themselves within it, so that its <term>acridity</term> must be viewed with suspicion <note>implying the resulting medicine might be too harsh or caustic for the patient</note>.

## §. 1.

**G**ummi Ammoniacum is so named because it flows from a type of rod-like stalk <note>original: "Ruthen"; referring to the tall, fennel-like stalks of the plant *Dorema ammoniacum*</note> which grows not far from the place where the oracle of **Jupiter Ammon** <note>original: "Jovis Ammonis"; an ancient Greco-Egyptian deity with a famous temple and oracle in the Libyan desert</note> once stood. The best variety is that which flows in thick "tears" or drops—yellowish on the outside and white on the inside—which are dry and clean, and possess a bitter, unpleasant taste.

§. 2. It is used internally in "opening" **electuaries** <note>original: "Opiatis"; in this context, the term refers to soft, paste-like medicinal confections used as a delivery system, rather than strictly narcotic opium preparations</note> for hard boils and swellings of the liver, the spleen, and the **mesentery** <note>original: "mesenterii"; the membrane that attaches the intestines to the abdominal wall</note>. Furthermore, it is applied externally in softening and **drawing plasters** <note>original: "Zug-Pflaster"; a medical dressing designed to "draw out" inflammation, pus, or foreign objects from the skin</note>.

§. 3. If one wishes to purify it, it is dissolved in wine vinegar, passed through a sieve, and all moisture is allowed to evaporate over a fire.

§. 4. By this method, it is cleansed of some dross and small impurities that it contains; however, because a portion of its **volatile spirits** <note>original: "volatilischen Spirituum"; in early modern chemistry, these were the light, active components thought to contain a substance's primary medicinal power</note>—in which its greatest strength consists—is lost in the process, and another portion is "fixed" or trapped by the **acid** <note>original: "acido"</note>, which always inhibits the movement of **volatiles** <note>original: "Volatilium"</note>, I advise no one to perform this **purification** <note>original: "Läuterung"</note>. I would rather one take the purest gum that can be obtained and simply grind it to powder alone in a **mortar** <note>original: "Mörsel"</note>, whereupon one with the

## Remarks.

### §. 3.

Although this **liquid** <note>original: "Liquor"</note>, which is improperly called an oil, is only the most soluble part of the myrrh that has been moistened by the humidity of the egg white and the cellar: yet it is the best among all those currently specified, whether they be prepared with **spirits of wine** <note>original: "Spiritu vini"; high-proof alcohol used as a solvent</note> or through the distillation of this **gum** <note>original: "Gummi"; referring to the resinous myrrh</note> over a **retort** <note>original: "Retorte"; a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances</note>. For with the **spirits of wine**, that which is most volatile in the myrrh departs and is lost, whether one allows it to be distilled or **evaporated** <note>original: "evaporiren"</note>: through the **retort**, however, one dries the substance out in such a way that it loses its best properties in the process. Through **deliquescence** <note>original: "deliqvium"; the process of a substance absorbing enough atmospheric moisture to dissolve into a liquid</note>, however, one preserves the volatile essence of this **gum** in its natural state, because the moisture mixed into it can neither destroy nor **alter** <note>original: "alteriren"</note> it.

# Third Part.
## Of the Actual Treatise of Chemistry.
### The Preface.
## Of Animals in General.

->§. 1.<-

<margin>Generally</margin>
It appears entirely as though every animal originates from an egg, and that it lies there enclosed in miniature, just as a plant is hidden and enclosed within its seed. However, because the eggs of all animals are not as common as the seeds of plants, and one cannot recognize the animal-egg through a **microscope** <note>original: "microscopium"; an early scientific instrument for magnifying small objects, which was still relatively new and improving in the early 18th century</note> as easily as one can the plant in the seed; therefore, this opinion is not universally accepted, and many **anatomists** <note>scientists who study the bodily structure of living things</note> and **philosophers** <note>at this time, "natural philosophers" were what we now call scientists</note> are found who cast doubt upon it.

§. 2. Be that as it may, once the animal is formed, the **nutritive juice** <note>original: "Nahrungs-Safft"; refers to the fluids, like chyle, thought to nourish the body</note> and its **humors** <note>original: "humores"; the vital bodily fluids believed in pre-modern medicine to control health and temperament</note> circulate through its body by means of the **spirits** <note>original: "Spirituum"; subtle, vaporous substances thought to animate the body and drive the movement of fluids</note> that propel them, so well that everything else therein

§. 3. To be sure, their substances are not all extracted with the same degree of volatility; some are more and others are less **volatile** <term>prone to evaporating or turning into gas</term>. The **volatile substances** <note>original: "Volatilia"</note> of the toad are not nearly as subtle as those of the **viper** <note>original: "Otter"; in 18th-century German medicinal contexts, this usually refers to the common European viper rather than the aquatic mammal</note>, just as those of **scorpions** do not reach the level of the latter. Hair, urine, and blood yield a much more volatile essence than **bones** <note>original: "Beine"; an archaic usage referring to bones in general, not just the legs</note>, and fish yield less than the animals on the earth. Moths, earthworms, and snails yield less than lizards and snakes. Deer, goats, dogs, wolves, foxes, beavers, cats, hares, rabbits, rats, and shrews give far more volatile principles than calves, **wethers** <note>castrated rams</note>, oxen, horses, and donkeys. Human parts are all filled with volatile matter, and I have encountered no other animal than the viper that possesses slightly more of the same. A bear also contains much of it within itself. **Hartshorn** <note>deer antler; a primary source for early chemists to produce ammonia, or "spirit of hartshorn"</note> yields more than ivory, and hair even more than anything else from a human. Milk, on the other hand, yields much less than other **liquids** <note>original: "Liqvores"</note> in animals.

§. 4. Depending on whether the animals, their parts, and their **excrements** <note>waste products or secretions</note> contain many or few volatile principles, and according to how they are bound together, they also possess different powers.

§ 5. Those whose **principles** <note>original: *principia*</note> are highly **volatile** <note>original: *volatilisch*; substances that evaporate or react easily</note> naturally possess a sweat-inducing power. Such substances include human blood, goat blood, the human skull, the adder, and hartshorn <note>the antlers of a male deer, often used to make smelling salts</note>. This is because when their **substances** are heated by the stomach, they spread throughout the entire body and exit through the pores <note>literally "air-holes"</note>.

§ 6. However, those whose **principles** are less **volatile** often have an opening power <note>a "deobstruent" that clears blockages in the body</note>, such as **prepared** toad, moths, and crayfish. This is because their salt possesses a certain weight and **precipitates** <note>original: *præcipitiret*</note> down into the blood, thereby opening the urinary tracts.

<margin>§ 7. The use of urine.</margin>
§ 7. Those that have fermented **principles**, such as beaver testicles <note>castoreum, a secretion used in perfumery and medicine</note>, urine, musk, civet, and the **excrement** of many animals, are on one hand excellently good for epilepsy <note>literally "heavy distress"</note>, stroke, and gout, and on the other hand for uterine complaints <note>original: *Mutterbeschwerungen*; "the mother" was a common term for the womb</note>. This is because when their **volatile substance** rises into the brain, it wonderfully strengthens the origin of the nerves. Urine is an excellent remedy for arthritis <note>literally "limb-sickness"</note>, as it raises the **humors** <note>the body's vital fluids</note> and drives them out through the pores, the bowels, and the urine. One may take perhaps two to three glasses of it a day; it is also good for flatulence.

## Chapter 1.
### Concerning the Viper.

->§. 1.<-

We do not wish to dwell upon the **fables of the ancients** <note>referring to myths, such as the belief that young vipers eat their way out of their mother's side</note> regarding the birth of the viper; rather, we shall only say this: it is a species of **snake** which comes out of its mother’s womb alive. For this reason, it was named *Vivipara* <note>Latin: "giving birth to living young"</note>, and corrupted into *Vipera* <note>the common name "Viper"</note>.

§. 2. This is a very common animal in **Dauphiné** and **Poitou** <note>provinces in France</note>, from where it is distributed throughout all of **France**. When it lives in the open fields, it eats many small creatures and lives off them; however, if one shuts it up, it can be kept alive for a whole summer without being given anything to eat, provided it is allowed **air**.

§. 11. Thus it also appears as if these thoughts were confirmed by some experience and experiment, which **Mr. Charas** <note>Moyse Charas (1619–1698), a French apothecary famous for his "New Experiments on Vipers"</note> brings forward in his book on the **viper** <note>original: "Otter"; though this word means "otter" in modern German, in this historical context it refers to the viper or adder</note>, where he not only shows how the **heated spirits** <note>early modern medical theory suggested that a viper’s "spirits" or vital essences became poisonous only when the animal was angry or provoked</note> were solely and uniquely the **viper-venom**, but also claims that the **yellow sap** in the socket of the large tooth, which was previously held to be the venom of this animal, was nothing of the sort: For even when this **liquid** <note>original: "Liquorem"</note> was poured onto the wounds of many beasts, they did not die from it; and what is more, those who even tasted it felt no discomfort at all. Nevertheless, **Mr. Redy** <note>Francesco Redi (1626–1697), an Italian physician and biologist often called the "founder of experimental biology"</note> was not satisfied with these experiments in a separate treatise on the viper.

§. 12. He says, on the contrary, that if one let this **yellow sap** flow onto the wounds of various animals, they died from it; and he concludes from this that the viper-venom must indeed be contained in this yellow sap, and does not lie solely in the heated and irritated spirits—even though the others have insisted upon it, because that cause appears to him all too **metaphysical** <note>original: "Methaphysisch"; Redi preferred physical, observable evidence over the abstract "vital spirits" favored by Charas</note>.

§. 13. Among so many different opinions and experiments, a **great man of our time** <note>This likely refers to a contemporary scientist like Richard Mead or perhaps the author's own mentor</note> has tried to establish a reconciliation and wrote that it could be that the yellow viper-sap has different effects according to the different places where these animals were born <note>original: "geworffen"; literally "thrown" or "whelped"</note>

## Chapter 2.

# A. Distillation of Urine and its Volatile Salt.

->§. 1.<-

This operation is a separation of the **volatile spirit of salt** <note>original: *Spiritus salis volatilis*; an early chemical term for what we now know as ammonium carbonate, a pungent salt</note> and oil in urine, where they are set apart from its **phlegm** <note>original: *phlegmate*; the watery, inactive portion of a distilled liquid</note> and its **earth** <note>original: *Erde*; the solid, mineral residue remaining after all liquids have evaporated</note>.

§. 2. Take 10 to 12 **measures** <note>original: *Mösel*; a historical liquid measure that varied by region, roughly equivalent to a pint or half-liter</note> of urine collected from **young people** <note>early modern chemists often specified the urine of children or healthy young men, believing it contained more "vital force" or "spirit"</note>. Let the moisture evaporate from it in a **stoneware** <note>original: *Gretz*; likely referring to "Grätzer" ware, a type of durable ceramic</note> or glass **cucurbit** <note>the gourd-shaped base of a distillation apparatus</note> over a **sand-fire** <note>a sand bath, used to distribute heat evenly and prevent the glass from cracking</note> until a substance as thick as honey remains.
