Maintain a gentle fire and let the rest of the **phlegm** distill. After this, gradually increase the heat; the **spirits** <note>volatile gases</note> will then rise in clouds along with some oil and consequently the **volatile salts**, which will attach themselves to the helm like **butterflies** <note>original: *Zweyfalter*; a poetic chemical term describing the delicate, leaf-like crystalline structures that form during sublimation</note>. Maintain the fire until nothing more passes over. Then, open the vessels and separate the volatile salt. Place it into a **matrass** <note>a long-necked glass flask</note> with a long neck, also pour the spirit into the recipient, and place a **blind helm** <note>a still-head without a spout, used when the goal is to collect solid crystals (sublimation) rather than liquid distillate</note> on the matrass. Lute the joints with a wet **bladder** <note>animal bladders were used as flexible, airtight seals that tightened as they dried</note>, set the matrass in sand, and **sublimate** <note>the process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then collects again as a solid</note> with a gen-

Filter the residue [in a] **matrass** <note>original: *Matras*; a long-necked glass chemical flask</note>; the **spirit** will run through, and a somewhat black and extremely foul-smelling oil will remain in the filter. This oil is good for the resolution of frostbitten limbs and for gout, and one allows those afflicted with **uterine complaints** <note>original: *Mutterbeschwerung*; historically known as "hysteria," a condition once thought to be caused by the womb moving through the body</note> to smell it.

§. 3. One can distill the **spirit** over a **sand-fire** <note>original: *Sand-Feuer*; a heat source where the glass vessel is buried in sand to distribute heat evenly</note> and thus separate it from a fat that remains below. One gives 8 to 20 drops in a tolerable **liquid**.

§. 4. Mix 2 drams with 2 **lots** <note>a historical unit of weight, roughly 1/32nd of a pound</note> of **brandy** <note>original: *aqvavit*; aqua vitae</note> and rub the limbs afflicted by gout with it; it is used in the same way for frostbite and for **sciatic paralysis** <note>original: *paralysin ischiaticam*</note>.

§. 5. If one **calcines** <note>reduces to ash through high heat</note> the mass that remains in the **cucurbit** <note>the lower vessel of the still</note> and makes a lye from it with water, one extracts—after the moisture has evaporated—a small quantity of **alkaline salt**, which has the same potency as other alkaline salts.

Ttt 3

->§. 6.<-

The urine of young people is superior to others because it contains a higher concentration of **salt**. It must be collected quite fresh and allowed to evaporate over a gentle fire so that fermentation and excessively strong heat do not cause the **volatile salts** <note>original: *volatilischen Saltze*; ammonium carbonate, a pungent chemical that evaporates quickly</note> to rise and escape with the **phlegm** <note>original: *Phlegmate*; in early chemistry, the watery, inactive portion of a distilled substance</note>. The **spirit** <note>original: *Spiritus*; the volatile, active liquid essence</note> is nothing more than a dissolved salt that has been liquefied in a small amount of phlegm. This salt is more effective than all others at purging through the urine, though it has an extremely foul odor.

->§. 7.<- The **volatile salt** <term>sal volatile</term> prepared in the manner just described is produced more easily and in far greater quantities during the winter than in the summer. For since a fermentation occurs immediately in collected urine during warm weather, a very large portion of the volatile salt is dispersed into the air along with the phlegm, no matter how tightly one tries to contain it. In winter, however, the cold concentrates the **volatile salt**, making it much easier to separate the phlegm.

->§. 8.<- Such **medicine** <note>original: *Artzeney*</note> should never be administered in **broth**. Because broth is taken warm, the heat would cause a portion of the volatile salts to evaporate before the patient can drink it.

### §. 53.

### §. 54.
The one is derived from the **pasture**: For it is certain that the herbs on certain grazing grounds are much more **spirituous** <note>original: *spirituöser*; containing more volatile essences or "animal spirits"</note> than in other regions. ### §. 55.
The other concerns the animals themselves, as these have been heated much more than others while being driven <note>referring to the exertion of driving livestock to market or the slaughterhouse</note> and cannot cool down again before slaughter. For because the **spirits** <term>spirits</term> <note>original: *Spiritus*; in early modern physiology, these were subtle, vaporous substances thought to circulate through the body and facilitate life and motion</note> are in great motion, they do not immediately lose their **agitation** <note>original: *Schwarm*; literally a "swarm," referring to the energetic movement of particles</note> even though the animal is dead. As long as they can move in all their fury, the **phosphorus** can be seen. But if the meat begins to smell foul, one no longer sees any light there, because its subtle spirits have dissipated, or have even gone astray through another **fermentation** <note>original: *Fermentation*; here meaning the process of decay or chemical breakdown</note> that has arisen.

§ 4. Although the **Bolognese Stone** <note>original: *Bolognesische Stein*; a variety of the mineral barite found near Bologna which, when treated, glows in the dark</note> is indeed found around the Italian city from which it takes its name, it was not so long ago that it was so unknown in that very city that no one could provide information about it, and very few had even heard it mentioned. For this reason, our **travelers** <term>travelers</term> <note>original: *Peregrinanten*; scholars or students on a "Grand Tour" of Europe for their education</note> learned nothing of it, and most believed that the **Bolognese Stone** discussed previously was an artificial **compound** <note>original: *Composition*</note> whose secret had been lost.

§. 5. Specifically, the **Bolognese Stone** is a gray, soft, yet heavy, **sulfurous** <note>original: *schwefflicht*</note> stone that sparkles in many places. However, these large stones are prized solely for their rarity; they are not otherwise the best for the production of **phosphorus** <note>original: *Phosphori*; in this era, the term referred to any "light-bearer" or substance that glowed in the dark, rather than the chemical element phosphorus discovered later</note> because they are usually dark. The powder must be fine <note>original: "subtil."</note> so that it adheres to the stone and, after **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to change its properties.</note>, can better capture and hold the light; for since the light only rests upon the surface, the fine dust will take in far more than a coarse powder, which does not have as much surface area.

§. 10. Even if one took poor and dark Bologna stones and covered them with the finest dust, the stones still performed well; conversely, if one covered fine and very transparent stones only with powder from poor ones, they performed no better than if they had been **calcinated** plainly without any application of powder—that is, they hardly glowed at all.

<margin>§. 22. At what time one places the stone in the light.</margin>
§. 22. If one lets calcined **Bologna stone** lie on top of a piece of polished **brass**, the brass will take on a silver-white color—not only where the stone lay, but all around it. This comes from a penetration which the salty **sulfur** of the stone performs into the brass: namely, as it changes the external polish of the metallic particles, it causes a different reflection of light in our eyes than one otherwise perceives when we look at brass.

§. 23. Before one brings the calcined stone into the light, it must first be well cooled: because it does not become as brightly glowing when it is still warm as when it comes into the light cold. If one wishes to make it glowing, it is not enough for it to absorb light in a closed place, room, or chamber; rather, one must bring it by hand to a window that opens onto a street or courtyard into the light, so that the rays of light fall straight and **perpendicularly** <note>original: "perpendiculariter"</note> down upon it from above. However, these must not be direct sun rays: because the sun would partly consume the **phosphorus** <note>Here referring to the glowing stone itself, which was often called "Bolognian Phosphorus" at the time.</note> too quickly with its heat, as it would extract too many of the necessary sulfur particles.

§. 24. When the sun sets, the stone captures a much more beautiful light than in the height of day. But if the sun has already gone down, the stone captures nothing more at all, even though it is still daylight. In foggy and very overcast weather, it becomes indeed brighter and more glittering than on a fine day; however, one may leave it out at night however one wishes, and it will not become even a little bit luminous from it. If the moon shines, it takes in a little light, and from torches even less.

<margin>§. 26. It glows in a vacuum.</margin>
§. 26. The air contributes nothing to this: for if one has pumped the air out of a glass or crystalline bottle, and brings the stone inside with great caution, and seals it with a glass stopper and **sealing wax** <note>original: "Spanischen Wachs," a high-quality resin-based wax used for airtight seals.</note>, then one need only place it in the light, and the stone—even though it is in a **vacuum** <note>original: "Vacuo"</note>—will draw in just as much light as if it were outside the bottle in the open air. Nevertheless, when covered with glass or crystal, it does not allow its fire to be seen as vividly, because the rays emanating therefrom, as they pass through this transparent wall, are somewhat refracted, so that they do not strike the sensitive membranes of the eye <note>original: "Augen-Häutlein"</note> as strongly as when the stone is free. This **phosphorus** <note>A general term used at the time for any substance that could emit light; here specifically referring to the Bologna stone.</note> is distinguished from that of urine <note>A reference to "white phosphorus," discovered in 1669 by Hennig Brand, which glows spontaneously upon exposure to oxygen.</note> in that the former requires light, while the latter requires only air.

§. 27. If one wishes to properly observe the bright radiance of the Bologna stone, one must make their surroundings completely dark and remain in the darkness for some time before looking at it. This allows the eyes to gradually "wean" themselves from the great light of day, making them much more adept at capturing the glow of the *phosphorus* <note>original: "Phosphori." In this era, "phosphorus" referred to any substance that could emit light after being "charged" by the sun, not just the chemical element phosphorus.</note> and judging its intensity. This must be done primarily on very bright and clear days; however, in cloudy and rainy weather, such **precaution** <note>original: "præcaution."</note> is not necessary, because our eyes are not then accustomed to such a brilliant light and can therefore better perceive the stone's delicate glow.

§. 28. The Bologna stone glows only on its **surface** <note>original: "superficie."</note>; for if it is broken, one sees no light inside it. However, if one also **calcines** <note>original: "calcinirt." Calcination involves heating the stone to high temperatures, a crucial step in "activating" the barium sulfate to make it phosphorescent.</note> the interior properly, it will give off light just like the rest of the exterior. Even the powder with which the stones were covered during **calcination** <note>original: "Calcination."</note> need only be brought into the light and then placed in the shade to appear entirely fiery on its top layer. Yet, if one stirs it all together, the powder that was underneath will be dark; but if one brings that first layer back to the top, it will give off light wherever it is viewed.

§. 29. Now that I have recounted many of the wonderful effects of the Bologna stone—which one may quite rightly call a **light sponge** <note>original: "Lichtschwamm." A metaphor suggesting the stone "soaks up" light like a sponge soaks up water.</note>—I have deemed it useful to look a little closer at this matter and offer some reasons which explain, as much as possible, how this stone is filled with light. In this regard, I wish to take two things into consideration: what kind of light it is, and what the condition of the stone must be to receive it. <margin>§. 29. Light sponge.</margin>

§. 30. Without concerning myself with everything the philosophers have proposed regarding light, I will only say this: it is a fire which goes out from the sun with power through large rays and divides itself into countless small rays, which are spread throughout the whole world and are weakened as soon as they move away from their center. Should anyone doubt this, they can immediately witness it with a <term>concave mirror</term> <note>original: "Speculo concavo." A curved, hollow mirror used in physics to focus light onto a single point.</note>, where the light falls together and is captured at a single point, creating fire. <margin>§. 30. Light is a fire.</margin>

The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile matter or change its state.</note>, this sulfur is so well united with the other principles of which the stone consists that it does not glow at all, and this stone gives off as little light as any other stone. §. 32. Having now presupposed these matters—which appear to me entirely indisputable—I conclude that the <term>calcined</term><note>Heated to a high temperature to drive off volatile components and change its chemical state.</note> <term>Bologna stone</term><note>A variety of the mineral barite that became famous in the 17th century for its ability to glow in the dark after being "activated" by fire.</note> becomes luminous when placed in the light because the light, acting as a fire, ignites the superficial sulfur <note>original: "superficialen Schwefel"; in early chemistry, sulfur was often used to refer to the "principle of flammability" within a substance.</note> and makes it appear fiery and burning, much like fire ignites a coal. Thus, we shall now see if I can respond to all experiments in this regard and resolve the difficulties.

§. 33. Through the process of calcination, the Bologna stone has been transformed into a type of lime. It appears entirely as though "fire-particles" have entered in place of the sulfur that escaped; these particles have become trapped and entangled within the remaining branching particles of the stone—a phenomenon I have demonstrated in many other calcined substances. These tiny fire-particles can now do much to help the stone's sulfur catch fire from this light. For even if these tiny <term>corpuscles</term><note>Small particles of matter, a central concept in the "corpuscular" physics of the era.</note> are enclosed within the air-pores of the material as if in small cells, they nevertheless do not cease to seek an exit with all their movement and force; they thus <term>volatilize</term><note>Turn into a vapor or gas.</note> and divide these sulfur particles so finely that even the weakest fire—such as light dimmed by clouds—can ignite them.

§. 34. Once the stone is ignited, it glow—

§. 36. §. 52. Thus, there must be a great *disposition* for motion within the particles of the matter. But as for the Bolognese stone, the sulfur within it has been so elevated <note>original: "erhöhet," meaning refined or concentrated through the process of calcination (heating)</note> and so well stripped of all its fatty particles that it has no need to be ignited by anything other than light: This sulfur, however, catches no fire at night, because nothing can then ignite it. §. 59. Sixthly, **urine-phosphorus** <note>original: "Urin-Phosphorus"; white phosphorus, which was famously first isolated from concentrated human urine by the alchemist Hennig Brand in 1669</note> is well-preserved in water, while the **Bolognese stone** <note>original: "Bologneserstein"; a variety of the mineral barite which, after being heated with charcoal, becomes phosphorescent—meaning it glows in the dark after being exposed to light</note> is well-preserved when dry. The reason for this is that urine-phosphorus is almost entirely a **sulfur** <term>sulfur: "Schwefel," referring here to the early modern chemical principle of "sulfur," which was believed to be the oily, combustible component of all matter, rather than just the element sulfur on the periodic table</term>; for water condenses its particles just as it does those of other sulfur, and does not allow the air to scatter them.

Whereas, on the other hand, the sulfurous particles of the Bolognese stone are surrounded by much **earth** <term>earth: "Erde," another alchemical principle representing solidity and dryness, which binds and stabilizes more volatile or "oily" components</term>, which holds them back so that they need no water for their preservation; it is enough to enclose the stone in a box in which some cotton has been placed. Thus it appears very much that as soon as these sulfurous particles move continuously about on the surface of the stone, a little of them is also scattered into the air. However, the greater part falls back again and occupies its **air-holes** <note>original: "Lufft-Löcher"; likely referring to the pores or structural gaps in the stone's surface where the light-bearing particles reside</note> once more, continuing to give off light until the sulfur is entirely consumed. 

Nevertheless, a much larger portion is used up when the stone is "ignited" <note>original: "angezündet"; here meaning the state where the stone is actively glowing after light exposure</note> than when it is extinguished. # E. Baldwin's Hermetic Phosphorus.
<note>Latin: Phosphorus Hermeticus Balduini; a luminescent salt discovered by Christian Adolph Balduin in 1674.</note>

->§. 1.<-

It is a mixture of **chalk** and the **acid of <term>aquafortis</term>**<note>Nitric acid.</note> that produces light.

§. 2. Let approximately 2 lbs. of chalk become glowing hot in the fire, then let it cool again, and turn it into powder.

§. 3. Take as much as you wish of aquafortis—for example, one pound—pour it into a large glass <term>cucurbit</term><note>A gourd-shaped chemical vessel used for distillation.</note>, and throw a spoonful of powder from your calcined chalk into it. A strong <term>ebullition</term><note>A bubbling or fizzing chemical reaction.</note> will occur. Once the matter is dissolved, add the same amount again, and continue doing so until no more ebullition occurs. Let the liquid stand, and pour it by tilting into a stoneware basin; place it in sand and let all the moisture evaporate over a small fire, and a certain salt will remain behind for you.

§. 4. Pour the salt into a <term>cupel</term><note>A shallow, porous vessel used in chemistry and assaying, often made of bone ash or clay.</note> or an earthenware dish that is not glazed; place your vessel in a small fire. As soon as the material has become warm, it swells up; maintain the small fire for one hour, or until the material has completely sunk down again. Once it has melted, you must wait for a yellow vapor which you will see rising through the holes of the lid. §. 5. You will find a streak of yellow matter on the sides of your vessel, which is sometimes as thick as a finger. That is the <term>phosphorus</term>, remove it, and keep it in a well-closed box in a dark place.

§. 6. If you wish to make it luminous, you must first place it in daylight for just a moment, and then bring it to a dark place.

although one also finds it in abundance in other places. Some *writers* <note>original: "Scribenten"</note> distinguish three types of it: a white, a green, and a black; however, here we require only the white. One *calcinates* <term>calcinates</term><note>To heat a substance to a high temperature to change its state or remove volatile parts.</note> it so that its sulfur <note>In the chemical language of the time, "sulfur" referred to the oily or combustible principle of a substance rather than the specific element.</note> is given more motion than it previously possessed, as the most subtle parts rise out of it, although one needs no more than what belongs to the making of the *phosphorus*.

### §. 2.

Although the chalk is resinous, it does not fail to be *alkaline* <note>original: "alcalinisch"</note>, because the few sulfurs found within cannot close its air-holes; indeed, the *calcination* opens it further and prepares this earth so that it can receive the impression of the *acid* <note>original: "acidi"</note> all the more easily. This is evident from the strong *ebullition* <term>ebullition</term><note>A vigorous bubbling or fizzing reaction resulting from the release of gas.</note> which occurs when one puts it into *aqua fortis* <note>original: "Aquafort"; literally "strong water," a historical name for nitric acid.</note>; the *cucurbit* <term>cucurbit</term><note>A gourd-shaped glass vessel used as the body of a still.</note> must be large, and the chalk must be added little by little so that the material does not run out over the top.

### §. 3.

The chalk is completely dissolved in the *aqua fortis*, and one adds so much of it until no more *ebullition* arises; this is a sign that the acidic spikes <note>Seventeenth-century chemists often imagined acids as microscopic needles or "spikes" that physically pierced and broke apart substances.</note> have exerted all the power of *rarefaction* <term>rarefaction</term><note>The process of a substance becoming less dense or expanding in volume.</note> that they are capable of, and are, as it were, bound and shackled to the particles of the matter which they hold up and aloft, so that they can do nothing more. Anything that one then adds in excess falls to the bottom. If the *aqua fortis* is good, it dissolves almost as much chalk as it itself weighs; the *distillate* <note>original: "distillation"</note> appears yellow.

### The 3rd Chapter.

## A. Concerning *Cornu cervi* <note>original: 'Cornucervi'; Latin for stag's horn</note> or Hartshorn.

§. 1.

The horns or antlers, which protrude from the head of the stag, are formed from a gluey moisture of the brain; for when this is driven forth by the *spirits* <term>spirits: 'spiritus' in early physiology were considered subtle, life-giving vapors or fluids that circulated through the body to animate the limbs</term> of the animal, it is first *sublimated* <term>sublimated: in this context, the process of a substance being raised up and hardened into a solid form</term> into two small, simple, and soft little antlers without tines; but because nourishment is carried there in abundance through the vessels formed within them, they visibly grow large and spread out into many tines, and become as hard as bone; and these are now the animal's weapons. It sheds its antlers every year in the spring, because the part attached to the head has become excessively hard over the winter, so that the slimy moisture driven from the brain in the spring can no longer penetrate into it; consequently, new little antlers form underneath

## Chapter 4.
# On the Human Skull and Brain.

### §. 1.
Although the human head contains a casing saturated with **phlegm** <term>phlegm: one of the four bodily humors, described here as a slimy moisture</term> <note>original: 'Pituite'</note>, it is nonetheless also a vessel for the most subtle **spirits** <term>spirits: in early modern medicine, these were invisible fluids or vapors believed to circulate through the body to provide life and movement</term> <note>original: 'Spirituum'</note> of the body, which move incessantly within it. Thus, one can be certain that it also contains many good and very useful **medicines** <term>medicines: original 'Arzney-Mittel'</term>.

### §. 2.
The head that one wishes to use in **medicine** <term>medicine: original 'Medicin'</term> must come from a young, **vigorous** <term>vigorous: original 'vigorösen'</term>, healthy person who has died a violent death very recently and is not yet buried, so that it still retains all its **active principles** <term>active principles: the chemically or medicinally potent components of a substance</term> <note>original: 'principia activa'</note>, as otherwise the most volatile part is lost into the earth.
<margin>§. 2. Selection of the skull.</margin>

### §. 3.
Dried, grated, and powdered human skull is considered good for the **falling sickness** <term>falling sickness: an archaic term for epilepsy</term> <note>original: 'schwehre Noth'</note> and other brain diseases. Between 10 **grains** <term>grain: a tiny apothecary unit of weight (approx. 65mg) based on the weight of a seed</term> <note>original: 'Gran'</note> and 2 **scruples** <term>scruple: an apothecary weight equal to 20 grains (approx. 1.3g)</term> <note>original: 'Scrupel'</note> are administered; it acts through its salt, which is entirely volatile.

§. 3. One must not, however, accept the method of many writers who insist that the skull must first be **calcined** <term>calcined: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to ash or powder</term> in fire before it is taken. This is because, through this calcination, the **volatile salt** <term>volatile salt: an early chemical term for ammonium carbonate, believed to be the active medicinal vapor of a substance</term> <note>original: 'sal volatile'</note> and oil—from which the skull derives its power—are dispersed in such a way that the residue rubbed onto the **porphyry** <term>porphyry: a hard, purple-red stone used as a surface for grinding medicinal ingredients</term> (which is then presented as **prepared human skull** <note>original: 'cranium humanum præparatum'</note>) is nothing more than an earthy alkaline matter. It no longer possesses any **active principles** <term>active principles: the chemically or medicinally potent components of a substance</term> <note>original: 'principia activa'</note> and possesses no other quality than its ability to sweeten the body's **acids** <note>original: 'acida'</note> and to stop diarrhea and the flow of blood.

Once the flesh and skin have decayed over this time, such moss grows upon the skull.

## B. Distillation of the Human Skull and the Brain.

->§. 1.<-

This operation is a separation of the <term>principles</term> <note>the fundamental chemical components—usually salt, sulfur, and mercury—thought to make up all matter</note> that are contained within the human head.

->§. 2.<-

Take the head of a young person who died a violent death <note>Early modern physicians believed that the "vital spirits" remained concentrated in the bodies of those who died suddenly while in peak health, such as executed criminals</note> in the prime of their youth and health. Strip away the skin and flesh from the outside, saw the skull into small pieces, and place them—along with everything inside—into two or three large, glazed <term>retorts</term> <note>teardrop-shaped glass vessels with downward-pointing necks</note> made of glass or <term>Graz earth</term> <note>original: "Gretz-Erde"; a type of heat-resistant clay from Graz</note>. These must only be filled halfway. Place them in one or more <term>reverberatory furnaces</term> <note>a furnace where the flame is deflected or "reverberated" off the roof onto the vessel</note>. Attach a large <term>receiver</term> <note>original: "Recipienten"; a vessel to catch the distilled liquid</note> or glass balloon to each retort, seal all the joints well with <term>lute</term> <note>an airtight clay or paste sealant</note>, and start a small charcoal fire beneath the retorts for four to five hours. This allows them to heat up gradually and distill the <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>the watery or moisture-heavy</note> part of the brain drop by drop. Increase the fire little by little up to the <term>third degree</term> <note>a traditional alchemical measure of heat intensity</note>, and white clouds will fill the receivers. Following this, a black oil and <term>volatile salt</term> <note>original: "sal volatile"; a substance that vaporizes easily and settles as crystals</note> will rise and deposit themselves on the walls of the glass. One continues to maintain the fire, finally increasing it to such an extent...

§. 5. The honey-water is allowed to boil until a fresh egg can float upon it: by which one recognizes that the liquid <note>original: "liqvor"</note> has enough consistency <note>In this context, consistency refers to the sugar density; if the sugar content is high enough, the egg will float due to buoyancy.</note> for its preservation: if it were too thin, the egg would fall to the bottom. Thus far, one uses only common honey-water or mead, which was called *Melicratum*, *Mulsa*, or *apomeli* <note>Ancient Greek and Latin terms for honey-water: "Melicratum" (from Greek *melikraton*), "Mulsa" (Latin *aqua mulsa*), and "apomeli" (a honey-water decoction).</note> by the ancients. However, through fermentation, it is made wine-like.

§. 6. One fills only two-thirds of the barrel so that the fermentation finds enough space to circulate and nothing overflows: during the fermentation, one must also plug the bunghole <term>Spundloch: the hole in a barrel through which it is filled and which is later sealed with a stopper</term> of the barrel only with paper or linen, so that the spirits <note>original: "Spiritus"; the volatile gases, specifically carbon dioxide, produced by the yeast during fermentation.</note> do not drive too much and too violently and push everything out. But once the great "tumult" <note>The phase of "stormy fermentation" where bubbling is most active.</note> is over and the liquid no longer surges upward, one bungs the barrel shut in the usual manner; if one wishes first to fill it completely with the wine-like honey-water or mead—as is practiced with wine barrels—it will keep better.

§. 7. The heat of the sun is far better than the warmth of warm baths for awakening the fermentation of the wine-mead; however, because one can only have the sun for one part of the day, the operation proceeds much faster if one places the barrel in bathing rooms <note>original: "Badstuben"; these were consistently heated rooms, often the only ones in a household kept warm day and night, making them ideal for maintaining fermentation temperatures.</note> that are warm day and night.

Regarding how wine-mead comes about, one must know that honey naturally contains an *essential acid salt* <note>original: "Sal acidum essentiale"; in early modern chemistry, "salts" were seen as active principles that gave substances their specific properties.</note> and oil <note>original: "Oel"; likely referring to the aromatic esters and fats found in honey.</note> within itself. From the heat, this salt is set in motion and seeks to break free; however, it finds an oily and hooked <note>original: "häckeligte"; describing a sticky or interlocking substance that provides resistance.</note> substance which holds it back. Because of this, it attacks the oil and *thins* <note>original: "rarificirt"; to make less dense or more porous.</note> and divides these small particles from one another so that it may gain its free movement: this is exactly what causes the *fermentation*, from which a wine-like *spirit* <note>original: "Spiritus"; the volatile, alcoholic essence of the drink.</note> comes. For because the oil is well-thinned and elevated by the salt, it becomes a *spirit*.

§. 9. As soon as the honey-water has become wine-like, the *fermentation* that has occurred ceases, because the acidic *salts* <note>original: "Salia"</note>—which are to be viewed as so many tiny knives—have cut apart everything together that resisted their movement: thus, no more force or impact, and consequently no more small swelling or bubbling, can occur in the *liquid* <note>original: "Liqvore"</note>.

§. 10. In the *fermentation* of wine-mead, exactly the same thing happens as occurs with Spanish wine <note>At this time, "Spanish wine" often referred to strong, fortified, or naturally high-alcohol wines like Sherry or Sack.</note>, because in both, the same *principles* and the same *arrangement* of particles are found. However, this difference remains: far more salt is found in the juice of the grapes than in the wine-mead; therefore, the *fermentation* there occurs very quickly, even if no external heat is added to it.

**§.12.** If one **rectifies** <note>original: "rectificirt"; the process of refining a substance through repeated distillation.</note> the butter of wax with clay or <term>bolus</term> <note>a medicinal earth or clay</note>, or through the heat of summer in the manner mentioned above, one draws out a good amount of such spirituous **liquors**. Early chemists believed acids had sharp, needle-like particles that lime could break or neutralize.</note> over it; and even though the fire gives some part of it back, it is nonetheless stripped of its **active principles**.

**§.13.** The spirit of wax is nothing but an acidic volatile salt, of which a very small amount has been dissolved in a great deal of phlegm. However, one should not believe everything written in the world: namely, that if one distills a large amount of wax, one only needs to put the extract into a **matrass** <note>a long-necked glass flask</note> with a long neck and, like others, allow the **volatile salt** <note>original: "Sal volatile"</note> to sublimate from it. For although this salt is indeed volatile, it cannot rise up by itself ahead of the phlegm. It is an **acid salt** <note>original: "Sal acidum"</note> very similar to that of **amber** <note>original: "succini"</note>, and has none of the nature of volatile **alkalis**, which sublimate as easily as people believe. Therefore, one must preserve this **spirit** as it is, or even allow half of it to evaporate away under very gentle heat so that it becomes all the stronger.

**§.14.** **Volatile salts** <note>original: "Salia volatilia"</note> are drawn out from many sulfurous materials as they exist in **compounds** <note>original: "Mixtis"</note>. Because they fall into soft and branch-like substances that yield before their movement, they do not shelter their sharp points at all when they try to break loose while being driven by the fire; thus they do not become entangled with as much earthy and fiery matter as is needed if one wishes to make them porous like volatile alkalis.

**§.15.** As it seems to me, this operation and another I have described using **amber** <note>original: "Succino"</note> further confirm what I presented in my notes on the **Principles** <note>original: "Principia"; the fundamental building blocks of matter</note>: that all salt in **compounds** <note>original: "Mixtorum"</note> is naturally **acid** and sour, and that **alkali** is merely a change brought about by fire.

**§.17.** <note>The numbering skips §.16 in the original text.</note> Otherwise, it also appears as if all experiments agree quite well with this conclusion. However, I do not think so highly of my own opinions that I would not gladly yield to another if it could be shown to me that theirs was better than mine; for I seek nothing other than
->to discover the truth.<-

**§.18. Volatile salt** of wax.

<summary>This page describes the chemical refinement of wax "butter" into spirit and oil, arguing that the resulting "spirit of wax" is an acidic volatile salt rather than an alkali. The author posits a broader theory that all natural salts are inherently acidic, and alkalinity is a byproduct of the distillation fire.</summary>
<keywords>distillation, wax butter, volatile salt, acid salt, alkali, chemical principles, amber, rectification, quicklime</keywords>

# ERRATA.

Even though the French original is the ninth edition, it is not without **printing errors**, as I have well experienced—so much so that the entire sheet "U u" was completely reversed. Therefore, the kind reader will hopefully overlook a few in this first German copy. Specifically, it should be read as:
I. page 19, in the marginal notes: **Mary's bath** <note>original: "baln. Mariæ" or bain-marie.</note> instead of **steam bath** <note>original: "B. vaporum."</note>.
I. page 72. line 14. **Small measure** <note>original: "Mäßlein"</note> or **Rose-measure** <note>original: "Rösel"</note> instead of **Measure**.
I. page 126. line 16. **Air-holes** instead of **Sulfur-holes**.
I. page 225. line 4. after the word **Color**: "so".
I. page 397. line 5. **Antimony** instead of **Mercury**.
II page 38. at the very bottom: **Salt of China-bark** <note>original: "Chinæ de China Saltz"; referring to Cinchona bark, the source of quinine.</note>.
II. page 237. **Purgatives** instead of **Plants** in the last line.
II. page 112 line 18. **Rupture** <note>original: "Bruch"</note> instead of **Custom** <note>original: "Brauch"</note>.
In the Appendix on the 3rd leaf: **Moss from a skull** <note>Usnea, mentioned on the previous page.</note> instead of **burnt skull**. The rest will have very few errors, or at least such errors that anyone can easily correct them.
